questions.text_verbatim: a) Discuss the significance of continuous survey of machinery onboard ships, outlining its key objectives, methodologies, and the impact of advanced technologies on this process. (8) b) Enumerate challenges that could be encountered in such surveys and propose viable solutions to ensure its effectiveness. (8)

subparts.text: Discuss the significance of continuous survey of machinery onboard ships, outlining its key objectives, methodologies, and the impact of advanced technologies on this process.

decomposition: What the continuous survey of machinery actually is - a class survey arrangement, not a statutory instrument - and where it sits against the five-year renewal cycle

The methodology: item groups, due dates and windows, opening-up and testing, Chief Engineer surveys, the approved planned maintenance alternative, crediting and the survey status report

blocks.h: 1. What the continuous survey of machinery is, and where it sits

blocks.p: A cargo ship's machinery must be surveyed by or on behalf of the Administration, and SOLAS chapter I regulation 10 fixes the outer interval: a renewal survey at intervals not exceeding five years, with intermediate and annual surveys inside the cycle. Regulation 6 is the survey and inspection obligation itself and the authority under which a recognized organization acts; regulation 11 requires the condition to be maintained after survey.

Taken literally, that means every surveyable machinery item is opened, examined and tested together, once every five years. Continuous Survey of Machinery (CSM) is the classification arrangement that breaks that block apart. The surveyable items are divided into groups with individual due dates spread across the cycle, so that roughly one fifth of the items fall due each year and every item is still examined within the five years. The interval is not relaxed. Only its distribution changes.

Two points of identity matter and both are commonly got wrong. CSM is a classification arrangement, not a statutory instrument — SOLAS sets the interval, class rules distribute it, and the Administration accepts the arrangement through the recognized organization. And CSM is a survey regime, not a maintenance regime: it says when class must see an item, not when the ship must overhaul it.

ul: The ship keeps trading. A whole-machinery renewal survey concentrates opening-up, dismantling and testing into one window that in practice forces an extended stay. Spreading it converts one long outage into many short ones taken alongside cargo work.
Workload is levelled. The engine department, the superintendent and the spares budget carry a steady annual load instead of a five-yearly spike that no crew complement can absorb.

Survey and maintenance converge. Items are shown to the surveyor when they are already open for planned overhaul. The same dismantling serves both purposes, which is the single largest saving in the scheme.
Condition is known continuously. Class holds a rolling picture of the machinery rather than a five-yearly snapshot, and deterioration is caught between renewals rather than at one.

It is the gateway to the modern alternatives. An approved planned maintenance scheme, and condition-based arrangements built on it, are grafted onto the continuous framework — without CSM there is nothing for them to attach to.

ol: To discharge the machinery renewal survey required within the five-year cycle, item by item, without relaxing the interval.
To maximise ship availability by removing the need for a single extended survey outage.
To distribute survey and maintenance workload evenly across the cycle and across crews.
To align class attendance with planned overhaul, so that one opening-up satisfies both.
To maintain a continuous, auditable record of machinery condition in the class survey status.
To detect deterioration early and allow corrective action before it becomes a defect or a casualty.
To support informed docking and repair planning from a known forward schedule of due items.

blocks.h: 4. Methodology - how the scheme actually runs

rows: Item register and grouping
Every surveyable machinery item is listed and assigned to a group with its own due date, spread so that the whole register is covered within five years
Survey status report
The class record of what is due, what is completed and what is overdue. It is the working document, and it is what a port State control officer, a vetting inspector or a buyer's surveyor asks for
Examination

Opening up and internal examination, dismantling where required, measurement of wear-down and clearances, pressure and hydraulic testing, non-destructive examination where called for, and functional testing of safety and control devices under working conditions
Attendance
A class surveyor attends, examines and credits the item. Crediting is the act that discharges it; work done without crediting has not been surveyed
Chief Engineer's survey

Subject to approval, defined items may be examined and recorded by a suitably qualified Chief Engineer, with the records confirmed by the surveyor at his next attendance. It is a delegation of examination, not of judgement
Approved planned maintenance scheme
Where class approves the ship's PMS, maintenance carried out under it is credited against continuous survey items, subject to periodical audit of the scheme and its records
Postponement
An item may be postponed only with class agreement and within limits set by the society. Postponement is a decision, not a delay
Overdue items
An item passing its due date without credit or postponement becomes overdue and attracts a condition of class or equivalent recommendation with a date by which it must be discharged

blocks.p: The commercial edge is the condition of class. Class status drives the hull and machinery cover, the P&I entry and the charterer's willingness to fix the ship. An overdue continuous survey item is therefore not an engineering irritation; it is a trading exposure, and that is why the survey status report is managed as a live document rather than filed.
Technology has changed how the evidence is produced, not what has to be proved:

ul: Condition monitoring. Vibration analysis, lubricating oil analysis, thermography and thermodynamic performance monitoring give a quantified picture of a machine that has not been opened. Where class approves a condition-based arrangement, that evidence can substitute for scheduled opening-up.

The shift from calendar to condition. The scheme's logic moves from open it because it is due to open it because the data says so. Unnecessary dismantling is itself a source of failure, so this is a genuine reliability gain and not only a cost one.

Remote survey. Streamed video, photographic and documentary evidence assessed ashore, established at scale from 2020 onward and by this sitting a routine route for a defined subset of items. It removes the surveyor's travel from the critical path.
Remote inspection techniques. Drones and crawlers for spaces that would otherwise need staging; borescopes and endoscopes in place of opening up.
Digital survey status. Live, shared status data replacing a periodically issued document, so that ship, office and society see the same forward schedule.

Data and analytics. Continuous machinery data trended against a baseline, with anomaly detection prompting attention before an alarm point is reached; and electronic certificates removing the paper-currency problem entirely.

blocks.p: The limits are worth a mark. None of this changes the interval, and none of it displaces the surveyor's judgement — the technology produces evidence and the society decides what it discharges. Data quality, calibration and a trustworthy baseline are preconditions, not by-products; and remote survey is accepted for a defined subset of items, never as a general substitute for attendance.

blocks.h: (b) Challenges, and the solution to each

ol: Due-date tracking across a five-year rotation. Dozens of items with individual dates, across crew changes and superintendent changes; items are missed on paper long before they are missed in the engine room.
Commercial schedule and access. Short port stays, continuous cargo work and voyage patterns that never coincide with a due item. Machinery that cannot be taken out of service cannot be opened.
Surveyor availability. The ship is where the surveyor is not. Attendance cost, travel and waiting time push owners toward postponement.

Crew competence and continuity. The Chief Engineer's survey depends on an individual approval, and a relief who does not hold it stops that route dead. Short tenures break the continuity the scheme assumes.

Record quality and integrity. Late entries, missing measurements, photographs without context, PMS records completed retrospectively. An audit that finds this withdraws the credit and can withdraw the scheme approval.
Spare parts and lead time. An item opened without the parts to close it becomes an unplanned immobilisation.
Unnecessary opening-up. Dismantling a healthy machine to satisfy a calendar introduces assembly error, contamination and gasket and fastener failures.
Condition-monitoring data quality. Sensor drift, no baseline, alarm flooding, and nobody aboard trained to interpret a spectrum.
Alignment with statutory and docking windows. Continuous items, harmonized statutory surveys and the docking cycle pull in different directions and can produce three separate outages.
Change of class or ownership. Survey status transfers with the ship, and an incomplete or disputed transfer surfaces as a block of overdue items on day one.
Overdue items becoming a condition of class. The consequence of every failure above, and the one with commercial teeth.

rows: Due-date tracking

A live survey-status matrix held by ship and office together, reviewed at a fixed monthly point, with a rolling twelve-month look-ahead and named ownership of each due item. Digital class status data rather than a periodic document
Commercial schedule

Plan due items against the trading pattern, not the calendar - identify the long port stays, ballast legs and lay-up windows a year out and place the heavy items there. Bring the commercial operator into the survey plan
Surveyor availability
Batch items so that one attendance credits several; use remote survey for the items the society accepts remotely; book attendance against the plan rather than against the due date
Crew competence

Obtain and maintain Chief Engineer survey approval as a fleet standard rather than an individual accident; hand over the survey status formally at every relief; train on measurement and recording, not only on maintenance
Record quality
Record at the machine and at the time - measurements, photographs with identification, the actual clearances against limits. Internal audit the records before the society does
Spares
A critical-spares policy driven by the due-item look-ahead; confirm parts on board before opening up; hold the wear parts for the next twelve months of due items
Unnecessary opening-up
Move to an approved planned maintenance scheme, and where the machinery and the data support it to a condition-based arrangement, so that opening-up follows evidence
Data quality

Establish a baseline when the machine is known good; calibrate and verify sensors; set alarm limits that mean something; train one competent analyst per ship and support the ship from a shore analysis capability
Window alignment
Build one integrated plan carrying continuous items, harmonized statutory surveys and the docking cycle together, and align the anniversary dates so the three windows overlap rather than compete
Change of class or ownership
Obtain and reconcile the full survey status before transfer; treat unreconciled items as outstanding until the new society credits them
Conditions of class
Treat any condition of class as a bridge-and-office level item with a named owner and a date, and close it early rather than at its limit

blocks.p: The single point that ties limb (b) together: almost every challenge above is a planning and information failure rather than an engineering one. The machinery is rarely the obstacle; the obstacle is that nobody knew the item was due until the window had passed. The solutions therefore cluster on visibility, on look-ahead and on approved schemes that let evidence already being generated aboard do the survey's work.

Limb (a) prints eight marks against four tasks — significance, objectives, methodologies, and the impact of advanced technologies. That is the tightest ratio on the paper and it dictates the shape: four visibly separate blocks, each short. A candidate who writes eight flowing paragraphs on how useful CSM is has answered one of the four tasks and will be marked on one.

The objectives go in a numbered list and the methodology in a table for the same reason: an examiner scanning for four discrete deliverables must be able to find each one without reading for it. The technology section closes on its limits, because a section that only enthuses reads as a brochure and the mark is for judgement.

Limb (b) prints the verb “enumerate”, which is an instruction about form. Enumerate the challenges — numbered, one line each — then pair each with its solution. Pairing them in a two-column table is what makes the second half of the limb legible; a candidate who lists eleven challenges and then eight unlabelled solutions forces the examiner to do the matching.

blocks.h: The distinction the whole question turns on

blocks.p: CSM does not extend the interval. It distributes it.

SOLAS chapter I regulation 10 fixes a machinery renewal survey at intervals not exceeding five years. The continuous arrangement changes nothing about that. It divides the surveyable items into groups with individual due dates so that about a fifth fall due each year and every item is still examined inside the five years. A candidate who writes that CSM lets a ship go longer between surveys has said the opposite of what the scheme does.

The second distinction: CSM is a class arrangement, not a statutory one. SOLAS sets the interval; class rules distribute it; the Administration accepts it through the recognized organization. And the third: a survey regime is not a maintenance regime. CSM says when class must see the item. The planned maintenance system says when the ship overhauls it. They are connected — an approved PMS lets the maintenance credit the survey — but they are not the same thing, and Q6 on this paper is about the other one.

rows: Continuous survey of machinery
When must class see this item?
Classification society, under the SOLAS interval
Planned maintenance system
When must we overhaul it?
The company, under the ISM Code
Condition monitoring
What state is it actually in?
The ship, feeding both of the above

blocks.p: An approved PMS is the bridge: it lets the middle column discharge the left one. A condition-based arrangement lets the right column discharge the middle one. Explaining that chain in one sentence is worth more than another paragraph on benefits.

ul: Saying CSM extends the survey interval. It does not; it distributes the same five years.
Treating CSM as a statutory requirement. It is a classification arrangement accepted in discharge of the statutory survey.
Confusing CSM with the planned maintenance system, or using the two terms interchangeably.
Answering “significance” and stopping — leaving objectives, methodology and technology unwritten when the limb names all four.
Writing about hull surveys, the enhanced survey programme or docking. The question says machinery.
Omitting crediting. Work done and not credited has not been surveyed.
Omitting the condition of class, which is the commercial consequence of the whole scheme.
Listing technologies with no statement of their limits, so the answer reads as sales material.
In limb (b), giving challenges without solutions, or solutions that do not match the challenges listed.
Proposing “better planning” as a solution. Say what plan, held by whom, reviewed when.
“Does continuous survey let you go more than five years?” No. The interval is unchanged; only the distribution changes.
“Who approves the arrangement?” The classification society, acting for the Administration as recognized organization.
“Roughly what proportion falls due each year?” About a fifth, which is what a five-year cycle divided into annual tranches means.
“Can the Chief Engineer survey items himself?” Only defined items, only with approval, and the surveyor confirms the records. The examination is delegated; the judgement is not.
“What happens if an item goes overdue?” A condition of class or equivalent recommendation with a date for discharge, and class itself is at risk if it is not met.
“Your PMS is approved. Do you still need class attendance?” Yes — the scheme is audited periodically and the surveyor still confirms and credits.
“What is the difference between crediting and doing the work?” Crediting is the class act that discharges the item. Uncredited work leaves the item open.
“Can a survey be done remotely?” For a defined subset of items that the society accepts remotely — not as a general substitute for attendance.
“What is the risk of opening a healthy machine?” Assembly error, contamination, gasket and fastener failure. Unnecessary dismantling causes defects, which is the argument for condition-based work.
Which SOLAS regulation sets the cargo ship machinery survey interval? Chapter I regulation 10 - not exceeding five years.
Which regulation requires the condition to be maintained after survey? Chapter I regulation 11.
Name three things a surveyor does at a continuous survey item. Opens and examines it, measures wear-down and clearances, and tests it under working conditions.
What document tells you what is due? The class survey status report.
What is a condition of class? A recorded requirement that specified work be completed by a stated date for class to be retained.
What must you have before you open the item? The spares to close it, and the item's due date confirmed.
Name three condition monitoring techniques. Vibration analysis, lubricating oil analysis and thermographic or performance monitoring.
Why is unnecessary opening-up a hazard? Because reassembly is where defects are introduced.
What happens to survey status if the ship changes class? It transfers with the ship and must be reconciled and credited by the new society.

blocks.p: For limb (a), four blocks in the order the limb names them: SIGNIFICANCE, OBJECTIVES, METHOD, TECHNOLOGY. Write the headings first, then fill them.
For the method, five words in the order a real item moves: LIST, DUE, OPEN, TEST, CREDIT — and one consequence word if it does not happen: OVERDUE.
For the technology, MONITOR, REMOTE, DATA, then one word of caution: LIMITS.

For limb (b), group the challenges under four heads and the solutions fall out by themselves: TIME (schedule, access, surveyor), PEOPLE (competence, continuity, records), PARTS (spares, unnecessary opening-up), PAPER (tracking, transfer, conditions of class).

ul: SOLAS chapter I regulation 6 — survey and inspection; the authority under which a recognized organization acts. Regulation 10 — surveys of hull, machinery and equipment of cargo ships; renewal at intervals not exceeding five years, with intermediate and annual surveys. Regulation 11 — maintenance of condition after survey.

A.1156(32) — Survey Guidelines under the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification, 2021. These are the operative guidelines at this sitting. The 33rd Assembly successor was adopted 6 December 2023, one month after the examination, and does not belong in this answer.

ISM Code as amended through MSC.353(92) (in force 1 January 2015) — section 10, maintenance of the ship and equipment, which generates the maintenance evidence an approved planned maintenance scheme relies on.

Classification society rules and the industry's unified requirements — these, and not SOLAS, are what actually constitute the continuous survey arrangement, the Chief Engineer's survey and the approved planned maintenance scheme. No rule or unified requirement is cited by number in this answer; see the uncertainty section.
India at this sitting: the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and the rules made under it.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of the evidence

blocks.p: The statutory frame is primary; the scheme itself is not, and the split is declared rather than hidden.

The SOLAS chapter I survey obligations and the operative Assembly survey guidelines are cited at identity level from instruments whose identity and amendment status are recorded in the True Source corpus. The continuous survey arrangement is a classification instrument, and the corpus holds no classification layer — its class directory returns nothing for continuous survey of machinery, and its reference resolver holds 320 entries of which every one is MARPOL Annex VI. The scheme is therefore described at authoritative-secondary level.

The consequences are deliberate. No unified requirement number is attributed and no class rule is quoted. No numerical value is given for a permitted postponement, a crediting window, or the limit up to which a Chief Engineer may survey — those differ between societies and no held source records them. The five-year cycle and the approximate annual fifth are stated, because they follow from the statutory interval itself, which is primary.

The condition-based and remote survey arrangements are described generically: no society, notation or acceptance criterion is named. The technology section is engineering judgement and industry practice, attributed as such.

Currency. The one live temporal edge is the survey guidelines. A.1156(32) governs at this sitting; its 33rd Assembly successor was adopted 6 December 2023, one month after the examination, and every later paper in the corpus correctly cites the successor. That is exactly the reversal a later editor would import, and it is the reason this section exists.

notes: NOVEMBER 2023 IS BOUNDARY-FREE AT DAY LEVEL. MEPC 80 adopted the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy on 7 July 2023, four months before this sitting; the 33rd Assembly adopted its resolutions on 6 December 2023, one month after it. Neither falls inside the sitting month, so no day-level reasoning is required for this question and none is used.

THE ONE LIVE REVERSAL IS THE SURVEY GUIDELINES. A.1156(32), the Survey Guidelines under the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification, 2021, is the operative Assembly instrument at this sitting. Its 33rd Assembly successor was adopted 6 December 2023 and is FUTURE by one month. It is not cited anywhere in this answer. Every later paper in the corpus correctly cites the successor, which is precisely why this is recorded.

SOLAS CHAPTER I IS STABLE ACROSS THIS WINDOW. Regulations 6, 10 and 11 - survey and inspection, cargo ship machinery survey at intervals not exceeding five years, and maintenance of condition after survey - are unamended in any respect touching this question. The SOLAS Consolidated Edition 2024 took effect 1 July 2024 and is eight months future; nothing in this answer depends on it.

THE ISM CODE POSITION AT THIS SITTING IS THE MSC.353(92) TEXT, IN FORCE 1 JANUARY 2015, which is the latest Code amendment recorded in the corpus amendment register. A.1188(33), the 2023 Guidelines on implementation of the ISM Code by Administrations, was adopted 6 December 2023 and is future by one month; it is not cited. questions.understand_first: Start from the problem the scheme solves. A ship's machinery has to be shown to the classification surveyor on a fixed cycle, and if every item is shown at once the ship stops for a long time to let it happen. So the items are split into groups with staggered dates, and the surveyor sees roughly a fifth of them each year. Nothing about the deadline changes — every item is still examined inside the same cycle — but the work is spread, and each item can be shown at the moment the engineers were going to open it anyway. That is the whole idea: the same interval, distributed. Two things follow. First, this is an arrangement the classification society operates on behalf of the flag, not a rule the ship reads out of a convention — the convention only fixes the outer deadline. Second, it is about when class must look, not about when the ship must overhaul, which is a different system run by the company. They meet at one point: if the society approves the ship's own maintenance scheme, the maintenance the crew is already doing can count as the examination. And the sting in the tail is what happens when an item slips past its date: it becomes an outstanding requirement recorded against the ship, with a deadline of its own, and the ship's standing with insurers and charterers follows that record.

steps.title: What the continuous survey of machinery is, and where it sits
points: SOLAS chapter I regulation 10 requires a cargo ship machinery renewal survey at intervals NOT EXCEEDING FIVE YEARS, with intermediate and annual surveys inside the cycle
regulation 6 is the survey and inspection obligation and the authority under which a recognized organization acts; regulation 11 requires the condition to be maintained after survey
taken literally that means every surveyable item is opened, examined and tested together once every five years
continuous survey of machinery divides the surveyable items into groups with individual due dates spread across the cycle
roughly a fifth of the items fall due each year and every item is still examined WITHIN the five years
THE INTERVAL IS NOT RELAXED - only its distribution changes
it is a CLASSIFICATION arrangement, not a statutory instrument: SOLAS sets the interval, class rules distribute it, the Administration accepts it through the recognized organization
it is a SURVEY regime, not a MAINTENANCE regime - it says when class must see the item, not when the ship must overhaul it

steps.title: Why it matters - the significance
points: the ship keeps trading - one long outage becomes many short ones taken alongside cargo work
workload is levelled across the cycle instead of spiking every five years beyond what any crew complement can absorb
survey and maintenance converge - the item is shown to the surveyor when it is already open for planned overhaul, and one dismantling serves both
condition is known continuously - class holds a rolling picture rather than a five-yearly snapshot
it is the framework onto which an approved planned maintenance scheme and condition-based arrangements are grafted

steps.title: Objectives
points: to discharge the machinery renewal survey within the five-year cycle item by item, without relaxing the interval
to maximise ship availability by removing the single extended survey outage
to distribute survey and maintenance workload evenly across the cycle and across crews
to align class attendance with planned overhaul so that one opening-up satisfies both
to maintain a continuous auditable record of machinery condition in the class survey status
to detect deterioration early, before it becomes a defect or a casualty
to support informed docking and repair planning from a known forward schedule

steps.title: Methodology - how the scheme actually runs
points: an item register, every surveyable machinery item assigned to a group with its own due date
the survey status report - the class record of what is due, completed and overdue, and the document PSC, vetting and buyers ask for

examination: opening up and internal examination, dismantling where required, wear-down and clearance measurement, pressure and hydraulic testing, NDE where called for, and functional testing of safety and control devices under working conditions
attendance and CREDITING by the surveyor - crediting is the act that discharges the item, and uncredited work has not been surveyed
the Chief Engineer's survey - defined items examined and recorded by an approved Chief Engineer, confirmed by the surveyor; examination is delegated, judgement is not
the approved planned maintenance scheme - maintenance credited against continuous survey items, subject to periodical audit
postponement only with class agreement and within society limits
an overdue item attracts a CONDITION OF CLASS or equivalent recommendation with a date for discharge
the commercial edge - hull and machinery cover, the P&I entry and the charterer's willingness to fix all follow class status

steps.title: The impact of advanced technologies
points: technology has changed how the evidence is produced, not what has to be proved
condition monitoring - vibration analysis, lubricating oil analysis, thermography, thermodynamic performance monitoring - quantifies a machine that has not been opened
where class approves a condition-based arrangement, that evidence can substitute for scheduled opening-up
the logic moves from OPEN IT BECAUSE IT IS DUE to OPEN IT BECAUSE THE DATA SAYS SO, and unnecessary dismantling is itself a source of failure
remote survey - streamed video, photographic and documentary evidence assessed ashore, established at scale from 2020 and routine for defined items by this sitting
remote inspection techniques - drones and crawlers in place of staging, borescopes in place of opening up
digital survey status - live shared data replacing a periodically issued document
data and analytics - continuous trending against a baseline with anomaly detection; electronic certificates removing the paper-currency problem
THE LIMITS - none of this changes the interval, none displaces the surveyor's judgement, data quality and baseline are preconditions, and remote survey covers a defined subset only

steps.title: Enumerated challenges
points: due-date tracking across a five-year rotation, through crew and superintendent changes
commercial schedule and access - short port stays and machinery that cannot be taken out of service
surveyor availability, attendance cost and travel pushing owners toward postponement
crew competence and continuity - the Chief Engineer's survey depends on an individual approval
record quality and integrity - late entries, missing measurements, retrospectively completed PMS records
spare parts and lead time - an item opened without parts becomes an unplanned immobilisation
unnecessary opening-up introducing assembly error, contamination and fastener failure
condition-monitoring data quality - sensor drift, no baseline, alarm flooding, nobody trained to interpret
alignment of continuous items with harmonized statutory surveys and the docking cycle
change of class or ownership, and an unreconciled survey status transferring with the ship
overdue items becoming a condition of class - the consequence with commercial teeth

steps.title: Matched solutions
points: a live survey-status matrix held by ship and office, reviewed monthly, with a rolling twelve-month look-ahead and named ownership of each item
plan due items against the TRADING PATTERN and place heavy items in the long stays, ballast legs and lay-up windows identified a year out
batch items so one attendance credits several, and use remote survey where the society accepts it
obtain and maintain Chief Engineer survey approval as a fleet standard; hand over survey status formally at every relief
record at the machine and at the time, with measurements against limits and identified photographs; internal audit before the society does
a critical-spares policy driven by the due-item look-ahead, with parts confirmed on board before opening up
move to an approved planned maintenance scheme, and where data supports it to a condition-based arrangement, so that opening-up follows evidence
establish a baseline when the machine is known good, calibrate sensors, set meaningful limits, and support the ship from a shore analysis capability
one integrated plan carrying continuous items, harmonized statutory surveys and docking together, with anniversary dates aligned so the windows overlap
reconcile the full survey status BEFORE a change of class or ownership and treat unreconciled items as outstanding
treat any condition of class as a named-owner item with a date and close it early rather than at its limit
THE COMMON ROOT - almost every challenge is a planning and information failure, not an engineering one

quick_revision.recall_15s: Continuous Survey of Machinery distributes the five-year interval; it does not extend it. SOLAS I/10 requires a cargo ship machinery renewal survey at intervals not exceeding five years; I/6 is the survey obligation; I/11 requires the condition to be maintained after survey. CSM is a classification arrangement, not a statutory one, and a survey regime, not a maintenance one. Items are grouped with individual due dates so about a fifth fall due each year and all are examined inside the cycle. Method: list, due, open, test, credit — and crediting by the surveyor is what discharges the item. Chief Engineer's survey for defined items with approval, confirmed by the surveyor. Approved PMS credits maintenance against survey items, subject to audit. An item passing its date becomes overdue and attracts a condition of class with a discharge date — and insurance, P&I and charter all follow class. Technology: condition monitoring, condition-based arrangements, remote survey, drones and borescopes, digital status, analytics — but the interval is unchanged, the surveyor still judges, and remote covers a defined subset only. Challenges cluster as TIME, PEOPLE, PARTS, PAPER, and the solutions are visibility, look-ahead and approved schemes. Operative survey guidelines at this sitting: A.1156(32), not the 33rd Assembly successor adopted one month later.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: SOLAS chapter I regulation 10 is the provision the whole scheme is built on: it requires the hull, machinery and equipment of a cargo ship to be surveyed on renewal at intervals not exceeding five years, with intermediate and annual surveys inside the cycle. Continuous Survey of Machinery does not touch that interval — it distributes it across the cycle item by item under classification society rules, accepted by the Administration through the recognized organization acting under regulation 6, with regulation 11 requiring the condition to be maintained after survey.
quick_revision.major_trap: Writing that continuous survey extends the interval between surveys. It does the opposite of relaxing anything: the five-year deadline in SOLAS chapter I regulation 10 is untouched and every item is still examined inside it — what changes is that the items are staggered rather than shown together. The paired traps are treating CSM as a statutory requirement when it is a classification arrangement accepted in discharge of the statutory survey, and confusing it with the planned maintenance system, which is the company's ISM-driven overhaul regime and the subject of Q6 on this same paper.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is continuous survey of machinery, in one sentence?
retrieval_cards.answer: A classification-society arrangement under which the machinery items that would otherwise be examined together at the five-yearly renewal survey are divided into groups with individual due dates spread across the cycle, so that about a fifth fall due each year and every item is still examined within the same five years.
retrieval_cards.why: The definition contains the distinction the question turns on - distribution, not extension.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does continuous survey allow a ship to go longer than five years between machinery surveys?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. SOLAS chapter I regulation 10 fixes the renewal interval at not exceeding five years and continuous survey does not touch it. Every item is still examined inside the five years; only the distribution of the examinations changes.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the commonest single error on this question and it inverts the whole scheme.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish continuous survey of machinery from the planned maintenance system.
retrieval_cards.answer: Continuous survey is a classification survey regime and answers when class must SEE the item. The planned maintenance system is the company's regime under the ISM Code and answers when the ship must OVERHAUL it. They meet where class approves the PMS, because approved maintenance can then be credited against continuous survey items, subject to periodical audit.
retrieval_cards.why: The two are routinely used interchangeably, and this paper sets both - Q1 and Q6.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Trace the life of one continuous survey item from register to discharge.
retrieval_cards.answer: Listed in the item register with a group and a due date; planned against the trading pattern with spares confirmed; opened and internally examined, clearances and wear-down measured, pressure tested where required and functionally tested under working conditions; then CREDITED by the surveyor, which is the act that discharges it. If the date passes without credit or agreed postponement the item goes overdue and attracts a condition of class with a discharge date.
retrieval_cards.why: List, due, open, test, credit - and the consequence if it does not happen.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which SOLAS regulations frame this, and what does each do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Chapter I regulation 6 - survey and inspection, and the authority under which a recognized organization acts. Regulation 10 - surveys of the hull, machinery and equipment of cargo ships, with renewal at intervals not exceeding five years and intermediate and annual surveys inside the cycle. Regulation 11 - maintenance of the condition after survey.
retrieval_cards.why: The statutory frame is the only primary material in the answer, and it must be attributed correctly.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The engineers overhauled and closed up a continuous survey item last month. Is the item discharged?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not unless it was credited. Crediting by the attending surveyor - or confirmation of an approved Chief Engineer's record, or credit under an approved planned maintenance scheme - is what discharges the item. Work carried out without crediting leaves the item open and it will still go overdue on its due date.
retrieval_cards.why: The distinction between doing the work and discharging the survey is a standard oral question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What has advanced technology changed about continuous survey, and what has it not changed?
retrieval_cards.answer: Changed: how the evidence is produced. Condition monitoring quantifies a machine that has not been opened; condition-based arrangements let that evidence substitute for scheduled opening-up; remote survey allows defined items to be assessed ashore from streamed and documentary evidence; drones, crawlers and borescopes replace staging and dismantling; digital status data and analytics replace a periodic report. Not changed: the interval, the surveyor's judgement, and the need for calibrated data against a trustworthy baseline. Remote survey covers a defined subset of items, never attendance generally.
retrieval_cards.why: The mark in this part of limb (a) is for balance - naming the limits, not only the tools.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What proportion of continuous survey items falls due each year, and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: About one fifth. It follows directly from the arithmetic of the scheme: the whole register must be covered within the five-year cycle set by SOLAS chapter I regulation 10, so dividing it into annual tranches puts roughly a fifth in each year.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the only safe number in the answer, because it follows from the statutory interval rather than from any society's rule.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a condition of class, and why does it matter commercially?
retrieval_cards.answer: A recorded requirement that specified work be completed by a stated date for class to be retained - the consequence of an item going past its due date without credit or agreed postponement. It matters because hull and machinery cover, the P&I entry and a charterer's willingness to fix the ship all follow class status, so an overdue survey item is a trading exposure and not just an engineering one.
retrieval_cards.why: It is where the whole scheme acquires commercial teeth, and it is what limb (b) is ultimately about.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Group the challenges of running a continuous survey scheme under four heads, with a solution for each head.
retrieval_cards.answer: TIME - schedule, access, surveyor availability: plan against the trading pattern a year out, batch items into one attendance, use remote survey where accepted. PEOPLE - competence, continuity, records: fleet-standard Chief Engineer approval, formal handover of survey status, recording at the machine. PARTS - spares lead time and unnecessary opening-up: spares driven by the due-item look-ahead, and an approved PMS so opening-up follows evidence. PAPER - tracking, class transfer, conditions of class: one live shared status matrix, reconciliation before transfer, conditions closed early.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (b) is eight marks and 'enumerate' asks for countable items; four heads make eleven challenges recallable under pressure.

questions.verification_status: ENGINEERING, NOT REGULATORY, AND THE PROVENANCE IS DECLARED ACCORDINGLY. The physics is P1 in the sense that matters for an engineering answer: mean piston speed is defined by the geometry of the crank mechanism as twice the stroke times the rotational speed, and the identity that power equals the product of mean effective pressure, piston area, mean piston speed and cylinder number follows from the definition of mean effective pressure itself. Both are derived in the answer rather than asserted. The propeller cube law is stated as the approximation it is, with its assumptions named. THE NUMERICAL RANGES ARE THE WEAK POINT AND ARE MARKED AS SUCH. Typical mean piston speeds for low-speed two-stroke, medium-speed four-stroke and high-speed engines are given as orders of magnitude drawn from general engineering practice; NO MAKER, ENGINE TYPE, POWER, RPM OR SFOC VALUE IS PRESENTED AS SOURCED, because the True Source corpus holds no engine-maker documentation and none was consulted. The position of the SFOC minimum is described as a region rather than a point for the same reason. The regulatory frame of limb c) - SEEMP Part III mandatory from 1 January 2023, the 2022 SEEMP guidelines MEPC.346(78) operative at this sitting, and 2023 as the first CII data year still running - is P1 by identity and status from the corpus amendment register, with the register's own supersession marking correctly reversed for this sitting.
sources: PRIMARY (derivation): mean piston speed is defined by the crank geometry. In one revolution the piston travels twice the stroke, so mean piston speed = 2 x stroke x rotational speed. Stated in metres per second with rotational speed in revolutions per second, or 2LN/60 with N in revolutions per minute.

PRIMARY (derivation): from the definition of mean effective pressure, indicated power = mean effective pressure x swept volume x cycles per second x number of cylinders. Substituting swept volume as piston area x stroke and grouping the stroke with the speed yields power proportional to mean effective pressure x piston area x mean piston speed x number of cylinders. Power is therefore the product of a PRESSURE term and a SPEED term, and mean piston speed is that speed term.

PRIMARY (identity and status): MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 - the SEEMP, with Part III mandatory from 1 January 2023 for ships to which the CII applies. Annex VI identity and the 1 November 2022 entry into force of MEPC.328(76) taken from the corpus record and TSCR-3.

PRIMARY (identity and status): MEPC.346(78), the 2022 SEEMP Guidelines, are the OPERATIVE guidelines at this sitting. The corpus amendment register marks them superseded by MEPC.395(82); that supersession is a 2024 event and is future here. The register is present-tense and its direction is reversed for this sitting.

PRIMARY (identity and status): the CII rating regime applies from 1 January 2023, so 2023 is the FIRST CII data year and it is still running at this November sitting. No ship has yet been issued a rating.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: the propeller law for a fixed-pitch propeller in unchanged hull and weather conditions - delivered power varies approximately as the cube of shaft speed and torque as the square. It is an approximation whose assumptions are stated in the answer.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: specific fuel oil consumption varies with engine load and passes through a minimum in the upper-middle part of the load range for a conventionally tuned engine, rising at both very high and low loads. The rise at low load is attributable to reduced compression and scavenge pressure, turbocharger mismatch and poorer atomisation.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: mechanical friction losses in the running gear increase with mean piston speed, so mechanical efficiency falls as mean piston speed rises; wear rate and cylinder oil demand rise with it too.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: the time available for injection, ignition delay and complete combustion in each cycle is inversely proportional to rotational speed, and therefore inversely proportional to mean piston speed at fixed stroke.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: typical mean piston speeds are of the order of 8 to 8.5 metres per second for large low-speed two-stroke engines at their rated output, 9 to 11 for medium-speed four-stroke engines and higher again for high-speed engines. These are orders of magnitude from general engineering practice, not maker data.

P3 INDUSTRY GUIDANCE: shipboard engine performance measurement practice - steady-state test points, correction to reference ambient conditions, indicator and electronic pressure measurement, flowmeter and sounding reconciliation, and hull and propeller performance monitoring.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT: the ordering of the limb c) methodology so that instrumentation and fuel measurement are proved before any engine conclusion is drawn, and the placing of hull, propeller and engine condition ahead of the choice of operating point.

INTERNAL REUSE VERIFIED: QP2503-Q8 and QP2307-Q7 for hull roughness management and condition-based propeller maintenance; QP2306-Q9 for the resistance vocabulary. Read for consistency; no prose taken.

blocks.h: (a) Mean piston speed and its significance for fuel consumption

blocks.p: Mean piston speed is the average speed of the piston over a complete revolution. In one revolution the piston travels twice the stroke — once down, once up — so:

rows: With speed in rev/s
cm = 2 × L × N
L in metres, N in rev/s, cm in m/s
With speed in rev/min
cm = 2LN / 60
N in rev/min

blocks.p: It is an average, not a maximum: the piston is momentarily stationary at each dead centre and reaches roughly half as much again as the mean near mid-stroke. As orders of magnitude, a large low-speed two-stroke runs about 8 to 8.5 m/s at its rated output, a medium-speed four-stroke about 9 to 11 m/s, and high-speed engines higher again.

Why engineers use it instead of rpm. Revolutions per minute compare nothing: 100 rpm on a three-metre stroke and 100 rpm on a one-metre stroke are entirely different duties. Mean piston speed puts every engine on one scale, because it measures what actually wears, heats and limits the machine — how fast the rubbing surfaces move and how little time each process has. It is the honest measure of how hard an engine is working mechanically.

The power identity. From the definition of mean effective pressure, indicated power is mean effective pressure × swept volume × cycles per second × number of cylinders. Writing swept volume as piston area × stroke, and grouping the stroke with the speed, gives:
Power ∝ pm × A × cm × i

So for a given engine, power is the product of a pressure term and a speed term. The pressure term is how much is burnt per stroke; the speed term is mean piston speed. Fuel burnt per hour is power × specific fuel oil consumption, so mean piston speed sits directly inside the consumption equation.

The cube law amplifies it. For a fixed-pitch propeller in unchanged hull and weather conditions, delivered power varies approximately as the cube of shaft speed. Since mean piston speed is proportional to shaft speed on a directly coupled engine:

ul: Power ∝ cm3, so fuel per hour falls very steeply as mean piston speed is reduced. A 10% reduction in mean piston speed removes roughly 27% of the power.
But the ship also goes slower, so the voyage takes longer. Consumption per mile falls roughly as the square, not the cube — still a large saving, and it is the figure that matters commercially.
That single distinction — per hour against per mile — is what makes slow steaming worth doing and is the most valuable sentence available in limb (a).

blocks.p: But lower is not always better, and this is the discriminating point. Specific fuel oil consumption is not constant. It passes through a minimum in the upper-middle part of the load range and rises at both ends:

ul: At high mean piston speed — mechanical friction losses rise with piston speed, so mechanical efficiency falls; thermal loading, wear rate and cylinder oil demand all rise; and combustion has less time to complete.

At low mean piston speed — compression pressure and temperature fall, the turbocharger is off its matched point so scavenge air pressure and air-fuel ratio fall, injection pressure and atomisation degrade, and the engine burns dirtier for every kilowatt it makes.

blocks.p: The consequence for the ship: there is an optimum band of mean piston speed, not a monotonic rule. Below it, the cube-law saving is being eaten by a rising specific consumption and by fouling, deposits and maintenance cost. Finding that band is exactly what limb (c) asks for.

blocks.h: (b) Relation to rpm and to ideal combustion

ul: For a given engine the stroke is fixed, so mean piston speed is directly proportional to rpm. Doubling rpm doubles mean piston speed exactly.
Across engines the relation breaks. Two engines at the same rpm have quite different mean piston speeds if their strokes differ — which is why rpm alone tells you nothing about duty.

This is the whole point of the long-stroke engine. Lengthening the stroke lets an engine reach its design mean piston speed — the mechanical duty it was built for — at lower rpm. Lower rpm permits a larger, slower-turning propeller of higher open-water efficiency, which is why modern low-speed engines are long-stroke and turn slowly.
Stroke-to-bore ratio is the design lever. A higher ratio buys propeller efficiency and combustion time at the cost of engine height and mass.

On a controllable-pitch installation the proportionality survives but the propeller law does not: shaft speed may be held constant while pitch varies, so mean piston speed stays fixed while power changes. The load, not the piston speed, then moves along the SFOC curve.

blocks.h: 4. Mean piston speed and ideal combustion

blocks.p: Ideal combustion needs four things together: enough air, well atomised fuel, adequate turbulence, and enough time. Mean piston speed sets the fourth directly and disturbs the other three indirectly.

rows: Time per cycle
Short. Injection, ignition delay and burn-out must all fit into fewer milliseconds
Long. Ample time, so time is not the constraint
Combustion quality
Afterburning - combustion continues into expansion, so heat is released too late to do useful work
Poor atomisation and low compression temperature give slow, incomplete burning
Air supply
Turbocharger well matched; air is normally adequate
Turbocharger off its matched point; scavenge pressure and air-fuel ratio fall; auxiliary blowers cut in
Symptoms
High exhaust temperatures, thermal overload, high wear and cylinder oil consumption
Fouled gas ways, sooty exhaust, deposits on rings, liner and turbine; risk of scavenge fire
Efficiency
Falls - mechanical friction and late heat release
Falls - incomplete combustion and unfavourable pressure development

blocks.p: The unifying statement. The maker matches injection timing and rate, nozzle geometry, compression ratio, turbocharger and scavenge arrangement to a design mean piston speed. Combustion is closest to ideal at that design point, and degrades in either direction away from it. That is why an engine run persistently far below its design point needs re-matching — turbocharger cut-out, variable turbine geometry, tuning kits, or de-rating — rather than merely being throttled back and left.

It is worth adding that combustion time is not the only casualty of high piston speed: the gas exchange itself is time-limited, so scavenging becomes less complete, residual gas rises and the following cycle starts with less fresh air.

blocks.h: (c) Methodology on an old ship - ascertaining optimum fuel use against desired mean piston speed
5. Establish the baseline, then prove the measurements

blocks.p: On an old ship the data is more suspect than the engine. Nothing below is worth doing until the instruments are trusted, and that is the order the answer is written in.

ol: Collect the design baseline. Shop trial and sea trial records, the maker's SFOC curve, rated power and speed, and the stroke. Calculate the design mean piston speed at rated output and at the service rating, so there is a target to compare against.

Collect the ship's history. Running hours, overhaul records, previous performance reports, docking and propeller polishing dates, and the last hull cleaning. An old ship's consumption has drifted for reasons that are recorded somewhere.

Calibrate and prove the instruments. Tachometer, torsionmeter if fitted, fuel flowmeters, temperature and pressure sensors, scavenge and exhaust instrumentation, and the indicator or electronic pressure-measurement equipment. Cross-check flowmeter against tank soundings.

Fix the fuel measurement in mass, not volume. Density at 15 °C from the bunker analysis, temperature correction applied, and the daily figure reported as tonnes of a known net calorific quality — otherwise every later comparison is contaminated by fuel quality and temperature.

blocks.h: 6. Run a structured performance test and reduce the data

ol: Choose steady test points. A series of shaft speeds spanning the intended range, each held genuinely steady in stable weather, at constant draught and trim, on the same fuel, with no auto-pilot hunting and no cargo work.

Record a full set at each point. Shaft speed and power, fuel rate, scavenge air pressure and temperature, exhaust temperatures before and after turbine, turbocharger speed, compression and maximum pressures per cylinder, ambient air and seawater temperature, draught, trim, wind and sea state.
Correct to reference ambient conditions before comparing anything to shop trial data. An uncorrected comparison against a test-bed figure is meaningless.
Reduce each point to the two numbers that matter. Compute cm = 2LN for each test point, and compute specific fuel oil consumption in g/kWh and fuel per nautical mile.

Plot them. SFOC against mean piston speed, and fuel per mile against mean piston speed. The optimum is read off the second curve, not the first — the ship is paid to move cargo, not to make kilowatts.

blocks.h: 7. Separate the engine from the hull, the propeller and the fuel

blocks.p: This is where an old ship differs from a new one, and where most answers stop too early. A high consumption at a given mean piston speed may have nothing to do with the engine:

ul: Hull and propeller. Fouling and propeller roughness shift the whole power-speed relation, so the engine must turn faster for the same ship speed. Establish hull and propeller condition — performance trend, inspection, polishing and cleaning history — before concluding the engine is inefficient.

Engine condition. Worn liners and rings, leaking exhaust valves, drifted fuel pump timing, worn or fouled injectors, a fouled turbocharger or air cooler, and fouled scavenge and gas ways. Overhaul and clean, then re-test; otherwise the optimum found is the optimum of a dirty engine.
Fuel quality. Calorific value, viscosity at injection temperature, and catalytic fines all move consumption independently of piston speed. This is where the fuel oil analysis report feeds in.
Loading condition. Draught and trim change resistance materially. Compare like with like or correct for it.

blocks.h: 8. Bound the answer by the real constraints

ul: Barred speed range from torsional vibration — a whole band of shaft speed, and therefore of mean piston speed, that may not be run continuously.
Minimum load at which the turbocharger sustains itself and the auxiliary blowers cut out; and the maker's stated minimum continuous load and low-load running instructions.
Cylinder lubrication — the feed rate and cylinder oil base number must be matched to the load and the fuel actually being burnt, or a low-load optimum is bought at the price of liner condition.
Manoeuvring, weather and schedule margin — a ship at its economic optimum must still be able to accelerate, keep steerage and make the berth.
Commercial obligations — charterparty speed and consumption warranties, laycan and schedule integrity. The optimum the engine wants may not be the optimum the charter permits.

Regulatory — the ship's SEEMP, with Part III mandatory since 1 January 2023, is where the chosen operating envelope is recorded and monitored. 2023 is the first CII data year and it is still running at this sitting, so this year's operating decisions are being logged into a rating that has not yet been issued to anybody.

blocks.h: 9. Decide, implement, and keep it under review

ol: Choose an operating band, not a single figure — the mean piston speed range that minimises fuel per mile subject to every constraint above.
Convert it into an order the bridge can follow: a shaft speed instruction, with the barred range excluded and the low-load limit stated.
Record it in the SEEMP and brief the engineers and the master on why it is what it is.
Monitor and trend continuously — a monthly performance report against the curves, so drift shows up as drift rather than as a surprise.
Re-establish the baseline after any step change — hull cleaning, propeller polish, docking, major overhaul or a change of fuel.

Escalate to hardware only if the mismatch is structural. If the ship genuinely now runs far below the engine's design mean piston speed, the answer is re-matching — turbocharger cut-out, variable turbine area, tuning kits, propeller re-pitch or de-rating — and that is a technical and commercial project, not a bridge order.

blocks.p: The closing judgement. The question asks for optimum use of fuel oil against a desired mean piston speed, and the honest answer is that the optimum is a negotiated band rather than a calculated point: the engine wants its design duty, the propeller law wants low revolutions, the charter wants the schedule and the liner wants a stable thermal load. A Chief Engineer joining an old ship earns his marks by measuring before deciding, by proving the instruments before blaming the engine, and by expressing the result in fuel per mile.

The marks are printed 5 + 5 + 6, and the shape follows them exactly. Limb (a) is worth five marks and prints the verb “illustrate”, which asks for the formula and the mechanism, not an essay: definition and formula first, then the two reasons it governs fuel — the power identity and the cube law — then the qualification that lower is not always better. Limb (b) is also five and has two named halves, rpm and combustion, so it gets one section each. Limb (c) carries the most marks and prints “formulate a methodology”, which is an instruction to produce numbered steps in a defensible order.

The single most valuable structural decision is in limb (c): instrumentation and fuel measurement come first. On an old ship the data is less trustworthy than the machinery, and a methodology that starts by testing the engine is a methodology that will produce a confident wrong answer.
The second is that the optimum is read off fuel per mile, not fuel per hour and not SFOC. The ship is paid to move cargo. A candidate who plots only SFOC has optimised the engine and not the voyage.

rows: Geometry
c<sub>m</sub> = 2LN
Converts any shaft speed into the engine's real mechanical duty
Power
Power ∝ p<sub>m</sub> × A × c<sub>m</sub> × i
Shows that power is a pressure term times a speed term, and mean piston speed is the speed term
Propeller
Power ∝ c<sub>m</sub><sup>3</sup> (fixed pitch, unchanged hull and weather)
Converts a small speed reduction into a large power reduction - the arithmetic of slow steaming

blocks.p: And the qualification that goes with the third: per hour the saving follows the cube; per mile it follows roughly the square, because the voyage takes longer. Get that pair right and limb (a) is secure.

blocks.h: Why the lowest mean piston speed is not the cheapest

blocks.p: This is the discriminating idea in the whole question. Two effects run in opposite directions as the engine is slowed:

ul: Power demand falls as the cube. This is the saving, and it is large.

Specific fuel oil consumption rises once the engine is well below its matched point — lower compression pressure and temperature, turbocharger off its matching, falling scavenge pressure and air-fuel ratio, degraded atomisation.

blocks.p: Below some point the second effect starts eating the first, and the cost of deposits, fouling, scavenge fires and extra maintenance is on top of it. So the deliverable of limb (c) is a band, and a candidate who writes “the slower the better” has missed the question.

ul: Giving the formula as LN rather than 2LN. The piston travels the stroke twice per revolution.
Quoting mean piston speed in m/min, or mixing rev/min into the rev/s form without dividing by 60.
Calling it the maximum piston speed. It is a mean; the peak near mid-stroke is roughly half as much again.
Saying fuel per mile falls as the cube. Per hour follows the cube; per mile follows roughly the square.
Treating SFOC as constant, and therefore concluding that the slowest speed is always the cheapest.
Answering limb (b) on rpm only and never reaching combustion, when the limb names both.
Discussing only the high piston speed case in combustion. The low-speed case — poor atomisation, turbocharger mismatch, fouling — is where the marks actually are for a slow-steaming era paper.
In limb (c), producing a list of things to look at rather than an ordered methodology with measurement first.
Forgetting that the ship is old: fouled hull, worn propeller, drifted pump timing and fouled turbocharger will all masquerade as an engine efficiency problem.
Omitting the constraints — barred speed range, minimum turbocharger load, cylinder oil feed rate, charterparty warranty.
“Write the formula.” cm = 2LN, or 2LN/60 with N in rev/min. Metres per second.
“Why 2?” Because the piston covers the stroke twice in one revolution.
“Two engines both run at 100 rpm. Same duty?” Only if the strokes are equal. Mean piston speed, not rpm, is the measure.
“Typical value for a large two-stroke?” Of the order of 8 to 8.5 m/s at rated output; medium-speed four-strokes rather higher.
“Why are modern engines long-stroke?” To reach the design mean piston speed at lower rpm, which allows a larger, slower, more efficient propeller.
“You halve the revolutions. What happens to power?” Approximately one eighth, by the cube law — stating the fixed-pitch and unchanged-conditions assumption.
“Then why not run at dead slow permanently?” Because SFOC rises off the matched point, combustion degrades, deposits and fouling increase, and the schedule and charter still have to be met.
“What happens to combustion at high piston speed?” Less time per cycle, so afterburning — heat released too late in expansion, high exhaust temperature, thermal loading.
“And at low piston speed?” Turbocharger off its match, low scavenge pressure and air-fuel ratio, poor atomisation, incomplete combustion, fouling and scavenge-fire risk.
“First thing you do on joining the old ship?” Prove the instruments and the fuel measurement. Not run a test.
“Which curve do you optimise?” Fuel per nautical mile against mean piston speed.
What are the units of mean piston speed? Metres per second.
How does mean piston speed relate to rpm? Directly proportional for a given engine, because the stroke is fixed.
What is stroke-to-bore ratio and why has it increased? It buys propeller efficiency and combustion time at the cost of engine height.
Name three measurements you take at each test point. Shaft speed and power, fuel rate, and scavenge air pressure and temperature - with maximum and compression pressures per cylinder.
Why correct to reference ambient conditions? Because ambient air and seawater temperature move the result, and the shop trial figure was taken at reference conditions.
What is afterburning? Combustion continuing into the expansion stroke, so the heat is released too late to do useful work.
Why do auxiliary blowers cut in? Because at low load the exhaust energy is insufficient to drive the turbocharger to the required scavenge pressure.
How does a fouled hull look on your data? As higher shaft speed and power for the same ship speed - an engine problem that is not an engine problem.
Where do you record the operating envelope you decide on? In the SEEMP.
What do you do if the ship is permanently mismatched to the engine? Re-match the hardware - turbocharger cut-out, variable turbine area, tuning kit, re-pitch or de-rate.

blocks.p: One formula and one word for it: TWICE THE STROKE, EVERY REVOLUTION — cm = 2LN.
For significance, two lines: POWER = PRESSURE × SPEED, and CUBE PER HOUR, SQUARE PER MILE.

For combustion, one word each way: too fast is TIME (afterburning); too slow is AIR (turbocharger off its match). Ideal combustion needs AIR, ATOMISATION, TURBULENCE, TIME — and mean piston speed sets the last and disturbs the first two.

For the methodology, six steps in a fixed order: BASELINE, CALIBRATE, TEST, REDUCE, SEPARATE, DECIDE. If it helps, remember that the first two are about trusting the numbers, the middle two about getting the numbers, and the last two about using them.

ul: The physics is not regulatory and none of limbs (a) and (b) rests on an instrument. cm = 2LN is geometry; the power identity follows from the definition of mean effective pressure; the cube law is the propeller law for a fixed-pitch propeller in unchanged hull and weather conditions.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of the evidence

blocks.p: This is an engineering question and the provenance is declared as such.

The two relationships the answer rests on are derived, not asserted. cm = 2LN follows from the crank geometry, and the identity that power is proportional to mean effective pressure × piston area × mean piston speed × number of cylinders follows from the definition of mean effective pressure itself. Both derivations appear in the answer.

The numbers are the weak point and are marked as such. The typical mean piston speed ranges — about 8 to 8.5 m/s for a large two-stroke, 9 to 11 for a medium-speed four-stroke — are orders of magnitude from general engineering practice. The True Source corpus holds no engine-maker documentation, none was consulted, and no maker, engine type, rated power, rated speed or SFOC figure is presented as sourced. For the same reason the SFOC minimum is described as a region in the upper-middle load range rather than as a percentage of rated output, and no figure is given for a barred speed range, an auxiliary-blower cut-in load or a minimum continuous load — those are ship-specific and are read off the ship's own documentation, which is what the methodology instructs.

The cube law is an approximation and its assumptions are stated where it is used: fixed-pitch propeller, unchanged hull condition, unchanged weather. No claim is made for its accuracy on a fouled hull, in a seaway, or on a controllable-pitch installation off its combinator curve.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three limbs of 5, 5 and 6 marks. Limb a) wants the definition, the formula and the mechanism by which mean piston speed governs fuel burn - the power identity and the propeller cube law - together with the qualification that specific consumption rises off the matched point so lower is not automatically cheaper. Limb b) wants two things and names them: the proportionality to rpm at fixed stroke and the reason long-stroke engines exist, and the effect of piston speed on combustion in BOTH directions. Limb c) wants an ordered, defensible shipboard methodology on a ship whose data is not to be trusted. The discriminating feature is whether the candidate knows that the optimum is a band rather than the lowest attainable speed.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 5 + 5 + 6, all printed. Limb a) gets a formula table and two short mechanism sections. Limb b) gets one section on rpm and one on combustion, the latter built as a two-column HIGH against LOW table because the low-speed case is where the marks are in a slow-steaming era and is what most answers omit. Limb c) carries the most marks and prints 'formulate a methodology', so it is written as five numbered stages in a defensible order, with measurement proved before the engine is judged and the constraints stated before the decision.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate writes 2LN and not LN; can show why power is a pressure term times a speed term; can convert a speed reduction into a power reduction by the cube law AND knows that consumption per mile follows roughly the square; can explain combustion degradation in both directions from the design point; and can produce a methodology that starts with calibration and fuel measurement rather than with the engine. A Chief Engineer who separates hull, propeller, engine condition and fuel quality before pronouncing on the engine is demonstrating the judgement the limb is testing.
primary_source_plan: Derive c_m = 2LN from the crank geometry rather than asserting it
Derive the power identity from the definition of mean effective pressure, so the significance for fuel follows rather than being claimed
State the propeller cube law WITH its assumptions - fixed pitch, unchanged hull and weather
Distinguish fuel per hour from fuel per mile explicitly, because that distinction is the whole commercial point
Describe the SFOC curve as passing through a minimum in the upper-middle load range, as a region and not a percentage figure
Give typical mean piston speed ranges as orders of magnitude only, and assert no maker, engine type, power, speed or SFOC value
Establish the SEEMP and CII position at this sitting from the corpus amendment register, reversing the register's present-tense supersession marking on MEPC.346(78)
State that 2023 is the first CII data year and that it is STILL RUNNING at this sitting
Order the limb c) methodology so that instruments and fuel measurement are proved first, and hull, propeller, engine condition and fuel quality are separated before the engine is judged
Name the retrofit hardware only as the exit route, leaving it to Q8 on this same paper
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - and it is entirely in one limb. The physics cannot date. The regulatory content of limb c) can, and one reversal applies: the corpus register marks the 2022 SEEMP guidelines superseded, which is true today and false at this sitting. The CII statement is the other live edge - 2023 is the first data year and it is STILL RUNNING in November 2023, so any inherited statement about ships holding ratings is false here.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The question is entirely technical and international. No Indian instrument is engaged; the domestic statute at this sitting is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and it is not cited because nothing in the answer needs it.
technical_ambiguities: Whether mean piston speed is 2LN or LN - it is 2LN, because the piston covers the stroke twice per revolution
Whether it is a mean or a maximum - a mean; the peak near mid-stroke is roughly half as much again
Whether rpm and mean piston speed are interchangeable - only within one engine, because the relation depends on the stroke
Whether fuel consumption follows the cube law - power per hour does, approximately; consumption per mile follows roughly the square because the voyage lengthens
Whether the lowest mean piston speed gives the lowest fuel cost - it does not; SFOC rises off the matched point and deposits, fouling and maintenance cost rise with it
Whether combustion degrades only at high piston speed - it degrades in BOTH directions from the design point, and the low-speed case is the one that matters in a slow-steaming era
Whether the propeller law applies to a controllable-pitch installation - not in the same way; shaft speed may be held while pitch varies, so mean piston speed is fixed while load moves

Whether a consumption problem on an old ship is an engine problem - often it is not; hull fouling, propeller roughness, drifted pump timing, a fouled turbocharger and fuel quality all present the same way
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Three printed limb headings. Under (a), a definition section with a two-row formula table and a significance section built on the power identity and the cube law, closing on why lower is not always better. Under (b), one bulleted section on the rpm relation including the long-stroke argument, and one section on combustion built as a HIGH against LOW table with a unifying paragraph on design-point matching. Under (c), five numbered stages - baseline and calibration, structured test and data reduction, separation of hull, propeller, engine and fuel, the real constraints, and the decision with its review - closing on the judgement that the optimum is a negotiated band.
