reverify_before_publication.claim: No ship-specific limit is given for a barred speed range, an auxiliary-blower cut-in load, a minimum continuous load or a cylinder oil feed rate
reverify_before_publication.why: These are properties of an individual installation and are read off the ship's own documentation, which is what the methodology instructs. No held source records them and none is asserted.

questions.understand_first: The idea underneath this question is simple and has nothing to do with regulations. However big an engine is, what really limits it is how fast the moving parts are sliding and how little time each burn has to finish. Revolutions per minute do not tell you that, because a long-stroke engine moves its piston much further in each turn than a short-stroke one does. So engineers use the average speed of the piston itself: in one turn the piston covers the stroke twice, so that average is simply twice the stroke times the turning speed. Once you have it, two things follow. First, the power an engine makes is the amount burnt in each stroke multiplied by how fast the strokes come — a pressure part and a speed part — so slowing the piston takes power straight out, and because a propeller resists much harder the faster it turns, a small slowdown removes a surprisingly large amount of fuel. Second, and this is where most people go wrong, slowing down forever does not keep saving. Everything on the engine — the injectors, the compression, the turbocharger — was matched to one design speed, and far below it the air supply falls away, the spray is coarse and the fuel burns badly. So there is a best band, not a best minimum. The last part of the question is really about honesty: on an old ship you cannot find that band until you can trust your own instruments, and you cannot blame the engine until you have ruled out a dirty hull, a rough propeller and bad fuel.
questions.memory_cue: One formula: TWICE THE STROKE (1). Two consequences: POWER = PRESSURE × SPEED (2) and CUBE PER HOUR, SQUARE PER MILE (2). Two failures: too fast is TIME, too slow is AIR (4). Six steps: BASELINE, CALIBRATE, TEST, REDUCE, SEPARATE, DECIDE (5, 6, 7, 9).

steps.title: Definition, formula and units
points: mean piston speed is the AVERAGE speed of the piston over a complete revolution
in one revolution the piston travels TWICE the stroke - down and up
c_m = 2 x L x N with L in metres and N in rev/s, giving metres per second; or 2LN/60 with N in rev/min
it is a mean, not a maximum - the piston is stationary at each dead centre and peaks near mid-stroke at roughly half as much again
orders of magnitude: about 8 to 8.5 m/s for a large low-speed two-stroke at rated output, 9 to 11 for a medium-speed four-stroke, higher for high-speed engines
why engineers use it instead of rpm - it puts every engine on one scale by measuring how fast the rubbing surfaces move and how little time each process has

steps.title: Why it governs fuel consumption
points: from the definition of mean effective pressure, indicated power = mean effective pressure x swept volume x cycles per second x number of cylinders
writing swept volume as piston area x stroke and grouping the stroke with the speed gives POWER PROPORTIONAL TO p_m x A x c_m x i
power is therefore a PRESSURE term times a SPEED term, and mean piston speed is the speed term
fuel per hour is power times specific fuel oil consumption, so mean piston speed sits inside the consumption equation
the propeller law amplifies it - for a fixed-pitch propeller in unchanged hull and weather conditions, power varies approximately as the CUBE of shaft speed
a 10% reduction in mean piston speed therefore removes roughly 27% of the power
BUT THE VOYAGE LENGTHENS - consumption per nautical mile falls roughly as the SQUARE, and that is the figure that matters commercially
lower is NOT automatically better: SFOC passes through a minimum in the upper-middle load range and rises at both ends
at high piston speed - friction losses rise, mechanical efficiency falls, thermal loading, wear and cylinder oil demand rise
at low piston speed - compression and scavenge pressure fall, the turbocharger is off its matched point, atomisation degrades
so there is an OPTIMUM BAND of mean piston speed, which is what limb c) sets out to find

steps.title: The rpm relation
points: for a given engine the stroke is fixed, so mean piston speed is DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL to rpm
across different engines the relation breaks - equal rpm with unequal strokes is unequal duty
this is the whole point of the long-stroke engine: a longer stroke reaches the design mean piston speed at LOWER rpm
lower rpm permits a larger, slower-turning propeller of higher open-water efficiency
stroke-to-bore ratio is the design lever, buying propeller efficiency and combustion time at the cost of engine height and mass
on a controllable-pitch installation the proportionality survives but the propeller law does not - shaft speed may be held while pitch varies, so load moves while mean piston speed stays fixed

steps.title: Mean piston speed and ideal combustion
points: ideal combustion needs four things together - enough AIR, good ATOMISATION, adequate TURBULENCE and enough TIME
mean piston speed sets the time directly and disturbs the others indirectly
HIGH piston speed - short time per cycle, so injection, ignition delay and burn-out must fit into fewer milliseconds
the failure mode is AFTERBURNING - combustion continues into expansion so heat is released too late to do useful work; high exhaust temperatures, thermal overload, wear and cylinder oil consumption
gas exchange is also time-limited, so scavenging becomes less complete and residual gas rises
LOW piston speed - turbocharger off its matched point, scavenge pressure and air-fuel ratio fall, auxiliary blowers cut in
low compression temperature and degraded atomisation give slow incomplete burning, fouled gas ways, sooty exhaust, deposits on rings, liner and turbine, and scavenge-fire risk
THE UNIFYING STATEMENT - the maker matches injection, compression ratio, turbocharger and scavenging to a DESIGN mean piston speed, and combustion degrades in EITHER direction away from it
an engine run persistently far below its design point needs re-matching, not merely throttling back

steps.title: Establish the baseline, then prove the measurements
points: ON AN OLD SHIP THE DATA IS MORE SUSPECT THAN THE ENGINE, and nothing else is worth doing until the instruments are trusted
collect the design baseline - shop and sea trial records, the maker's SFOC curve, rated power and speed, and the STROKE; calculate design mean piston speed at rated and service output
collect the ship's history - running hours, overhauls, previous performance reports, docking, propeller polishing and hull cleaning dates
calibrate and prove the instruments - tachometer, torsionmeter, fuel flowmeters, temperature and pressure sensors, and the indicator or electronic pressure-measurement equipment
cross-check flowmeter against tank soundings
fix the fuel measurement in MASS, not volume - density at 15 degrees C from the bunker analysis, temperature correction applied

steps.title: Run a structured performance test and reduce the data
points: choose steady test points across the intended speed range, each held genuinely steady in stable weather at constant draught and trim, on the same fuel

record a full set at each point - shaft speed and power, fuel rate, scavenge air pressure and temperature, exhaust temperatures before and after turbine, turbocharger speed, compression and maximum pressures per cylinder, ambient air and seawater temperature, draught, trim, wind and sea
correct to reference ambient conditions before comparing anything to shop trial data
reduce each point to c_m = 2LN, to specific fuel oil consumption in g/kWh, and to fuel per nautical mile
plot SFOC against mean piston speed, and fuel per mile against mean piston speed
READ THE OPTIMUM OFF THE FUEL-PER-MILE CURVE, not off SFOC - the ship is paid to move cargo, not to make kilowatts

steps.title: Separate the engine from the hull, the propeller and the fuel
points: a high consumption at a given mean piston speed may have nothing to do with the engine, and this is where an old ship differs from a new one
hull and propeller - fouling and roughness shift the whole power-speed relation, so the engine turns faster for the same ship speed
establish hull and propeller condition from trend, inspection and cleaning history BEFORE concluding the engine is inefficient
engine condition - worn liners and rings, leaking exhaust valves, drifted fuel pump timing, worn or fouled injectors, fouled turbocharger, air cooler and gas ways
overhaul and clean, THEN re-test, or the optimum found is the optimum of a dirty engine
fuel quality - calorific value, viscosity at injection temperature and catalytic fines all move consumption independently of piston speed
loading condition - draught and trim change resistance materially; compare like with like or correct for it

steps.title: Bound the answer by the real constraints
points: barred speed range from torsional vibration - a band of shaft speed that may not be run continuously
minimum load at which the turbocharger sustains itself and the auxiliary blowers cut out, and the maker's minimum continuous load and low-load instructions
cylinder lubrication - feed rate and cylinder oil base number matched to the load and the fuel actually burnt
manoeuvring, weather and schedule margin - the ship must still accelerate, keep steerage and make the berth
commercial obligations - charterparty speed and consumption warranties, laycan and schedule integrity
regulatory - the SEEMP, with PART III MANDATORY SINCE 1 JANUARY 2023, is where the operating envelope is recorded and monitored
2023 IS THE FIRST CII DATA YEAR AND IT IS STILL RUNNING AT THIS SITTING - this year's decisions are being logged into a rating nobody has yet been issued

steps.title: Decide, implement, and keep it under review
points: choose an operating BAND, not a single figure - the range that minimises fuel per mile subject to every constraint
convert it into a shaft speed instruction the bridge can follow, with the barred range excluded and the low-load limit stated
record it in the SEEMP and brief the engineers and the master on the reasoning
monitor and trend continuously, with a monthly performance report against the curves so drift shows as drift
re-establish the baseline after any step change - hull cleaning, propeller polish, docking, major overhaul or a change of fuel
escalate to hardware only if the mismatch is structural - turbocharger cut-out, variable turbine area, tuning kits, re-pitch or de-rating
THE CLOSING JUDGEMENT - the optimum is a negotiated band, because the engine wants its design duty, the propeller law wants low revolutions and the charter wants the schedule

quick_revision.recall_15s: cm = 2LN — twice the stroke, every revolution, in m/s. It is a mean, not a maximum. Orders of magnitude: large two-stroke about 8 to 8.5 m/s at rated output, medium-speed four-stroke 9 to 11. It is used instead of rpm because it puts every engine on one scale of mechanical duty. Power ∝ pm × A × cm × i — a pressure term times a speed term. With a fixed-pitch propeller in unchanged conditions, power ∝ cm3, so a 10% speed cut removes about 27% of the power — but the voyage lengthens, so fuel per mile falls roughly as the square. Lower is not automatically cheaper: SFOC has a minimum in the upper-middle load range and rises at both ends. Rpm: directly proportional at fixed stroke; long-stroke engines reach the design piston speed at lower rpm, allowing a larger, more efficient propeller. Combustion needs air, atomisation, turbulence, time — too fast costs time (afterburning, high exhaust temperature); too slow costs air (turbocharger off match, low scavenge pressure, poor atomisation, fouling, scavenge-fire risk). Old-ship method: baseline, calibrate, test, reduce, separate, decide — prove the instruments and the fuel mass measurement first, rule out hull, propeller, engine condition and fuel quality, respect the barred speed range and minimum turbocharger load, and read the optimum off fuel per mile. Record the envelope in the SEEMP; Part III has been mandatory since 1 January 2023 and 2023 is the first CII data year, still running.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: Limbs (a) and (b) rest on no instrument at all - they are geometry, the definition of mean effective pressure and the propeller law. The only regulatory content is in limb (c): the operating envelope decided there is recorded and monitored in the ship's SEEMP under MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4, with Part III mandatory since 1 January 2023, and the operative guidance at this sitting is the 2022 SEEMP Guidelines, MEPC.346(78) - not the 2024 successor, which is future here.
quick_revision.major_trap: Concluding that the lowest mean piston speed gives the lowest fuel bill. Two effects run against each other: power demand falls as the cube of speed, which is the saving, but specific fuel oil consumption rises once the engine is well below its matched point, because compression and scavenge pressure fall, the turbocharger is off its match and atomisation degrades. There is therefore an optimum band, not a monotonic rule. The paired traps are writing the formula as LN instead of 2LN, and claiming that fuel per mile follows the cube - per hour follows the cube, per mile follows roughly the square, because the voyage takes longer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define mean piston speed and give its formula and units.
retrieval_cards.answer: The average speed of the piston over a complete revolution. Because the piston covers the stroke twice per revolution, c_m = 2 x L x N, with L the stroke in metres and N the rotational speed in rev/s, giving metres per second; equivalently 2LN/60 with N in rev/min.
retrieval_cards.why: The factor of two is the mark, and it is the single most commonly dropped item in the whole question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why do engineers use mean piston speed rather than rpm?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because rpm compares nothing across engines. The same rpm on a three-metre stroke and a one-metre stroke are entirely different duties. Mean piston speed puts every engine on one scale by measuring what actually wears, heats and limits the machine - how fast the rubbing surfaces move and how little time each process has.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the conceptual point behind limb (b) and it explains the long-stroke engine in one line.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Derive the relationship between power and mean piston speed.
retrieval_cards.answer: From the definition of mean effective pressure, indicated power = mean effective pressure x swept volume x cycles per second x number of cylinders. Swept volume is piston area x stroke; grouping the stroke with the speed gives power proportional to p_m x A x c_m x i. Power is therefore a pressure term times a speed term, and mean piston speed is the speed term.
retrieval_cards.why: It converts 'mean piston speed matters' from an assertion into a derivation, which is what limb (a) means by illustrate.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You reduce mean piston speed by 10%. What happens to fuel per hour, and to fuel per mile?
retrieval_cards.answer: Per hour, power falls by roughly 27% by the cube law, for a fixed-pitch propeller in unchanged hull and weather conditions. Per mile the saving is smaller - roughly the square - because the ship is slower and the voyage takes longer. The per-mile figure is the one that matters commercially.
retrieval_cards.why: Claiming the cube for per-mile consumption is the classic error in every slow-steaming answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is the lowest mean piston speed not the most economical?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because specific fuel oil consumption is not constant. It passes through a minimum in the upper-middle load range and rises as the engine goes well below its matched point: compression pressure and temperature fall, the turbocharger is off its matching so scavenge pressure and air-fuel ratio fall, and atomisation degrades. Deposits, fouling, scavenge-fire risk and maintenance cost rise on top of that. The deliverable is an optimum band, not a minimum.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the discriminating idea in the question and the thing limb (c) exists to find.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What happens to combustion at high mean piston speed, and at low?
retrieval_cards.answer: High: less time per cycle for injection, ignition delay and burn-out, so afterburning - heat released into expansion too late to do useful work - with high exhaust temperatures, thermal overload, wear and cylinder oil demand; gas exchange is also time-limited so scavenging is less complete. Low: the turbocharger is off its matched point, scavenge pressure and air-fuel ratio fall, auxiliary blowers cut in, compression temperature and atomisation degrade, giving incomplete burning, fouled gas ways, deposits and scavenge-fire risk.
retrieval_cards.why: Most answers cover only the high case; the low case is where a slow-steaming era paper puts its marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why are modern low-speed engines long-stroke?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because a longer stroke lets the engine reach its design mean piston speed - the mechanical duty it was built for - at lower rpm. Lower rpm permits a larger, slower-turning propeller of higher open-water efficiency, and gives more time per cycle for combustion. The cost is engine height and mass.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the cleanest illustration that mean piston speed, not rpm, is the design constraint.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You join an old ship. What do you do BEFORE testing the engine?
retrieval_cards.answer: Prove the numbers. Collect the design baseline - shop and sea trial records, the SFOC curve, rated power and speed, and the stroke - and the ship's own history of overhauls, docking and hull cleaning. Then calibrate the tachometer, torsionmeter, flowmeters, pressure and temperature instrumentation and the indicator equipment, cross-check flowmeter against tank soundings, and fix fuel measurement in mass using density at 15 degrees C with temperature correction.
retrieval_cards.why: On an old ship the data is more suspect than the machinery; a methodology that starts with the engine produces a confident wrong answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do you reduce performance test data to find the optimum?
retrieval_cards.answer: Hold each test point genuinely steady in stable weather at constant draught and trim on the same fuel; record shaft speed and power, fuel rate, scavenge and exhaust conditions, turbocharger speed, compression and maximum pressures, and ambient conditions; correct to reference ambient conditions; then compute c_m = 2LN, SFOC in g/kWh and fuel per nautical mile for each point, and plot both against mean piston speed. Read the optimum off the fuel-per-mile curve.
retrieval_cards.why: The correction step and the choice of curve are the two places candidates lose the marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Consumption is high at the usual mean piston speed. Name four causes that are NOT the engine.
retrieval_cards.answer: Hull fouling and propeller roughness, which shift the whole power-speed relation so the engine must turn faster for the same ship speed; fuel quality - calorific value, viscosity at injection temperature and catalytic fines; loading condition, since draught and trim change resistance materially; and instrument error, which on an old ship is the first suspect of all.
retrieval_cards.why: An old ship's consumption problem usually is not an engine problem, and saying so is what distinguishes a Chief Engineer's answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where is the chosen operating envelope recorded, and what is the regulatory position at this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: In the ship's SEEMP under MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4, with Part III mandatory since 1 January 2023. The operative guidance at this sitting is the 2022 SEEMP Guidelines, MEPC.346(78). 2023 is the first CII data year and it is still running at this November sitting, so no ship has yet been issued a rating.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the only regulatory content in the question, and both the guidelines edition and the CII data year are easy to import wrongly from a later paper.

questions.subpart_marks_note: Four limbs of four marks each, all printed. The question number is printed as "Q3)" with a round bracket, unlike the full stop used on seven of the nine questions. Limb c) prints "on-hire Survey" with a capitalised S mid-sentence, and limb d) prints "which of the above three Survey is the most demanding" - a SINGULAR noun after a plural numeral. Both are preserved exactly as printed and neither is corrected; the answer reads limb d) as the examiner plainly meant and says so once in the study guide.
questions.recurrence_adjudication: Seven bare host tokens with no question numbers and no sitting identifier MIW can resolve. None was used. The canonical position is that limb a) alone has family members in the built set, and limbs b), c) and d) have none.
decomposition: What a bill of lading is - the three functions, which is the whole of limb a) and must be delivered in four marks
The types that matter commercially, kept short because the limb asks what it IS
The legal regime that governs it, and the Indian statute in force at this sitting
The precautions common to signing ANY bill of lading - quantity, condition, date, description, originals
The precautions specific to a VOYAGE charter, which turn on incorporation of the charterparty and on preserving the owner's lien
The precautions specific to a TIME charter, which turn on the employment clause, signing as presented, and the indemnity that protects the owner
What an on-hire survey is FOR, so that the three variants can be differentiated by purpose rather than by checklist
The three variants differentiated - bareboat, voyage and time - by what each survey has to protect and over what period
The judgement in limb d), argued from the Chief Engineer's own position: the bareboat survey, and the reasons must be reasons, not assertions
reuse_evidence: LIMB-LEVEL DONORS ONLY, AND ONLY FOR LIMB a). QP2403-Q2 and QP2510-Q2 (Bill of Lading - definition, significance, types and obligations) and QP2302-Q6 (February 2023 - the main function of a bill of lading, why it is made out 'to order', and when it becomes the contract of carriage) all set the definitional task that limb a) sets. Their route for that limb was used. QP2302-Q6 is the SAME-YEAR member and was read first.

QP2507-Q3 and QP2512-Q7 were read for the charterer's influence on the ship. None of them donated prose.

LIMBS b), c) AND d) ARE FRESH. No MIW paper, solved or held as intelligence, sets the precautions before signing a bill of lading or sets the on-hire survey. A search of all 342 solved questions for 'on-hire' and 'off-hire' returns nothing, and the only occurrences anywhere in the 549-question six-year window are the term 'Off-hire' inside a define-these-terms list (QP2103-Q4, QP2110-Q7, QP2112-Q5), which sets no survey. Three of the four limbs are therefore authored without a donor, which is why the tier is C and reused_from is null despite limb a) having a family.
questions.verification_status: AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY THROUGHOUT, DECLARED, AND THE REASON IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN ACCIDENTAL. This question is answered out of commercial practice and out of instruments the True Source corpus does not hold and is not intended to hold. The corpus's reference resolver contains 320 entries and every one of them is MARPOL Annex VI; it holds no carriage-of-goods statute, no charterparty form and no bill of lading. THE THREE FUNCTIONS OF A BILL OF LADING - receipt, evidence of the contract of carriage, and document of title - are uncontroversial and consistently recorded, and are carried at authoritative-secondary level. The Hague-Visby Rules and their Indian implementation through the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993, and the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856, are named at IDENTITY level; NO ARTICLE, RULE OR SECTION IS QUOTED AND NO ARTICLE NUMBER IS ATTRIBUTED A SUB-PARAGRAPH. The standard charterparty and bill of lading forms are NAMED ONLY - no clause of any form is quoted, numbered or paraphrased as though read, because the forms are copyright industry documents and none is held. The on-hire survey content of limbs c) and d) is commercial practice and engineering judgement, attributed as such: no survey report format, no scope-of-work document and no industry checklist is cited. The one hard legal position asserted without qualification is that a clean bill of lading must not be signed for cargo that is not in apparent good order and condition, and that a letter of indemnity offered in exchange for one is worthless - that is stated as settled practice and as the standing P&I position, not as a quotation.
sources: AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: a bill of lading performs three functions - it is a receipt for goods received or shipped, stating their quantity, marks and apparent order and condition; it is evidence of the contract of carriage; and it is a document of title to the goods, transferable by endorsement and delivery where it is made out to order.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: where a charterparty exists, the bill of lading is evidence of the contract of carriage but is not itself the contract as between owner and charterer, the charterparty being that contract. In the hands of a third-party holder who is not the charterer, the bill of lading contains or evidences the contract on which that holder sues.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: the principal distinctions between a shipped or on-board bill and a received-for-shipment bill; between a clean bill and a claused or foul bill; and between an order bill, a straight bill naming a consignee, and a bearer bill. A sea waybill is not a document of title and goods under it are delivered against identification rather than against presentation.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (identity only): the Hague-Visby Rules, given effect in India by the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993; and the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856, which is the statute in force at this sitting. No article, rule or section is quoted.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: settled practice and the standing protection-and-indemnity position that a clean bill of lading must not be issued for cargo which is not in apparent good order and condition, that a letter of indemnity offered in exchange for a clean bill is unenforceable as against the party defrauded, and that issuing a false bill or a misdated bill prejudices the owner's club cover.
AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: the mate's receipt records the quantity and apparent order and condition as ascertained by the ship, and any clausing on it must be carried through onto the bill of lading.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: standard forms are NAMED ONLY in this answer - the voyage charter and its associated bill, the time charter forms, and the bareboat form. No clause of any form is quoted, numbered or paraphrased as though read.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: under a bareboat or demise charter the charterer takes possession and control of the ship, mans, operates, maintains and insures her for the charter period, and redelivers her in like condition, fair wear and tear excepted. Under a time charter the owner retains crewing and maintenance while the charterer directs employment and pays hire and bunkers. Under a voyage charter the owner retains the ship entirely and is paid freight for carrying a cargo between named ports.

P3 INDUSTRY GUIDANCE: on-hire and off-hire survey practice - bunkers, fresh water and lubricating oil remaining on board, hold and tank condition and cleanliness, hatch cover weathertightness, cargo gear and its test certification, and the recording of existing damage at the moment of delivery.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT: the differentiation of the three on-hire surveys by WHAT EACH HAS TO PROTECT and OVER WHAT PERIOD, rather than by checklist; and the reasoning in limb d) that the bareboat survey is the most demanding because it is the only one that must survive years rather than a voyage or a period, and because machinery condition, class survey status and spares inventory - the Chief Engineer's own domain - are its largest and most contentious parts.

INTERNAL REUSE VERIFIED: QP2302-Q6 (February 2023) for the functions of the bill of lading and the 'to order' reasoning; QP2403-Q2 and QP2510-Q2 for the definitional route; QP2410-Q2 for charter party types and the parties' rights. All read in full; no prose taken.
unresolved: NO CARRIAGE-OF-GOODS INSTRUMENT IS HELD BY THE CORPUS. The Hague-Visby Rules, the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993, and the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 are named at identity level. No article, rule or section is quoted and no article number is attributed a sub-paragraph.

NO CHARTERPARTY OR BILL OF LADING FORM IS HELD. Standard forms are named only. No clause is quoted, numbered or paraphrased as though read, and no incorporation, lien, employment or indemnity clause is reproduced.

The carrier's package or unit limitation figures under the Hague-Visby Rules are NOT stated. They are unit-of-account figures whose Indian conversion is not held, and nothing in this question requires them.

The on-hire survey content is commercial and engineering practice. No survey report format, no standard scope of work and no industry checklist is cited, and no time or cost figure is given for any of the three surveys.

No P&I club rule or circular is cited for the letter of indemnity position. It is stated as settled practice and as the standing club position, which is uncontroversial, rather than as a quotation from a held rule.

Whether a voyage charter attracts an 'on-hire survey' at all is a matter of terminology rather than law. The answer records the point expressly - no hire is paid under a voyage charter, so the survey done is a pre-loading condition and cargo-worthiness survey - and then answers the limb as the examiner asked it.

The successor legislation that later recodifies the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 postdates this sitting. Its identity is not asserted; only the fact that the 1856 Act is the statute in force in November 2023 is stated.

blocks.h: (a) What a bill of lading is

blocks.p: A bill of lading is a document issued by or on behalf of the carrier to the shipper when goods are received for shipment or are shipped on board. Four marks buy the three functions, and the three functions are the answer:

ol: A receipt. It acknowledges that the carrier has received the stated goods — quantity, marks and numbers — in the apparent order and condition stated on its face. This is the function the ship controls and the one the master signs to.

Evidence of the contract of carriage. It records the terms on which the goods are carried. Note the precision: where a charterparty exists, the charterparty is the contract between owner and charterer and the bill is only evidence of it; but in the hands of a third party who is not the charterer, the bill of lading is the contract on which that holder sues.

A document of title. Where it is made out “to order”, it is transferable by endorsement and delivery, and the goods are delivered only against surrender of an original. This is what allows cargo to be sold while it is still at sea and financed by documentary credit — and it is the reason a bill of lading matters far more than a receipt.

blocks.h: 2. The types worth naming, and the law that governs

rows: Shipped (on board) against received for shipment
Only the shipped bill certifies the goods are actually on board. Letters of credit normally demand it
Clean against claused (foul)
A clean bill carries no notation of defective condition. A claused bill is normally unacceptable under a letter of credit - which is why pressure is put on the master to sign clean
Order against straight against bearer
Only the order bill is freely negotiable by endorsement. A straight bill names its consignee and is not
Bill of lading against sea waybill
A sea waybill is not a document of title; goods under it are delivered against identification, not presentation
Charterparty bill against liner bill
A charterparty bill incorporates the terms of a named charterparty, which is what limb (b) turns on

blocks.p: The governing law. Carriage under a bill of lading is governed internationally by the Hague-Visby Rules, given effect in India by the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993; the transfer of rights under the bill is governed by the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856, which is the statute in force at this sitting. The ship itself operates under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.

blocks.h: (b) Precautions before signing a bill of lading
3. The precautions that apply under any charter

blocks.p: The master signs, and what he signs binds the owner. These come first because they apply whatever the charter:

ol: Sign only for what is actually on board. Compare the bill against the mate's receipts and the ship's own tally, ullage or draught survey.

Carry the clausing across. Any remark on the mate's receipt — wet, rusty, torn bags, short, stained, atmospheric rust — must appear on the bill. A mate's receipt claused and a bill signed clean is the classic loss.

Never sign a clean bill for cargo that is not in apparent good order and condition, and never accept a letter of indemnity in exchange for one. Such an indemnity is unenforceable against the party it deceives, and issuing a knowingly false bill prejudices the owner's P&I cover. Clause the bill and refer to owners.

Quantity. Where the ship cannot verify the figure, sign for the ship's figures or qualify the shipper's figure appropriately — never adopt a shore figure the ship has not checked as though the ship had checked it.
Date it correctly. The date is the date loading completed. Ante-dating or post-dating is fraud, however commercially convenient, and it voids cover.
Check the particulars — description, marks and numbers, ports of loading and discharge, consignee and notify party, freight terms. Do not certify “freight prepaid” unless authorised.
Account for the originals. Note how many originals are issued and that delivery is against surrender of one original.
Deck cargo must be stated as carried on deck; and never sign a bill for cargo not shipped.
Check the authority to sign. If an agent signs, obtain written authority, and see that it is expressed as being for and on behalf of the master.

blocks.h: 4. Under a VOYAGE charter - protect the incorporation and the lien

blocks.p: Here the owner keeps the ship and is paid freight. The bill will reach a receiver who has never seen the charterparty, and the risk is that the owner ends up bound to a stranger on terms wider than the charter he agreed.

ul: Confirm the incorporation clause — that the bill incorporates the terms of the charterparty, identified by its date. An incorporation clause with no charterparty date is a standing defect.

Confirm that the lien survives. The owner's lien on cargo for freight, deadfreight and demurrage must be preserved through the bill, or the only security for unpaid freight is gone once the cargo is delivered.
Confirm the Paramount Clause, so that the applicable carriage regime and its defences and limits apply.
Check the cargo quantity against the charter — the minimum and maximum quantity, the deadweight and the deadfreight position.
Do not accept terms inconsistent with the charter — a different discharge port, a different description of the cargo, or a freight-prepaid notation where freight has not been paid.
Refer anything unusual to owners before signing. Under a voyage charter the master is the owner's man and has no reason to sign anything he is not comfortable with.

blocks.h: 5. Under a TIME charter - signing as presented, and the indemnity

blocks.p: Here the charterer directs the employment of the ship and normally presents the bills. The employment clause obliges the master to sign bills as presented — but that obligation is not unlimited, and the boundary is where the marks are:

ul: The obligation to sign as presented does not extend to a bill that is inconsistent with the mate's receipts, that is false, that is misdated, or that would impose on the owner a liability materially beyond the charter. The master may and should refuse.
Where the charterer or his agents sign on the master's behalf, obtain the written authority, and see that the authority is limited to signing in conformity with mate's receipts.
The employment and indemnity clause is the owner's protection for complying with charterer's orders — but it protects a master who acted properly. It is not a licence to sign anything.
Check the incorporation and the Paramount Clause as under a voyage charter, and check that the charterer has not presented a bill that turns a period contract into an unlimited carriage liability.

Switch bills, and delivery without production of an original against a letter of indemnity, are the two demands that most often arrive under a time charter. Both go to owners and P&I before anything is signed. Neither is the master's decision alone.
Freight is not the ship's concern here — the owner is paid hire, not freight — so the lien question is different, and the charterer's freight arrangements are not certified by the ship.

blocks.h: (c) On-hire survey under three charter types
6. What the on-hire survey is for, and the common core

blocks.p: An on-hire or delivery survey fixes the condition of the ship and the quantities on board at the moment responsibility changes hands, so that a dispute months or years later can be settled against a record rather than against recollection. It is a commercial survey between the parties — it is not a class or statutory survey, and it credits nothing.

Common to all three: date and time of delivery, bunkers remaining on board by grade and quantity, fresh water and lubricating oils, hold and tank condition, hatch cover condition, cargo gear, existing damage recorded and photographed, and the certificates on board.
What differs is what the survey has to protect, and for how long:

headers: What passes, and for how long
What the survey must therefore establish
rows:
1) Bare-boat
(demise)
Possession and control, for years. The charterer mans, operates, maintains, insures and drydocks her as if owner, and redelivers her in like condition, fair wear and tear excepted

The whole asset baseline: main and auxiliary machinery condition, running hours and recent overhauls; class survey status with every outstanding condition of class, due dates, thickness measurements and the docking cycle; all certificates; tank and hold coatings; and an item-by-item inventory of spares, stores, tools, plans, manuals and publications. Joint attendance with independent surveyors and often class; days. Mirrored by an off-hire survey years later
2) Voyage charter
Nothing. The owner keeps the ship entirely and is paid freight to carry one cargo between named ports

Cargo-worthiness for this cargo only: hold or tank cleanliness against the previous cargo, hatch cover weathertightness testing, cargo gear and its certification, a draught survey, and the certificates this voyage and this cargo need. Often one cargo surveyor; hours. No mirror survey
3) Time charter
The employment of the ship, for a period. The owner keeps crewing and maintenance; the charterer pays hire and bunkers

The hire, bunker and performance baseline: bunkers by grade and quantity, fresh water and lubricating oils; cargo spaces clean and ready for the intended trade; cargo gear and its test certification; existing damage recorded; certificate due dates falling inside the period; and the speed and consumption baseline against the description warranties. Joint independent surveyors; about a day. Mirrored by an off-hire survey at redelivery, bunkers again central

blocks.p: One point of terminology, stated once. Strictly, a voyage charter attracts no on-hire survey at all, because no hire is paid and the ship is never delivered into anyone's service. What is done is a pre-loading condition and cargo-worthiness survey. The limb asks for the differentiation, so it is given — but saying why the voyage case is the odd one out is itself worth a mark.

blocks.h: (d) Which survey is the most demanding and exhaustive
8. The bareboat survey - and the reasons

blocks.p: The bare-boat delivery survey, by a wide margin. As Chief Engineer I would expect to be committed to it for days, and to carry the consequences of it for the whole charter. Six reasons, in order of weight:

ol: It is the only one where the whole ship changes hands. Under a bareboat charter the charterer takes possession and becomes responsible for manning, operating, maintaining, insuring and drydocking her. Everything therefore has to be recorded, because everything is now someone else's obligation.

It is the only baseline that has to survive years. Redelivery is in like condition, fair wear and tear excepted, and "like condition" can only be argued against what was written down at delivery. A voyage survey is spent when the cargo is discharged; a time charter survey is answered at redelivery within the period; the bareboat record has to hold for the life of the charter.

Its scope is the entire technical inventory. Machinery condition and running hours, performance data, class survey status and every outstanding condition of class, thickness measurement records, docking and survey due dates, tank and hold coatings, and a spares, stores, tools, plans, manuals and publications inventory taken item by item. No other survey opens the store rooms.

The contentious parts are the engineer's parts. In my own experience the disputes are almost never about the hull. They are about machinery condition, running hours since overhaul, and what spares were on board — exactly the three things only the Chief Engineer can properly record, and the three things that are most expensive to argue about afterwards.

The consequences reach beyond the charter. A bareboat charter can carry a change of flag, of manager and of insurers, and may sit under a finance or bareboat-registration arrangement. Errors in the delivery record propagate into insurance, mortgage and registration questions, not merely into a hire dispute.

Nothing in it can be repeated. The ship sails, the crew changes, and the moment cannot be re-created. A cargo survey missed can be re-done next voyage; a bareboat delivery survey missed is simply gone.

blocks.p: The ranking, and why the other two sit where they do. The time charter survey is second: it is genuinely joint and it establishes bunkers, cargo readiness and the speed-and-consumption baseline against which performance claims will run — substantial, but bounded by the period and by the fact that the owner still maintains the ship. The voyage survey is third and narrowest: one cargo, one voyage, essentially a cargo-worthiness inspection, and the owner never lets go of the ship at all.

The principle behind the ranking is worth stating in one line: the depth of a delivery survey is set by how much responsibility passes and for how long. Bareboat passes everything, for years. Time charter passes employment, for a period. Voyage charter passes nothing at all.

Four limbs, four marks each, all printed — so the discipline is that no limb may be allowed to eat another. Limb (a) is the one candidates over-write: it asks what a bill of lading is, and four marks buy the three functions plus a short types-and-law paragraph. A page on types with the three functions missing scores badly.

Limb (b) names two charters, so it gets three blocks: the precautions common to both first, then one block each. That ordering is deliberate — most of the marks are in the common block, and the charter-specific material is what separates a good answer from an average one.

Limb (c) prints the word “differentiate” against three named charters, which is an instruction to build a comparison table with the three as columns. A candidate who writes three separate paragraphs has not differentiated; he has described three times.

Limb (d) prints “explain with reasons” and “as a Chief Engineer”. Both matter. It wants a decision stated at the top, numbered reasons underneath, and at least one of them argued from the engineer's own position rather than from a textbook.

blocks.h: The printed anomaly in limb (d), and how it is handled

blocks.p: The paper prints “which of the above three Survey is the most demanding and exhaustive” — a singular noun after a plural numeral, and capitalised mid-sentence. It is preserved exactly as printed and not corrected.

The intended sense is plain — which of the three surveys — and the answer reads it that way. This is the house rule and it is worth understanding rather than resenting: a candidate sitting that paper saw exactly this, and MIW records what was printed. Limb (c) prints “on-hire Survey” with a capital S for the same reason, and the question number itself is printed “Q3)” where seven of the nine questions print a full stop.

blocks.h: The one legal point never to get wrong

blocks.p: A clean bill of lading is never signed for cargo that is not in apparent good order and condition, and a letter of indemnity offered in exchange for one is worthless.

The indemnity is unenforceable against the party it deceives, and issuing a bill the master knows to be false prejudices the owner's P&I cover — so the owner is left with the liability and no insurance behind it. The same applies to misdating: the date is the date loading completed, and ante-dating to catch a letter of credit expiry is fraud however routine it is made to sound.

The correct action is always the same: clause the bill to match the mate's receipt, and refer to owners and the club. It is not a decision the master takes alone under commercial pressure at three in the morning, and saying so is worth a mark.

blocks.h: Voyage against time: the one-line difference for limb (b)

rows: Owner is paid
Freight
Hire
Who presents the bill
Normally through the owner's own chain
The charterer, and the employment clause requires signature as presented
Main risk to the owner
Being bound to a stranger on terms wider than the charter, and losing the lien for freight, deadfreight and demurrage
Signing a bill that is false, misdated, or inconsistent with the mate's receipts, in reliance on an employment clause that does not protect him if he does
The precaution that matters most
Incorporation clause with the charterparty date, and the lien preserved
Written authority where agents sign, and the limit of "as presented" understood

ul: In limb (a), listing types of bill of lading and never stating the three functions.
Saying flatly that the bill of lading is the contract of carriage. It is evidence of it — and becomes the contract in the hands of a third-party holder, which is the precise point.
Calling a sea waybill a document of title. It is not.
In limb (b), giving one undifferentiated list when the limb names two charters.
Omitting the letter of indemnity point, which is the most examinable thing in the limb.
Saying the master must sign whatever the time charterer presents. The obligation to sign as presented stops at bills that are false, misdated or inconsistent with the mate's receipts.
In limb (c), describing three surveys instead of differentiating them.
Treating the on-hire survey as a class or statutory survey. It is a commercial survey between the parties and credits nothing.
Missing that a voyage charter involves no hire and no delivery, so the survey there is a cargo-worthiness survey.
In limb (d), giving an answer with no reasons, or reasons that are assertions. “Explain with reasons” means the reasons are the marks.
Answering limb (d) without using the Chief Engineer's viewpoint the limb expressly gives you — machinery condition, running hours and spares inventory.
“Give the three functions.” Receipt; evidence of the contract of carriage; document of title.
“Is the bill of lading the contract?” Between owner and charterer, no — the charterparty is. In a third-party holder's hands, it is the contract he sues on.
“Why 'to order'?” Because it makes the bill negotiable by endorsement, so the cargo can be sold afloat and financed.

“Shipper wants a clean bill for rust-stained steel and offers an LOI. What do you do?” Clause the bill to match the mate's receipt, refuse the LOI, refer to owners and the club. The LOI is unenforceable and cover is prejudiced.
“What date goes on the bill?” The date loading completed. Nothing else.
“Charterer's agent wants to sign for you.” Written authority, limited to signing in conformity with mate's receipts.
“Discharge without an original bill, against an LOI?” Owners and P&I decide, not the master.
“Why does the incorporation clause need the charterparty date?” Because a clause incorporating an unidentified charterparty may incorporate nothing.
“Who is on hire under a voyage charter?” Nobody — freight is paid, not hire. It is the trap inside limb (c).
“What is the single largest item in a bareboat delivery survey?” The inventory — spares, stores, tools, plans and publications, taken item by item.
“What condition is a bareboat ship redelivered in?” Like condition, fair wear and tear excepted — measured against the delivery record.
What is a mate's receipt and why does it matter? The ship's own record of quantity and apparent order and condition; its clausing must be carried onto the bill.
What is a claused bill? One bearing a notation that the goods were not in apparent good order and condition.
Which rules govern carriage under a bill of lading, and how do they apply in India? The Hague-Visby Rules, through the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993.
Which Indian Act governs transfer of rights under a bill of lading at this time? The Bills of Lading Act, 1856.
What is a switch bill and why is it dangerous? A replacement set issued for the same cargo; two sets in circulation is a fraud risk, and it is never the master's decision.
What is the owner's lien for, and how is it lost? For freight, deadfreight and demurrage; it is lost if the bill does not preserve it or the cargo is delivered without it being exercised.
Name three things recorded at any on-hire survey. Bunkers by grade and quantity, hold and tank condition, and existing damage.
Who attends a bareboat delivery survey? Independent surveyors for both parties, often with class in attendance.
Why is a speed and consumption baseline taken at a time charter delivery? Because performance claims under the description warranties will be measured against it.

blocks.p: Limb (a) is three words: RECEIPT, EVIDENCE, TITLE. Nothing else in that limb is worth more than those three.

Limb (b) is five checks before the pen touches paper: QUANTITY, CONDITION, DATE, TERMS, AUTHORITY — and one rule that overrides all of them: NO CLEAN BILL FOR DIRTY CARGO, AND NO LOI. Then one word for each charter: voyage is INCORPORATION (and the lien); time is AS PRESENTED (and its limits).

Limb (c) is one question asked three times: WHAT PASSES, AND FOR HOW LONG? Bareboat — everything, for years. Time — employment, for a period. Voyage — nothing, for one voyage. Every difference in the table falls out of that.
Limb (d) is the same idea used as the answer: the more that passes and the longer it passes for, the deeper the survey.

ul: Hague-Visby Rules — the international carriage regime applied through the bill of lading's Paramount Clause. Named at identity level; no article is quoted.
Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993 (India) — the statute giving effect to the Hague-Visby Rules.
Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 — transfer of rights under a bill of lading. This is the Act in force at this sitting; any later recodification postdates the examination.
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 — the governing Indian shipping statute at this sitting. The 2025 Act commenced 15 March 2026 and is prohibited here.

Standard charterparty and bill of lading forms — the voyage form and its associated bill, the time charter forms and the bareboat form are named only. No clause of any form is quoted or numbered; see the uncertainty section.
P&I — the club position on false and misdated bills and on letters of indemnity is settled practice, not a quoted rule.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of the evidence

blocks.p: This question is answered out of commercial practice, and the corpus was never going to hold its sources.

The True Source corpus's reference resolver holds 320 entries and every one of them is MARPOL Annex VI. It holds no carriage-of-goods statute, no charterparty form and no bill of lading. That is not a gap in this session's research; it is the shape of the corpus. The three functions of a bill of lading are uncontroversial and consistently recorded, and are carried at authoritative-secondary level.

The consequences are deliberate. The Hague-Visby Rules, the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993, and the Bills of Lading Act, 1856 are named at identity level and nothing is quoted from any of them; no article or section number is attributed a sub-paragraph. The Hague-Visby package and unit limitation figures are not stated, because the Indian conversion is not held and nothing in this question needs them. The standard forms are named only — no incorporation, lien, employment or indemnity clause is reproduced, numbered or paraphrased as though read, because the forms are copyright industry documents.

The on-hire survey material in limbs (c) and (d) is commercial practice and engineering judgement. No survey report format, standard scope of work or industry checklist is cited, and no time or cost figure is given for any of the three surveys. The ranking in limb (d) is a reasoned judgement, offered as such, and its principle — depth follows how much responsibility passes and for how long — is stated so that the reasoning can be tested rather than merely accepted.

Currency. Two Indian statutes are at their pre-recodification stage here and both are stated as at the sitting. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 governs — the 2025 Act commenced 15 March 2026, twenty-eight months after this examination. The Bills of Lading Act, 1856 is likewise the Act in force; its successor postdates the sitting and its identity is not asserted. Neither may be updated by a later editor without falsifying the paper.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Four limbs of four marks each, running from a definition through a practical precaution list to a comparison and finally to a judgement. Limb a) is definitional and the examiner wants the THREE FUNCTIONS. Limb b) names two charters and the marks are in the difference between them. Limb c) prints 'differentiate' against three named charters, which asks for a comparison and not three descriptions. Limb d) prints 'explain with reasons' and 'as a Chief Engineer', which asks for a decision, numbered reasons, and at least one reason argued from the engineer's own domain. The discriminating features are the letter of indemnity rule in b), the fact that a voyage charter involves no hire and therefore no on-hire survey properly so called in c), and the ability in d) to state a PRINCIPLE rather than a preference.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4, all printed. Equal marks means no limb may consume another, and limb a) is where that discipline is hardest: four marks buys the three functions plus a short types-and-law table, not an essay on documentary credits. Limb b) gets three blocks - common precautions, then voyage, then time - because most of the marks are in the common block and the charter-specific material is what separates answers. Limb c) is built as a single nine-row table with the three charters as columns, which is what 'differentiate' asks for. Limb d) states the answer in its first line and then gives six numbered reasons in order of weight, closing on the principle that generates the ranking.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate can state the three functions without prompting; knows that the bill is EVIDENCE of the contract between owner and charterer but IS the contract in a third-party holder's hands; will not sign a clean bill for damaged cargo and knows why a letter of indemnity does not cure it; understands that the time charterer's right to have bills signed as presented has limits; can differentiate the three delivery surveys by what passes and for how long rather than by checklist; and can defend the bareboat ranking with reasons drawn from machinery condition, class survey status and spares inventory - the Chief Engineer's own ground.

questions.understand_first: Two quite different documents are being asked about and it is worth keeping them apart from the first line. The first is the piece of paper that travels with the cargo. It does three jobs at once: it is the ship's admission that she has the goods and what state they looked to be in; it records the terms on which they are carried; and — this is the surprising one — it is treated as standing for the goods themselves, so whoever holds it can sell them while they are still at sea and the ship must hand the cargo to whoever produces it. That third job is why signing one carelessly is so dangerous: a signature saying the cargo looked sound is relied on by a buyer thousands of miles away who will never see the ship, and no private promise from the shipper can undo the harm to him. The second document is about the ship. When a ship is handed over to a charterer, somebody writes down what state she is in and what is aboard at that exact moment, because when she comes back the two records will be compared. How thorough that has to be depends entirely on how much of the ship has been handed over and for how long. Hand over a single voyage and you need only prove she is fit for that cargo. Hand over her employment for a year and you need the fuel, the readiness and a performance yardstick. Hand over the whole ship — crew, upkeep, insurance, everything — for years, and you need to record the machinery, the certificates and every spare in the store, because nobody will remember any of it when she returns.
questions.memory_cue: Limb (a): RECEIPT, EVIDENCE, TITLE (1). Limb (b): QUANTITY, CONDITION, DATE, TERMS, AUTHORITY (3), then INCORPORATION for voyage (4) and AS PRESENTED for time (5). Limbs (c) and (d) are one question: WHAT PASSES, AND FOR HOW LONG (7, 8).

steps.title: The three functions
points: a bill of lading is issued by or on behalf of the carrier to the shipper when goods are received for shipment or shipped on board
RECEIPT - it acknowledges the stated goods, marks and numbers, in the APPARENT ORDER AND CONDITION stated on its face; this is the function the ship controls
EVIDENCE OF THE CONTRACT OF CARRIAGE - it records the terms on which the goods are carried
the precision that earns the mark: where a charterparty exists, the charterparty is the contract between owner and charterer and the bill is only EVIDENCE of it
but in the hands of a third party who is not the charterer, THE BILL IS THE CONTRACT on which that holder sues
DOCUMENT OF TITLE - where made out 'to order' it is transferable by endorsement and delivery, and goods are delivered only against surrender of an original
this is what allows cargo to be sold afloat and financed by documentary credit

steps.title: The types worth naming, and the law that governs
points: shipped (on board) against received for shipment - only the shipped bill certifies the goods are aboard, and letters of credit normally demand it
clean against claused or foul - a clean bill carries no notation of defective condition, and a claused bill is normally unacceptable under a letter of credit
order against straight against bearer - only the order bill is freely negotiable by endorsement
bill of lading against SEA WAYBILL - a waybill is NOT a document of title and goods are delivered against identification
charterparty bill against liner bill - the charterparty bill incorporates a named charterparty, which is what limb b) turns on
governing law: the Hague-Visby Rules, given effect in India by the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993
transfer of rights under the bill: the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856, the statute in force at this sitting
the ship herself operates under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958

steps.title: The precautions that apply under any charter
points: the master signs and WHAT HE SIGNS BINDS THE OWNER
sign only for what is actually on board - compare against the mate's receipts and the ship's own tally, ullage or draught survey
CARRY THE CLAUSING ACROSS - any remark on the mate's receipt must appear on the bill; a claused receipt and a clean bill is the classic loss
NEVER sign a clean bill for cargo not in apparent good order and condition, and NEVER accept a letter of indemnity in exchange for one
such an indemnity is unenforceable against the party it deceives and a knowingly false bill prejudices the owner's P&I cover; clause the bill and refer to owners
quantity - sign for the ship's figures or qualify the shipper's figure; never adopt an unchecked shore figure as though checked
DATE IT CORRECTLY - the date loading completed; ante-dating or post-dating is fraud and voids cover
check description, marks and numbers, load and discharge ports, consignee and notify party, and freight terms; do not certify 'freight prepaid' unless authorised
account for the number of originals issued, and that delivery is against surrender of one original
deck cargo must be stated as carried on deck, and never sign for cargo not shipped
check the authority to sign - written authority where an agent signs, expressed as for and on behalf of the master

steps.title: Under a VOYAGE charter - protect the incorporation and the lien
points: the owner keeps the ship and is paid FREIGHT; the bill will reach a receiver who has never seen the charterparty
the risk is the owner being bound to a stranger on terms wider than the charter he agreed
confirm the INCORPORATION CLAUSE and that it identifies the charterparty BY ITS DATE - an incorporation clause with no date is a standing defect
confirm the owner's LIEN on cargo for freight, deadfreight and demurrage survives through the bill
confirm the Paramount Clause so the applicable regime, its defences and its limits apply
check the cargo quantity against the charter minimum and maximum, the deadweight and the deadfreight position
accept no term inconsistent with the charter - a different discharge port, a different cargo description, or freight prepaid where freight is unpaid
refer anything unusual to owners before signing

steps.title: Under a TIME charter - signing as presented, and the indemnity
points: the CHARTERER directs employment and normally presents the bills, and the employment clause obliges the master to sign AS PRESENTED
THAT OBLIGATION IS NOT UNLIMITED - it does not extend to a bill inconsistent with the mate's receipts, false, misdated, or imposing liability materially beyond the charter
where the charterer or his agents sign on the master's behalf, obtain WRITTEN AUTHORITY limited to signing in conformity with mate's receipts
the employment and indemnity clause protects a master who acted PROPERLY; it is not a licence to sign anything
check incorporation and the Paramount Clause as under a voyage charter
SWITCH BILLS and delivery without production of an original against a letter of indemnity are the two demands that arrive most often - both go to owners and P&I before anything is signed
freight is not the ship's concern here, the owner being paid hire; the lien question is different and the charterer's freight arrangements are not certified by the ship

steps.title: What the on-hire survey is for, and the common core
points: it fixes the condition of the ship and the quantities on board AT THE MOMENT RESPONSIBILITY CHANGES HANDS
so that a dispute months or years later is settled against a record rather than against recollection
it is a COMMERCIAL survey between the parties - not a class or statutory survey, and it credits nothing
common to all three: date and time of delivery, bunkers remaining on board by grade and quantity, fresh water and lubricating oils
hold and tank condition, hatch cover condition, cargo gear, existing damage recorded and photographed, and the certificates on board
what differs is WHAT THE SURVEY HAS TO PROTECT AND FOR HOW LONG

steps.title: The three differentiated
points: BAREBOAT - possession and control pass; the charterer mans, operates, maintains, insures and drydocks the ship as if owner, for YEARS

bareboat survey: full machinery condition survey, class survey status and outstanding conditions of class, thickness measurements, docking and survey due dates, coatings, and an ITEM-BY-ITEM inventory of spares, stores, tools, plans, manuals and publications
VOYAGE - nothing passes; the owner keeps the ship and is paid freight to carry a cargo
voyage survey: cargo-worthiness for THIS cargo - hold or tank cleanliness and previous cargo, hatch cover weathertightness testing, cargo gear, draught survey, certificates needed for this voyage
TIME - the employment of the ship passes for a period; the owner keeps crewing and maintenance, the charterer pays hire and bunkers

time charter survey: bunkers by grade and quantity as the central figure, cargo spaces clean and ready for the intended trade, cargo gear and its test certification, defects recorded, and the SPEED AND CONSUMPTION BASELINE against the description warranties
attendance and duration scale the same way - bareboat days with joint independent surveyors and often class, time charter a day or so jointly, voyage often hours with a single cargo surveyor
bareboat and time charter each have a MIRROR off-hire survey at redelivery; the voyage charter has none

THE TERMINOLOGY POINT - strictly a voyage charter attracts no ON-HIRE survey at all, because no hire is paid and the ship is never delivered; what is done is a pre-loading condition and cargo-worthiness survey

steps.title: The bareboat survey - and the reasons
points: THE BARE-BOAT DELIVERY SURVEY, BY A WIDE MARGIN - days of work, and the consequences carried for the whole charter
it is the only one where the WHOLE SHIP changes hands - possession passes and the charterer becomes responsible for manning, operating, maintaining, insuring and drydocking
it is the only baseline that has to survive YEARS - redelivery is in like condition, fair wear and tear excepted, and 'like condition' can only be argued against what was written at delivery

its scope is the entire technical inventory - machinery condition and running hours, performance data, class survey status and every outstanding condition of class, thickness measurements, docking and survey due dates, coatings, and a spares, stores, tools, plans and publications inventory item by item
NO OTHER SURVEY OPENS THE STORE ROOMS
the contentious parts are the ENGINEER'S parts - machinery condition, running hours since overhaul and what spares were aboard, which only the Chief Engineer can properly record

the consequences reach beyond the charter - change of flag, manager and insurers, and bareboat registration or finance arrangements, so errors propagate into insurance, mortgage and registration questions
and nothing in it can be repeated - the ship sails, the crew changes, and the moment cannot be re-created
THE RANKING: bareboat first, time charter second because it is joint and establishes bunkers, readiness and the performance baseline but is bounded by the period, voyage third and narrowest
THE PRINCIPLE BEHIND THE RANKING - the depth of a delivery survey is set by how much responsibility passes and for how long

quick_revision.recall_15s: Bill of lading = RECEIPT, EVIDENCE of the contract of carriage, DOCUMENT OF TITLE. Between owner and charterer the charterparty is the contract and the bill is evidence; in a third party's hands the bill IS the contract. Order bills are negotiable by endorsement; a sea waybill is not a document of title. Law: Hague-Visby, through the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended 1993; transfer of rights under the Bills of Lading Act, 1856; ship under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. Before signing anything: quantity against mate's receipts, clausing carried across, correct date = date loading completed, particulars, originals accounted for, authority to sign. Never a clean bill for damaged cargo and never an LOI for one — unenforceable, and it prejudices P&I cover. Voyage charter: incorporation clause naming the charterparty by date, and the lien for freight, deadfreight and demurrage preserved. Time charter: sign as presented — but not if false, misdated or inconsistent with the mate's receipts; written authority where agents sign; switch bills and delivery without an original go to owners and P&I. On-hire survey fixes condition and quantities when responsibility changes hands; it is commercial, not class. Bareboat — everything passes, for years: machinery, class status, item-by-item inventory. Time — employment for a period: bunkers, readiness, speed-and-consumption baseline. Voyage — nothing passes: cargo-worthiness for one cargo. Most demanding: bareboat, because depth follows how much passes and for how long.
keywords: Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925
critical_numbers: Three functions of a bill of lading: receipt, evidence of the contract of carriage, document of title
The bill of lading date is the date LOADING COMPLETED - no other date is permissible
Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993 - the Indian statute giving effect to the Hague-Visby Rules
Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 - the Act in force at this November 2023 sitting
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 - the governing Indian shipping statute at this sitting
Three charter types, three survey depths: bareboat (years, everything), time charter (a period, employment), voyage charter (one voyage, nothing)
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Carriage under a bill of lading is governed by the Hague-Visby Rules, given effect in India by the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993, and applied to a particular bill through its Paramount Clause. Transfer of rights under the bill is governed at this sitting by the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856, and the ship operates under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. None of these instruments is quoted in this answer and no article, rule or section is attributed a sub-paragraph.
quick_revision.major_trap: Signing a clean bill of lading for cargo that is not in apparent good order and condition, in reliance on a letter of indemnity. The indemnity is unenforceable against the party it deceives — the receiver or bank who relied on the clean bill — and issuing a bill the master knows to be false prejudices the owner's P&I cover, so the owner carries the liability with no insurance behind it. The same applies to ante-dating to catch a letter of credit expiry. The correct action is always to clause the bill to match the mate's receipt and refer to owners and the club. The second trap, in limb (c), is forgetting that a voyage charter involves no hire and no delivery, so it attracts no on-hire survey properly so called.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the three functions of a bill of lading.
retrieval_cards.answer: A receipt for the goods received or shipped, stating quantity, marks and apparent order and condition. Evidence of the contract of carriage. And a document of title, transferable by endorsement and delivery where made out to order, against surrender of which the goods are delivered.
retrieval_cards.why: Four marks, three functions - it is the whole of limb (a) and the most reliably examined item in the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is a bill of lading the contract of carriage?
retrieval_cards.answer: As between owner and charterer, no - the charterparty is the contract and the bill is evidence of it. But in the hands of a third-party holder who is not the charterer, the bill of lading contains or evidences the contract on which that holder sues, so for him it operates as the contract.
retrieval_cards.why: The distinction is the difference between a correct answer and a nearly correct one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The shipper wants a clean bill for rust-stained steel and offers a letter of indemnity. What do you do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Clause the bill to match the mate's receipt, refuse the letter of indemnity, and refer to owners and the P&I club. The indemnity is unenforceable against the receiver or bank it deceives, and issuing a bill known to be false prejudices the owner's cover - so the owner is left with the liability and no insurance.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the single most examinable point in limb (b) and it is a real commercial pressure at the loading berth.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What date goes on a bill of lading, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: The date on which loading was completed. Ante-dating or post-dating - typically to catch a letter of credit expiry or a laycan - is fraud, however routine it is made to sound, and it voids the owner's P&I cover.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the most common commercial pressure put on a master and the least defensible thing to give way on.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must you check before signing under a VOYAGE charter that you would not check under a time charter?
retrieval_cards.answer: That the bill incorporates the charterparty and identifies it BY ITS DATE, and that the owner's lien on cargo for freight, deadfreight and demurrage survives through the bill. Under a voyage charter the owner is paid freight and the lien is his only security for it; under a time charter he is paid hire and the freight arrangements are not the ship's concern.
retrieval_cards.why: The incorporation-and-lien pair is what makes the voyage half of limb (b) specific rather than generic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Under a time charter, must the master sign whatever bill the charterer presents?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The employment clause obliges him to sign as presented, but that obligation does not extend to a bill that is false, misdated, inconsistent with the mate's receipts, or that would impose on the owner a liability materially beyond the charter. The employment and indemnity clause protects a master who acted properly; it is not a licence.
retrieval_cards.why: The limits of 'as presented' are exactly where the marks are in the time charter half of limb (b).

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is an on-hire survey, and what is it NOT?
retrieval_cards.answer: A commercial survey between the parties that fixes the condition of the ship and the quantities on board at the moment responsibility changes hands, so a later dispute is settled against a record. It is NOT a class or statutory survey and it credits nothing against any survey cycle.
retrieval_cards.why: Confusing the commercial delivery survey with the class survey regime is the structural error in limb (c) - and Q1 on this same paper is the other one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Differentiate the on-hire survey under bareboat, time and voyage charter in one line each.
retrieval_cards.answer: Bareboat - possession passes for years, so the survey is a full asset baseline: machinery condition and running hours, class survey status and outstanding conditions, thickness measurements, coatings, and an item-by-item inventory of spares, stores, tools and publications. Time charter - employment passes for a period, so the survey establishes bunkers by grade and quantity, cargo readiness for the intended trade, and the speed-and-consumption baseline. Voyage charter - nothing passes, so what is done is a pre-loading cargo-worthiness survey for one cargo.
retrieval_cards.why: Differentiate means compare; three one-line contrasts beat three paragraphs of description.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who is on hire under a voyage charter?
retrieval_cards.answer: Nobody. The owner is paid freight for carrying a cargo and the ship is never delivered into anyone's service, so there is no on-hire survey properly so called. What is carried out is a pre-loading condition and cargo-worthiness survey - hold or tank cleanliness against the previous cargo, hatch cover weathertightness, cargo gear and a draught survey.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the trap buried inside limb (c), and naming it is itself worth a mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which delivery survey is the most demanding, and what principle decides it?
retrieval_cards.answer: The bareboat delivery survey. It is the only one where possession of the whole ship passes, the only baseline that must survive years to a redelivery in like condition fair wear and tear excepted, the only one covering machinery condition, class survey status and an item-by-item inventory, and the only one whose errors reach into insurance, mortgage and registration. The principle: the depth of a delivery survey is set by how much responsibility passes and for how long.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (d) says 'explain with reasons' - the principle is what turns six reasons into an argument.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which instruments govern a bill of lading in India at this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Hague-Visby Rules, given effect by the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993; the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 for transfer of rights under the bill; and the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 as the governing shipping statute. All three are the instruments in force in November 2023.
retrieval_cards.why: The Indian layer is where an answer inherited from a later sitting would silently update two statutes and falsify the paper.
