questions.subpart_marks_note: All three limbs print their own mark figure. Limb a) prints "responding to and preventing oil pollution incidents" - OPRC is a preparedness, response and co-operation instrument and is expressly NOT a prevention convention, prevention being MARPOL's work. The stem is preserved exactly as printed; the answer gives the limb what it asks and states the boundary once, explaining the sense in which preparedness does reduce the consequences of an incident.
questions.recurrence_adjudication: The host prints a single self-referential annotation and claims no earlier sitting. MIW's own canonical position is that QP2504-Q4 sets substantially the same examiner task seventeen months later, which the host does not and could not know.
decomposition: What OPRC is - its full title, its dates, and the casualty that produced it
Its objectives, which are the three nouns of its own title, and the two things it deliberately is not
The key provisions, article by article, as the architecture a Party has to build
The prevention question the printed limb raises, answered honestly rather than dodged
The role of a Member State - and the precision that OPRC binds PARTIES, of which the ship's flag State is only one capacity
The State's duties separated into its flag, coastal and international capacities, because the limb asks about the State as a whole and not only as flag State
The challenges of implementation, analysed rather than listed, because the limb prints 'analyse'
The two document sets - what a Member State maintains, and what the ship carries - and the fact that the shipboard duty is actually delivered by MARPOL
reuse_evidence: NEAR RECURRENCE. QP2504-Q4 (April 2025, +17 months) sets substantially the same examiner task: the purpose and objectives of the OPRC Convention, the responsibilities of a State under it, and the documents required to be carried on board. BOTH PRINTED STEMS WERE READ IN FULL BEFORE THE DONOR WAS ACCEPTED. Its route was taken and its verified reading of MARPOL Annex I regulation 37 was re-used.

THE DELTA IS SUBSTANTIAL AND RUNS IN THREE DIRECTIONS. First, the donor is printed as ONE unlimbed 16-mark block; this paper prints THREE limbs at 6, 6 and 4. Second, the donor asks for the responsibilities of the FLAG STATE and expressly excludes the article 6 national system as being owed in the coastal capacity; THIS PAPER ASKS ABOUT MEMBER STATES, which pulls the article 6 national system back INTO scope and makes it the centre of limb b) rather than an excluded aside. Third, this paper sets a CHALLENGES task and a MEMBER STATE DOCUMENTS task that the donor does not set at all, and both are authored fresh.

THE DONOR IS SEVENTEEN MONTHS LATER AND ITS CURRENCY NOTE IS REVERSED. QP2504-Q4 carries a B_CURRENCY_CHECK flag on MEPC.384(81), the amendment to MARPOL Protocol I which regulation 37.2.1 cross-refers to, recorded there as adopted but not yet in force. At THIS sitting MEPC.384(81) DOES NOT YET EXIST - it is an MEPC 81 output of 2024, five months future - so the note is dropped entirely rather than merely re-stated. No inherited sitting-relative prose survives.
questions.question_delta: The donor prints one unlimbed 16-mark block asking for purpose and objectives, FLAG STATE responsibilities, and documents carried on board. This paper prints three limbs at 6+6+4 and changes the subject of the second task from the flag State to MEMBER STATES, which brings the article 6 national system - contingency plan, competent national authority, operational contact point, pre-positioned equipment, exercises and training - from being expressly excluded in the donor to being the centre of the limb here. It also adds an IMPLEMENTATION CHALLENGES task, which the donor does not set, and extends the document task from documents carried on board to documents maintained by MEMBER STATES AND on board. Limb a) additionally prints 'responding to and preventing', which the donor does not, and which requires the prevention boundary to be stated rather than assumed. The donor's MEPC.384(81) currency note is future at this sitting and is dropped.
questions.verification_status: MIXED PROVENANCE, DECLARED, AND THE SPLIT RESTS ON A VERIFIED READING RATHER THAN ON AN ASSUMPTION. The shipboard document limb is P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED. MARPOL Annex I as revised is held in the True Source corpus with a full extractable text layer as resolution MEPC.117(52), and regulation 37 was read from it in full for QP2504-Q4: the 150 GT oil tanker and 400 GT other-ship thresholds, approval by the Administration, preparation on Organization guidelines and in the working language of the master and officers, the four mandatory contents at 37.2.1 to 37.2.4 with the words 'at least', the combination rule with the Annex II regulation 17 plan at 37.3 and the resulting title, and the shore-based damage stability access requirement for oil tankers of 5,000 tons deadweight or more at 37.4. That reading is re-used here and was re-checked against the record of it; it is not re-quoted from an unverified source. THE OPRC CONVENTION ITSELF IS NOT HELD. Its adoption and entry-into-force dates, its article structure and the substance of articles 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 12 are carried at AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY level, as is the OPRC-HNS Protocol 2000. No article of OPRC is quoted verbatim anywhere in this answer and no article is attributed a sub-paragraph. The implementation-challenges analysis in limb b) is ENGINEERING AND POLICY JUDGEMENT, attributed as such: no compliance statistic, party count or national capability assessment is asserted. The Indian national system is described in OUTLINE ONLY, as the shape an article 6 system takes, because no Indian contingency-plan instrument or DG Shipping circular is held.
sources: PRIMARY: MARPOL Annex I regulation 37.1, from the held official text of resolution MEPC.117(52) - every oil tanker of 150 gross tonnage and above and every ship other than an oil tanker of 400 gross tonnage and above shall carry on board a shipboard oil pollution emergency plan approved by the Administration.

PRIMARY: MARPOL Annex I regulation 37.2 - the plan shall be prepared based on guidelines developed by the Organization and written in the working language of the master and officers, and shall consist AT LEAST of four items.

PRIMARY: MARPOL Annex I regulation 37.2.1 to 37.2.4 - the reporting procedure required by article 8 and Protocol I; the list of authorities or persons to be contacted; the detailed description of immediate action by persons on board; and the procedures and point of contact for co-ordinating shipboard action with national and local authorities.
PRIMARY: MARPOL Annex I regulation 37.3 - where Annex II regulation 17 also applies the plan may be combined, and the combined plan is titled 'Shipboard marine pollution emergency plan'.

PRIMARY: MARPOL Annex I regulation 37.4 - all oil tankers of 5,000 tons deadweight or more shall have prompt access to computerized, shore-based damage stability and residual structural strength calculation programs.

PRIMARY (identity and status): the corpus amendment register records only two MARPOL Annex I amendments beyond the held base - MEPC.359(79), in force 1 May 2024, and MEPC.384(81), an MEPC 81 output of 2024. BOTH ARE FUTURE AT THIS SITTING and neither touches regulation 37.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: the International Convention on Oil Pollution Preparedness, Response and Co-operation was adopted on 30 November 1990 and entered into force on 13 May 1995, following the Exxon Valdez grounding of 1989 which exposed the absence of any international framework for co-ordinated response.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: OPRC article 3 requires each Party to require ships flying its flag to have on board an oil pollution emergency plan as required by and in accordance with provisions adopted by the Organization, with parallel requirements for offshore units, sea ports and oil handling facilities under its jurisdiction.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: OPRC article 4 requires reporting without delay of any event involving a discharge or probable discharge of oil, to the nearest coastal State; article 5 governs assessment and notification of States whose interests are affected, together with the Organization.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: OPRC article 6 requires each Party to establish a national system for responding promptly and effectively, including a national contingency plan and a designated competent national authority and operational contact point, and within its capabilities a minimum level of pre-positioned response equipment, a programme of exercises and training, and detailed plans and communication capabilities.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: OPRC articles 7 to 10 provide for co-operation in response on request, research and development, technical co-operation with developing countries, and the promotion of bilateral and multilateral agreements; article 12 places the institutional and information-clearing role with IMO.
AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: the OPRC-HNS Protocol, 2000 extends the same preparedness, response and co-operation architecture to hazardous and noxious substances.

CONTEXT: UNCLOS article 199 obliges States to develop and promote contingency plans for responding to pollution incidents; article 194 is the general obligation on which the response architecture rests.

ENGINEERING AND POLICY JUDGEMENT: the implementation-challenges analysis in limb b) - resource asymmetry, the gap between a plan on paper and a rehearsed capability, equipment obsolescence and stockpile geography, customs and immigration friction on cross-border assistance, inter-agency co-ordination, funding and cost recovery, training and turnover, and the difficulty of exercising at realistic scale.

No article of OPRC is quoted verbatim in this answer and no article is attributed a sub-paragraph, because that precision cannot be sourced from a held text. The corpus should acquire the Convention and the OPRC-HNS Protocol.
The number of Parties to OPRC and to the OPRC-HNS Protocol is not stated. Those figures change and no held source records them.

No compliance statistic, national capability assessment or comparative implementation study is cited in limb b). The challenges analysed are structural and are offered as reasoned judgement, not as findings.

The Indian implementation - the national oil spill disaster contingency plan and the role of the Indian Coast Guard as the designated response authority - is described in OUTLINE ONLY, as the shape an article 6 national system takes. No Indian contingency-plan instrument and no DG Shipping circular is held by the corpus, so no provision of either is cited.

The IMO guidelines for the development of shipboard oil pollution emergency plans, which regulation 37.2 requires the plan to be based on, are not held. They are named as the basis the regulation names and none of their content is asserted.

No response equipment specification, stockpile quantity or tier-response threshold is quoted. Tiered response classification is industry practice rather than a Convention requirement and no held source records it.

The list of documents a Member State maintains is derived from what articles 3, 5, 6, 7, 10 and 12 require a Party to establish and communicate. It is NOT a schedule printed in the Convention, and the answer says so rather than presenting it as one.

blocks.h: (a) Key provisions and objectives, and the significance of the Convention
1. What OPRC is, and what it deliberately is not

blocks.p: The International Convention on Oil Pollution Preparedness, Response and Co-operation, 1990 was adopted on 30 November 1990 and entered into force on 13 May 1995. It was developed after the Exxon Valdez grounding of 1989, which showed that even a well-resourced State could be overwhelmed by a major spill and that there was no framework for asking anyone else for help.

It is a framework convention. It sets no discharge standard and prescribes no construction requirement. It obliges its Parties to build and maintain a capability — plans, authorities, equipment, exercises — and to make that capability available to one another. Its architecture was extended to chemicals by the OPRC-HNS Protocol, 2000.
The objectives are the three nouns of its own title:

ol: Preparedness — plans, designated authorities, pre-positioned equipment, trained people and rehearsed procedures existing before the incident.
Response — the ability to act promptly and effectively, through a known chain of command and known contact points.
Co-operation — that States assist one another, with the legal and administrative friction that delays cross-border assistance removed in advance.

blocks.h: 2. The key provisions, article by article

blocks.p: The substantive articles hold as a sequence — plan, report, react, build, share:

rows: 3 — emergency plans

Each Party requires ships flying its flag to carry an oil pollution emergency plan in accordance with provisions adopted by the Organization, with parallel requirements on offshore units, sea ports and oil handling facilities under its jurisdiction
4 — reporting
Masters and persons in charge report without delay any event involving a discharge or probable discharge of oil, to the nearest coastal State
5 — action on a report
The Party receiving it assesses the incident and notifies all States whose interests may be affected, together with the Organization
6 — national and regional systems

The core building obligation. A national contingency plan, a designated competent national authority and an operational contact point; and within the Party's capabilities a minimum level of pre-positioned response equipment, a programme of exercises and training, and detailed plans and communications capability
7 — co-operation in response
Advisory services, technical support and equipment on request, subject to capabilities and resources
Research and development; technical co-operation with developing countries; and the promotion of bilateral and multilateral agreements, from which regional arrangements grow
The institutional role — information services, education and training, and technical services placed with IMO

blocks.h: 3. Significance - in response, and in the sense in which it touches prevention

blocks.p: In response, its significance is direct. Before OPRC, a coastal State facing a major spill had no reliable mechanism to obtain foreign equipment or expertise, no agreed reporting route, and often no single authority in charge of its own response. OPRC supplies all three. Its real achievement is institutional: it converted oil spill response from an improvised national reaction into a standing, funded, exercised system with a named authority and a contact point that answers at three in the morning.

The limb also says “preventing”, and that deserves an honest answer rather than a silent one. Strictly, OPRC is not a prevention convention: preventing pollution — discharge limits, oil filtering equipment, segregated ballast, double hulls — is MARPOL's work, and liability and compensation belong to the CLC, FUND and Bunkers regime. OPRC begins where prevention has already failed. But it contributes to prevention in three real and defensible ways:

ul: It prevents escalation. The quantity of oil that reaches the shoreline is decided in the first hours, and preparedness is what shortens them. A spill contained at source is a spill that never becomes a pollution incident in any meaningful sense.
Reporting is preventive. Article 4 requires reporting of a probable discharge as well as an actual one — so the machinery is engaged before oil is in the water.

Preparedness disciplines operations. The exercises, the drills and the plan required by article 6 and by the shipboard plan raise awareness and expose weaknesses in bunkering and transfer procedures, which is where most operational spills begin.

blocks.p: Set beside its neighbours, the division of labour is clean: MARPOL prevents, OPRC prepares and responds, and CLC, FUND and Bunkers compensate. Above all of them, UNCLOS article 199 obliges States to develop and promote contingency plans for responding to pollution incidents, and OPRC is how that obligation was given operational content.

blocks.h: (b) The role of Member States, and the challenges of implementation
4. The role - and a point of precision first

blocks.p: OPRC binds Parties, not ships. A State's obligations arise in three different capacities, and an answer that runs them together loses the analysis the limb asks for. (Strictly, the Convention speaks of Parties rather than Member States: a State is a Member of IMO, and a Party to OPRC, and the two sets are not identical.)

rows: As flag State

Require ships flying its flag to carry the plan (art 3); approve it, through MARPOL Annex I reg 37.1; require reporting without delay (art 4); ensure the plan is usable in the working language of the master and officers; survey, inspect and enforce; ensure crews are drilled on it
As coastal and territorial State

The article 6 national system — the national contingency plan, the competent national authority, the operational contact point, the pre-positioned equipment, the exercise and training programme; and the article 5 duty to assess a report and notify affected States and IMO. It also imposes the plan requirement on offshore units, sea ports and oil handling facilities under its jurisdiction
As a member of the international community

Co-operate on request (art 7); take part in research and development and technical co-operation (arts 8 and 9); conclude bilateral and regional agreements (art 10); and support IMO's clearing-house role (art 12)
Domestically

Give the Convention force in national law — in India, at this sitting, through the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and the rules made under it, with a national oil spill contingency plan and a designated response authority answering to the shape article 6 requires

blocks.p: The analytical point: the question asks about Member States and not only about flag States, which means the article 6 national system is squarely in scope. That is the heaviest obligation in the Convention and the one that costs money every year whether or not there is a spill.

ol: Resource asymmetry. Article 6 obliges a Party to build capability “within its capabilities”. That qualification is what made the Convention ratifiable, and it is also its central weakness: the obligation is genuine but elastic, and a developing coastal State with a long shoreline and a small budget may comply in form while lacking any real Tier 2 capability. Articles 9 and 10 — technical co-operation and regional agreements — exist precisely to bridge that gap, and their success is uneven.

Plans on paper against rehearsed capability. A national contingency plan is cheap to write and expensive to exercise. The gap only becomes visible during an incident, which is the worst moment to discover it. Exercising at realistic scale — multi-agency, at night, in weather — is rare because it is disruptive and costly.

Inter-agency co-ordination. A national response typically involves the maritime administration, the coastguard or navy, the environment ministry, port authorities, customs, fisheries and local government. The single competent national authority required by article 6 has to have real authority over all of them, and in many States it has influence rather than command.

Equipment: obsolescence and geography. Booms, skimmers and dispersant stocks degrade, need maintenance and periodic replacement, and must be positioned where the risk is. A national stockpile a thousand miles from the casualty is a line in a plan, not a capability. Dispersant approval regimes also differ between States, which complicates assistance.

Friction on cross-border assistance. This is the challenge OPRC was written to solve and the one that keeps recurring: customs clearance for equipment, immigration for response personnel, liability and indemnity for the assisting State, and cost recovery. Unless these are pre-agreed in bilateral or regional arrangements, help arrives after it would have mattered.

Funding and cost recovery. Preparedness is a standing cost with no visible return in the years when nothing happens, so it is politically easy to defer. Recovering response costs afterwards depends on the separate CLC and FUND regime and on the polluter being identified and solvent.

Training, retention and turnover. Competence decays. Trained responders move on; contact lists go stale; the person named in the plan retired two years ago. Currency of the plan is itself a continuing obligation, not a one-off act.

Reporting quality at the sharp end. Article 4's duty is only as good as what actually reaches the coastal State, and reporting is often delayed by uncertainty aboard, by fear of consequences or by unclear contact routes — which is exactly why the shipboard plan must carry a procedure and a contact list, and why they must be current.

Scope creep and modern spill types. The Convention was written for persistent crude in the era of the very large tanker. Non-tanker bunker spills, container-ship casualties and lost-container incidents now form a large share of real events, and OPRC's architecture must be stretched to cover them — part of why the OPRC-HNS Protocol was needed.

blocks.p: The analysis in one sentence: OPRC's obligations are almost all institutional and continuing rather than technical and one-off, and institutional obligations are the kind that decay quietly. The Convention's real implementation problem is not knowing what to do; it is sustaining a capability nobody wants to pay for in the years when it is not needed.
These are derived from what articles 3, 5, 6, 7, 10 and 12 require a Party to establish and communicate. The Convention does not print them as a schedule, and it is honest to say so:

ul: The National Oil Spill Contingency Plan — the central article 6 document.
The record of the designated competent national authority and the operational contact point, kept current and communicated to IMO.
The inventory of pre-positioned response equipment, with its location, condition and maintenance record.
The exercise and training programme and its records.
Bilateral and regional agreements concluded under article 10.
Reports and notifications to IMO and to affected States under articles 5 and 12, and the national reporting arrangements that support them.
The national legislation and rules giving the Convention effect — in India, the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and the rules made under it.

blocks.h: 7. What the ship carries - and why it comes out of MARPOL

blocks.p: The operative document is the Shipboard Oil Pollution Emergency Plan (SOPEP). OPRC article 3 requires the Party to require it; the detail is supplied by MARPOL Annex I regulation 37. That is the single most important structural fact in this question.

ul: Regulation 37.1 — every oil tanker of 150 gross tonnage and above, and every ship other than an oil tanker of 400 gross tonnage and above, shall carry a shipboard oil pollution emergency plan approved by the Administration. The two thresholds differ and the tanker threshold is the lower.

Regulation 37.2 — prepared on guidelines developed by the Organization, written in the working language of the master and officers, and containing “at least” four things: the reporting procedure (37.2.1, referring to MARPOL article 8 and Protocol I); the list of authorities or persons to be contacted (37.2.2); a detailed description of immediate action by persons on board (37.2.3); and the procedures and point of contact for co-ordinating shipboard action with national and local authorities (37.2.4). “At least” makes the list a floor, not a ceiling.

Regulation 37.3 — where Annex II regulation 17 also applies, the plan may be combined, and the combined plan is titled “Shipboard marine pollution emergency plan” — the SMPEP. This is why a chemical tanker carries an SMPEP and not a SOPEP.
Regulation 37.4 — all oil tankers of 5,000 tons deadweight or more shall have prompt access to computerized, shore-based damage stability and residual structural strength calculation programs.

blocks.p: Kept with the plan, and correctly labelled as belonging to other instruments: the coastal State contact list maintained current as part of the plan; the Oil Record Book Part I, and Part II for tankers, under Annex I regulation 17; and the IOPP Certificate and its Supplement. Listing these is fine; listing them as OPRC documents is not.

The closing point that shows the two instruments have been read together: OPRC binds States; MARPOL Annex I regulation 37 binds the ship. A single document in the wheelhouse discharges an obligation created in one convention and specified in another, and it is enforced through MARPOL's machinery — verified at statutory survey, and checked by a port State control officer — because OPRC itself gives nobody any power over a ship.

The marks are printed 6 + 6 + 4 and the shape follows them. Limb (a) prints “Briefly”, so identity and objectives are short and the article-by-article provisions go in a table — seven rows an examiner can scan in fifteen seconds rather than a page of prose. Limb (b) prints “analyse”, which is a different instruction from “list”: the role goes in a four-row capacity table, and the challenges are given as numbered items each with its reason, closing on a single sentence that says what the challenges have in common. Limb (c) prints “enlist”, which asks for lists, and it has two of them because the limb names two holders — Member States and ships.

The highest-value paragraph in the answer is the last one, and it is worth writing even under time pressure: OPRC binds States, MARPOL Annex I regulation 37 binds the ship. It is what explains why limb (c)'s shipboard half is answered out of a different convention from the one the question names.

blocks.h: The printed word 'preventing', and how to handle it

blocks.p: Limb (a) asks about the Convention's significance in “responding to and preventing oil pollution incidents”. OPRC is not a prevention convention — that is MARPOL — and the stem is preserved as printed rather than corrected.

The wrong responses are to ignore the word, or to write a paragraph on double hulls. The right response is the one that earns marks in both directions: state the boundary, then give three defensible senses in which preparedness is preventive — it prevents escalation, because the quantity reaching the shoreline is decided in the first hours; article 4's reporting duty covers a probable discharge and so engages before oil is in the water; and the plans, drills and exercises discipline the operations, principally bunkering and transfer, where most operational spills begin.

This is a general technique worth carrying into other questions: where a stem contains a term the instrument does not actually support, name the boundary once and then answer generously within it. Never silently ignore a printed word.

blocks.h: Three conventions, one incident, three questions

rows: MARPOL
How do we stop it happening?
Before — construction, equipment, discharge standards
OPRC
Is anyone ready, and can they help each other?
Before and during — plans, authorities, equipment, response
CLC / FUND / Bunkers
Who pays?
After — liability and compensation

blocks.h: Member State, not flag State - and why that changes the answer

blocks.p: This is the most important difference between this question and every other OPRC question. A question about the flag State's duties excludes the article 6 national system, because the contingency plan, the pre-positioned equipment and the national response organisation are owed by the State in its territorial and coastal capacity, not because it registers ships.

This question asks about Member States, so article 6 is squarely in scope — and it is the centre of the limb. It is the heaviest obligation in the Convention and the one that costs money every year whether or not there is a spill. A candidate who answers this limb as though it were a flag State question has left out the most substantial thing the Convention requires.
One further precision, worth a line: the Convention speaks of Parties, not Member States. A State is a Member of IMO and a Party to OPRC, and the two sets are not identical.

ul: Describing OPRC as a pollution prevention convention without qualification — or, at the other extreme, refusing to engage with the printed word “preventing” at all.
Bringing liability, limitation or compensation into it. That is CLC, FUND and Bunkers.
Saying OPRC directly requires ships to carry a SOPEP. It requires Parties to require it; MARPOL Annex I regulation 37 imposes it on the ship.
Answering limb (b) as a flag State question and omitting the article 6 national system.
Listing challenges in limb (b) when the verb is analyse — each challenge needs its reason.
Giving one tonnage threshold for both tankers and other ships. It is 150 for tankers, 400 for others.
Omitting the approval requirement or the working-language requirement.
Treating the four SOPEP contents as exhaustive when regulation 37.2 says at least.
Calling a combined plan a SOPEP — it is retitled SMPEP.
Listing the Oil Record Book, IOPP Certificate and Garbage Management Plan as OPRC documents without labelling their real source.
Missing regulation 37.4 entirely.
In limb (c), giving only the shipboard list when the limb expressly names Member States and ships.
“When was OPRC adopted and when did it enter into force?” Adopted 30 November 1990; in force 13 May 1995.
“Which casualty led to it?” The Exxon Valdez grounding of 1989.
“Does OPRC prevent pollution?” Not directly — prevention is MARPOL. It prevents escalation, requires reporting of a probable discharge, and disciplines operations through drills.
“Which article is the heaviest obligation?” Article 6 — the national system. And it is owed in the coastal capacity, not the flag capacity.

“Name three things article 6 requires.” A national contingency plan; a competent national authority and operational contact point; a minimum level of pre-positioned equipment with exercises and training.
“Your ship is 380 GT and not a tanker. Does it need a SOPEP?” No — regulation 37.1 catches other ships at 400 GT and above. A 380 GT oil tanker would, because the tanker threshold is 150 GT.
“Who approves the SOPEP?” The Administration.
“What language must it be in?” The working language of the master and officers.
“Name the four things the plan must contain.” Reporting procedure; contact list; immediate action description; shipboard co-ordination procedures and point of contact.
“Your chemical tanker has one combined plan. What is it called?” A Shipboard marine pollution emergency plan — regulation 37.3 fixes the title.
“What extra does a 30,000 dwt tanker need?” Prompt access to computerized shore-based damage stability and residual structural strength calculation programs — the 5,000 dwt threshold at 37.4.
“Whom does the master report to after a spill?” Under article 4, without delay to the nearest coastal State.
“What is the single biggest obstacle to cross-border assistance?” Administrative friction — customs for equipment, immigration for people, and liability and cost recovery for the assisting State.
What do the letters OPRC stand for? Oil Pollution Preparedness, Response and Co-operation.
Which article requires the emergency plan? Article 3.
Which article requires reporting, and to whom? Article 4 - without delay, to the nearest coastal State.
Which article requires assessment and notification of affected States? Article 5.
Which Protocol extends OPRC to chemicals? The OPRC-HNS Protocol, 2000.
Which MARPOL regulation actually requires the SOPEP? Annex I regulation 37.
Where does the Organization's role sit? Article 12 - information services, education and training, and technical services.
What does India's national system look like in outline? A national oil spill contingency plan with a designated response authority - the shape article 6 requires.
Which UNCLOS article obliges contingency planning? Article 199.
Name two documents a State maintains under OPRC. The national contingency plan, and the record of its competent national authority and operational contact point communicated to IMO.

blocks.p: Start from the title, because the title is the objectives: PREPAREDNESS, RESPONSE, CO-OPERATION. Then the negative in one line: not prevention, not compensation — and then the three senses in which it is preventive, so the printed word is answered.
For the provisions, five verbs in article order: PLAN (3), REPORT (4), REACT (5), BUILD (6), SHARE (7 to 10), with IMO (12) on the end.
For the role, three hats: FLAG, COAST, WORLD — and remember that because the question says Member State, the coastal hat is in.

For the challenges, four words: MONEY, PRACTICE, PEOPLE, BORDERS. For the documents, two holders and one number pair: the State keeps the PLAN, AUTHORITY, EQUIPMENT, AGREEMENTS; the ship keeps the SOPEP — 150 and 400, and REPORT, CONTACT, ACT, CO-ORDINATE.

ul: OPRC 1990 — adopted 30 November 1990, in force 13 May 1995. Unamended.

Article 3 emergency plans; article 4 reporting without delay to the nearest coastal State; article 5 assess and notify; article 6 national and regional systems; article 7 co-operation on request; articles 8 to 10 R&D, technical co-operation and bilateral agreements; article 12 IMO's institutional role.
OPRC-HNS Protocol, 2000 — the same architecture for hazardous and noxious substances.

MARPOL Annex I regulation 37 — the shipboard duty. 37.1 thresholds and approval; 37.2 guidelines, working language and the four contents; 37.3 combination and the SMPEP title; 37.4 shore-based damage stability access for tankers of 5,000 dwt and above. Unamended at this sitting.
MARPOL article 8 and Protocol I — the reporting obligation regulation 37.2.1 cross-refers to. Annex I regulation 17 — the Oil Record Book. Annex II regulation 17 — the NLS emergency plan.
UNCLOS article 199 — contingency plans against pollution; article 194 — the general duty.
India at this sitting: the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and rules made under it.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of the evidence

blocks.p: The evidence splits cleanly and the split is declared rather than hidden.

The shipboard document limb is primary. MARPOL Annex I as revised is held in the True Source corpus with a full extractable text layer — resolution MEPC.117(52) — and regulation 37 was read from it in full. The thresholds, the approval requirement, the language rule, the four contents, the combination rule and the 5,000 dwt provision all come from that text.

The OPRC Convention itself is not held. That is an acquisition gap already recorded in the corpus's own question-mapping records, not an oversight of this session. The Convention's dates and its article-by-article content are carried at authoritative-secondary level; no article of OPRC is quoted verbatim anywhere in this answer and no article is attributed a sub-paragraph.

The list of documents a Member State maintains is derived, not quoted. It is what articles 3, 5, 6, 7, 10 and 12 require a Party to establish and communicate. The Convention does not print it as a schedule, and the answer says so rather than presenting a derived list as a printed one.

The challenges analysis is reasoned judgement. No compliance statistic, party count, national capability assessment or comparative study is cited, and none is available from a held source. The Indian national system is described in outline only — the shape an article 6 system takes, and the statute in force at the sitting — because no Indian contingency-plan instrument or DG Shipping circular is held. No response equipment specification, stockpile quantity or tier-response threshold is quoted; tiered response is industry practice, not a Convention requirement.

Currency, and one reversal. OPRC is unamended and regulation 37 is unamended at this sitting. The corpus records two MARPOL Annex I amendments beyond the held base — MEPC.359(79), in force 1 May 2024, and MEPC.384(81), an MEPC 81 output of 2024 — and both are future at November 2023. The later paper in this family carries a currency note on MEPC.384(81) because it amends the Protocol I that regulation 37.2.1 cross-refers to; here that amendment does not yet exist, so the note is dropped entirely rather than re-stated. Nothing about container loss reporting belongs in this answer.

notes: NOVEMBER 2023 IS BOUNDARY-FREE AT DAY LEVEL. MEPC 80 is four months past and the 33rd Assembly one month future; neither falls inside the sitting month and neither touches this question.

OPRC WAS ADOPTED 30 NOVEMBER 1990 AND ENTERED INTO FORCE 13 MAY 1995, AND IT HAS NOT BEEN AMENDED. There is no amendment window to police and no edition question to resolve. The OPRC-HNS Protocol, 2000 is likewise stable.
MARPOL ANNEX I REGULATION 37 CARRIES THE SHIPBOARD DOCUMENT DUTY AND IS UNAMENDED AT THIS SITTING. The held base text is the revised Annex I, MEPC.117(52), in force 1 January 2007.

THE DONOR'S CURRENCY NOTE IS REVERSED AND DROPPED, NOT MERELY RE-STATED. QP2504-Q4 (April 2025) flags MEPC.384(81), the amendment to MARPOL Protocol I, as adopted but not yet in force. MEPC.384(81) is an MEPC 81 output of 2024 and at November 2023 IT DOES NOT YET EXIST - it is five months future. So the correct treatment here is not 'adopted but not in force' but ABSENCE, and the whole note is dropped. Nothing about container loss reporting belongs in this answer.
THE OTHER RECORDED ANNEX I AMENDMENT IS ALSO FUTURE. MEPC.359(79) enters into force 1 May 2024, six months after this sitting, and does not touch regulation 37 in any event.

THE MEMBER STATE FRAMING CHANGES WHAT IS IN SCOPE, AND THAT IS A DONOR DELTA RATHER THAN A TEMPORAL ONE, BUT IT IS RECORDED HERE BECAUSE IT WOULD OTHERWISE BE MISTAKEN FOR ONE. The donor answers FLAG STATE duties and expressly excludes the article 6 national system; this paper asks about MEMBER STATES, so article 6 is in scope and is the centre of limb b).

FUTURE CONTAMINATION EXCLUDED: no instrument adopted after November 2023 is cited. MEPC.384(81), MEPC.359(79), the whole A.118x(33) set, the 34th Assembly of December 2025, the Hong Kong Convention of June 2025 and the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 are all absent. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is the Indian implementing statute at this sitting.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three limbs at 6, 6 and 4. Limb a) wants identity, objectives and the key provisions, and prints the word 'preventing' against a Convention that is expressly not about prevention - so the boundary must be stated and then answered generously rather than ignored. Limb b) prints 'analyse' and asks about MEMBER STATES, not flag States, which brings the article 6 national system into scope as the centre of the limb; and it asks for implementation challenges, which the donor does not set at all. Limb c) prints 'enlist' and names TWO holders - Member States and ships - so it needs two lists, and the shipboard list is answered out of MARPOL rather than OPRC. The discriminating feature is whether the candidate knows that OPRC binds States and MARPOL Annex I regulation 37 binds the ship.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 6 + 6 + 4, all printed. Limb a) prints 'Briefly', so identity and objectives are compressed and the seven substantive articles go into a scannable table, leaving room for the prevention adjudication which is where the limb's own wording puts a mark. Limb b) carries equal marks and prints 'analyse': the role goes into a four-row capacity table and the nine challenges are numbered with a reason attached to each, closing on one sentence stating what they have in common. Limb c) at four marks gets two tight lists and one closing paragraph on why the shipboard list comes out of MARPOL.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate can state the three nouns of the Convention's own title as its objectives; can give the article architecture in order; can distinguish what a State does as flag State from what it does as coastal State AND know that a Member State question includes both; can analyse rather than list; can name the SOPEP correctly with its two thresholds and four contents; and can say why the ship's document obligation is specified in MARPOL although created in OPRC. Engaging honestly with the printed word 'preventing' rather than ignoring it is itself a mark of a candidate who read the stem.

questions.understand_first: The most useful thing to hold about this Convention is what it deliberately is not. It is not about stopping oil getting into the sea — a different instrument does that, with discharge limits and hull construction. It is not about who pays afterwards — that is yet another set of rules. This one starts from the assumption that the spill has already happened and asks a much more practical question: is anybody ready, and can they help each other? Its three ideas are in its own name — be prepared, be able to respond, and co-operate — and every article serves one of them. The second thing to hold is structural, and it is where most answers go wrong: this Convention binds countries, not ships. It tells each country to require its own ships to carry an emergency plan; the rule that actually reaches the vessel, with tonnage thresholds and a list of what the plan must contain, lives in the pollution-prevention convention instead. So a question about what the ship must carry is answered out of a different instrument from the one being asked about — and saying so is the best single sentence available here. The third thing is that when a question asks about a country's role rather than a flag's, the biggest obligation comes into view: building and paying for a national response system — a plan, an authority someone can telephone at any hour, equipment sitting in a shed, and exercises — every year, whether or not anything spills.
questions.memory_cue: The title is the objectives: PREPAREDNESS, RESPONSE, CO-OPERATION (1). Provisions in article order: PLAN, REPORT, REACT, BUILD, SHARE (2). Three hats: FLAG, COAST, WORLD (4). Challenges: MONEY, PRACTICE, PEOPLE, BORDERS (5). Documents: the State keeps the plan, the ship keeps the SOPEP (6, 7).

steps.title: What OPRC is, and what it deliberately is not
points: the International Convention on Oil Pollution Preparedness, Response and Co-operation, 1990
adopted 30 November 1990, entered into force 13 May 1995
developed after the Exxon Valdez grounding of 1989 showed there was no framework for co-ordinated response or for asking anyone else for help
it is a FRAMEWORK convention - it sets no discharge standard and prescribes no construction requirement
it obliges Parties to BUILD AND MAINTAIN A CAPABILITY and to make it available to each other
extended to hazardous and noxious substances by the OPRC-HNS Protocol, 2000
the objectives are the three nouns of its own title - PREPAREDNESS, RESPONSE, CO-OPERATION
preparedness - plans, authorities, equipment, trained people and rehearsed procedures BEFORE the incident
response - the ability to act promptly and effectively through a known chain of command and contact points
co-operation - mutual assistance, with the legal and administrative friction removed in advance

steps.title: The key provisions, article by article
points: the sequence to hold is PLAN, REPORT, REACT, BUILD, SHARE
article 3 - oil pollution emergency plans for ships flying the flag, and for offshore units, sea ports and oil handling facilities under the Party's jurisdiction
article 4 - reporting without delay of any event involving a discharge or PROBABLE discharge, to the nearest coastal State
article 5 - action on receiving a report: assess, and notify all States whose interests may be affected together with the Organization
article 6 - THE CORE BUILDING OBLIGATION: a national contingency plan, a designated competent national authority and an operational contact point
and within the Party's capabilities a minimum level of pre-positioned response equipment, a programme of exercises and training, and detailed plans and communications capability
article 7 - international co-operation in response: advisory services, technical support and equipment ON REQUEST, subject to capability
articles 8 to 10 - research and development, technical co-operation with developing countries, and the promotion of bilateral and multilateral agreements
article 12 - the institutional role, placing information services, education and training and technical services with IMO

steps.title: Significance - in response, and in the sense in which it touches prevention
points: before OPRC a coastal State had no reliable mechanism to obtain foreign equipment or expertise, no agreed reporting route, and often no single authority in charge of its own response
its real achievement is INSTITUTIONAL - it converted response from improvisation into a standing, exercised system with a named authority and a contact point that answers at three in the morning
THE PRINTED WORD 'PREVENTING' MUST BE ANSWERED, NOT IGNORED
strictly OPRC is NOT a prevention convention - prevention is MARPOL's work, and liability is CLC, FUND and Bunkers
but it prevents ESCALATION - the quantity reaching the shoreline is decided in the first hours, and preparedness shortens them
reporting is preventive - article 4 covers a PROBABLE discharge, so the machinery engages before oil is in the water
preparedness disciplines operations - exercises and drills expose weaknesses in bunkering and transfer, where most operational spills begin
the division of labour: MARPOL prevents, OPRC prepares and responds, CLC and FUND compensate
UNCLOS article 199 obliges States to develop contingency plans, and OPRC is how that obligation was given operational content

steps.title: The role - and a point of precision first
points: OPRC BINDS PARTIES, NOT SHIPS, and a State's obligations arise in THREE capacities
the Convention speaks of PARTIES rather than Member States - a State is a Member of IMO and a Party to OPRC, and the sets are not identical

AS FLAG STATE - require the plan under article 3, approve it through MARPOL Annex I reg 37.1, require reporting under article 4, ensure the working language, survey and enforce, and ensure crews are drilled
AS COASTAL AND TERRITORIAL STATE - the article 6 national system, the article 5 duty to assess and notify, and the plan requirement on offshore units, sea ports and oil handling facilities

AS A MEMBER OF THE INTERNATIONAL COMMUNITY - co-operate on request under article 7, research and technical co-operation under articles 8 and 9, bilateral and regional agreements under article 10, and support IMO's clearing-house role under article 12
DOMESTICALLY - give the Convention force in national law; in India at this sitting through the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and rules made under it
THE ANALYTICAL POINT - because the question asks about MEMBER STATES and not only flag States, the article 6 national system is squarely in scope, and it is the heaviest obligation in the Convention

steps.title: The challenges - analysed
points: RESOURCE ASYMMETRY - article 6 obliges capability 'within its capabilities', a qualification that made the Convention ratifiable and is also its central weakness; articles 9 and 10 exist to bridge the gap and their success is uneven
PLANS ON PAPER AGAINST REHEARSED CAPABILITY - a contingency plan is cheap to write and expensive to exercise, and the gap becomes visible only during an incident

INTER-AGENCY CO-ORDINATION - the single competent national authority must have real authority over the administration, coastguard, environment ministry, ports, customs, fisheries and local government, and often has influence rather than command

EQUIPMENT OBSOLESCENCE AND GEOGRAPHY - booms, skimmers and dispersant stocks degrade and must be positioned where the risk is; a stockpile a thousand miles away is a line in a plan, and dispersant approval regimes differ between States

FRICTION ON CROSS-BORDER ASSISTANCE - customs for equipment, immigration for personnel, liability and indemnity for the assisting State, and cost recovery; unless pre-agreed, help arrives after it would have mattered

FUNDING AND COST RECOVERY - preparedness is a standing cost with no visible return in quiet years, and recovery afterwards depends on the separate CLC and FUND regime and on a solvent identified polluter
TRAINING, RETENTION AND TURNOVER - competence decays, contact lists go stale, and currency of the plan is a continuing obligation rather than a one-off act
REPORTING QUALITY AT THE SHARP END - article 4 is only as good as what reaches the coastal State, and reporting is delayed by uncertainty, fear of consequences or unclear routes

SCOPE AND MODERN SPILL TYPES - the Convention was written for persistent crude in the era of the very large tanker, and non-tanker bunker spills and container-ship casualties now form a large share of real events

THE ANALYSIS IN ONE SENTENCE - OPRC's obligations are institutional and continuing rather than technical and one-off, and the real problem is sustaining a capability nobody wants to pay for in the years when it is not needed

steps.title: What a Member State maintains
points: THESE ARE DERIVED FROM WHAT ARTICLES 3, 5, 6, 7, 10 AND 12 REQUIRE A PARTY TO ESTABLISH AND COMMUNICATE - the Convention prints no schedule, and saying so is part of the answer
the National Oil Spill Contingency Plan - the central article 6 document
the record of the designated competent national authority and the operational contact point, kept current and communicated to IMO
the inventory of pre-positioned response equipment, with location, condition and maintenance record
the exercise and training programme and its records
bilateral and regional agreements concluded under article 10
reports and notifications to IMO and to affected States under articles 5 and 12
the national legislation and rules giving the Convention effect - in India, the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and rules made under it

steps.title: What the ship carries - and why it comes out of MARPOL
points: the operative document is the SHIPBOARD OIL POLLUTION EMERGENCY PLAN; OPRC article 3 requires the Party to require it and MARPOL Annex I regulation 37 supplies the detail
regulation 37.1 - every oil tanker of 150 GT and above and every ship other than an oil tanker of 400 GT and above, APPROVED BY THE ADMINISTRATION; the thresholds differ and the tanker one is lower
regulation 37.2 - prepared on guidelines developed by the Organization, written in the working language of the master and officers, containing AT LEAST four things
37.2.1 the reporting procedure, referring to MARPOL article 8 and Protocol I; 37.2.2 the list of authorities or persons to be contacted
37.2.3 a detailed description of immediate action by persons on board; 37.2.4 the procedures and point of contact for co-ordinating shipboard action with national and local authorities
'AT LEAST' MAKES THE LIST A FLOOR, NOT A CEILING
regulation 37.3 - where Annex II regulation 17 also applies the plan may be COMBINED, and the combined plan is titled 'Shipboard marine pollution emergency plan', the SMPEP
regulation 37.4 - all oil tankers of 5,000 tons deadweight or more shall have prompt access to computerized shore-based damage stability and residual structural strength calculation programs
kept with the plan but belonging to other instruments - the coastal State contact list, the Oil Record Book under Annex I regulation 17, and the IOPP Certificate and Supplement

THE CLOSING POINT - OPRC binds States, MARPOL Annex I regulation 37 binds the ship, and the plan is enforced through MARPOL's machinery at survey and at port State control because OPRC gives nobody power over a ship

quick_revision.recall_15s: OPRC 1990 — adopted 30 November 1990, in force 13 May 1995, after the Exxon Valdez. Objectives are its three title words: preparedness, response, co-operation. It is not prevention (MARPOL) and not liability (CLC/FUND/Bunkers) — but it prevents escalation, article 4 covers a probable discharge, and drills discipline bunkering and transfer. Provisions: art 3 emergency plans (ships, offshore units, ports, oil handling facilities); art 4 report without delay to the nearest coastal State; art 5 assess and notify affected States and IMO; art 6 national system — contingency plan, competent national authority, operational contact point, pre-positioned equipment, exercises and training; art 7 co-operate on request; arts 8–10 R&D, technical co-operation, bilateral agreements; art 12 IMO. Member State, not flag State: three hats — flag (require, approve, enforce), coastal (the article 6 system, which is IN scope here), international (co-operate, agree, support IMO). Challenges: money, practice, people, borders — resource asymmetry under 'within its capabilities', plans not exercised, inter-agency authority, equipment obsolescence and geography, customs and immigration friction, funding, turnover and stale contact lists. Documents: the State keeps the national plan, the authority and contact point notified to IMO, the equipment inventory, the exercise records and the regional agreements — derived, not a printed schedule. The ship keeps the SOPEP under MARPOL Annex I reg 37: tankers 150 GT, others 400 GT, approved by the Administration, in the working language of master and officers, containing at least reporting procedure, contact list, immediate actions and co-ordination point; combined with the Annex II plan it is retitled SMPEP (37.3); tankers of 5,000 dwt need shore-based damage stability access (37.4). OPRC binds States; regulation 37 binds the ship.
critical_numbers: OPRC adopted 30 November 1990; entered into force 13 May 1995
SOPEP threshold: oil tankers of 150 gross tonnage and above
SOPEP threshold: ships other than oil tankers of 400 gross tonnage and above
MARPOL Annex I regulation 37.2 lists FOUR mandatory contents and says 'at least'
Regulation 37.4 - oil tankers of 5,000 tons deadweight or more need prompt access to shore-based damage stability and residual structural strength programs
OPRC-HNS Protocol adopted 2000
The reporting cross-reference is MARPOL article 8 and Protocol I
quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL Annex I regulation 37 is the provision that actually reaches the ship, and it is unamended at this sitting. Regulation 37.1 requires every oil tanker of 150 gross tonnage and above and every other ship of 400 gross tonnage and above to carry a shipboard oil pollution emergency plan approved by the Administration; 37.2 requires it to be based on the Organization's guidelines, written in the working language of the master and officers, and to consist at least of the reporting procedure, the contact list, the description of immediate action and the shipboard co-ordination procedures and point of contact. OPRC article 3 obliges the Party to require the plan; regulation 37 is what specifies it.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering limb (b) as though it were a flag State question. It is not — it asks about Member States, and that puts the article 6 national system squarely in scope: the national contingency plan, the competent national authority and operational contact point, the pre-positioned equipment and the exercise and training programme. That is the heaviest obligation in the Convention and it is owed in the coastal and territorial capacity, so an answer confined to flag duties omits the most substantial thing OPRC requires. The paired traps are believing that OPRC itself requires the ship to carry a SOPEP — it binds States, and MARPOL Annex I regulation 37 binds the ship — and ignoring the printed word “preventing” instead of stating the boundary and answering within it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State OPRC's full title, its dates, and its three objectives.
retrieval_cards.answer: The International Convention on Oil Pollution Preparedness, Response and Co-operation, 1990. Adopted 30 November 1990; entered into force 13 May 1995, developed after the Exxon Valdez grounding of 1989. Its three objectives are the three nouns of its title: preparedness - plans, authorities, equipment and training in place beforehand; response - the ability to act promptly and effectively; and co-operation - mutual assistance with the friction removed in advance.
retrieval_cards.why: The title carries the objectives, which makes this the cheapest structured mark on the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The question says OPRC is significant in PREVENTING oil pollution. Is that right?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not directly - prevention is MARPOL's work and OPRC begins where prevention has failed. But three senses are defensible: it prevents escalation, because the quantity reaching the shoreline is decided in the first hours; article 4 requires reporting of a PROBABLE discharge, so the machinery engages before oil is in the water; and the plans, drills and exercises discipline bunkering and transfer operations, where most operational spills begin.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem prints the word, so it has to be answered - stating the boundary and then answering generously within it is the technique.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does a MEMBER STATE question about OPRC differ from a FLAG STATE one?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the article 6 national system - the contingency plan, the competent national authority and operational contact point, the pre-positioned equipment and the exercise and training programme - is owed by the State in its coastal and territorial capacity, not because it registers ships. A flag State question excludes it; a Member State question puts it at the centre, and it is the heaviest obligation in the Convention.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the single feature that separates this question from every other OPRC question in the corpus.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the OPRC articles in order with one phrase each.
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 3 emergency plans - ships, offshore units, sea ports and oil handling facilities. Article 4 reporting without delay to the nearest coastal State. Article 5 assess the report and notify affected States and the Organization. Article 6 the national system - contingency plan, competent authority, contact point, pre-positioned equipment, exercises and training. Article 7 co-operation in response on request. Articles 8 to 10 research and development, technical co-operation, bilateral and multilateral agreements. Article 12 IMO's institutional role.
retrieval_cards.why: Plan, report, react, build, share - the sequence is how the architecture stays recallable under pressure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does OPRC require ships to carry a SOPEP?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not directly. Article 3 requires each Party to REQUIRE ships flying its flag to have an oil pollution emergency plan in accordance with provisions adopted by the Organization. Those provisions are MARPOL Annex I regulation 37, which supplies the thresholds, the approval requirement, the language rule and the contents. OPRC binds States; regulation 37 binds the ship.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the structural fact the whole question turns on, and it explains why limb (c)'s shipboard half is answered out of MARPOL.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the SOPEP tonnage thresholds and say who approves the plan.
retrieval_cards.answer: MARPOL Annex I regulation 37.1: every oil tanker of 150 gross tonnage and above, and every ship other than an oil tanker of 400 gross tonnage and above. The plan must be approved by the Administration. The thresholds differ and the tanker one is the lower.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates routinely give a single figure for both, which loses the mark outright.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the four mandatory contents of a SOPEP.
retrieval_cards.answer: Under regulation 37.2, and the plan shall consist AT LEAST of: the procedure for the master or person in charge to report an oil pollution incident, as required by MARPOL article 8 and Protocol I; the list of authorities or persons to be contacted; a detailed description of the action to be taken immediately by persons on board; and the procedures and point of contact on the ship for co-ordinating shipboard action with national and local authorities.
retrieval_cards.why: Report, contact, act, co-ordinate - and that is also the order the plan is used in during a real incident.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What documents does a Member State maintain under OPRC?
retrieval_cards.answer: The national oil spill contingency plan; the record of its competent national authority and operational contact point, communicated to IMO; the pre-positioned equipment inventory with location and maintenance record; the exercise and training programme and its records; bilateral and regional agreements under article 10; and the national legislation giving the Convention effect. The list is DERIVED from what the articles require a Party to establish - the Convention prints no schedule of State documents.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (c) names two holders, and most answers give only the shipboard half.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A chemical tanker carries one combined pollution emergency plan. What is it called and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: A Shipboard marine pollution emergency plan (SMPEP). Regulation 37.3 permits the SOPEP to be combined with the plan for noxious liquid substances required by MARPOL Annex II regulation 17, and provides that the combined plan shall be so titled.
retrieval_cards.why: The retitling is expressly in the regulation and explains why chemical tankers do not carry a document called a SOPEP.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name four structural challenges in implementing OPRC, with the reason for each.
retrieval_cards.answer: Resource asymmetry - article 6 requires capability 'within its capabilities', which made the Convention ratifiable but leaves the obligation elastic. Plans against practice - a contingency plan is cheap to write and expensive to exercise, and the gap shows only during an incident. Cross-border friction - customs for equipment, immigration for responders, liability and cost recovery, all of which must be pre-agreed or assistance arrives too late. People - competence decays and contact lists go stale, so currency of the plan is a continuing obligation.
retrieval_cards.why: The limb prints 'analyse', so each challenge must carry its reason - money, practice, people, borders.

retrieval_cards.prompt: MARPOL, OPRC, CLC and FUND all touch the same oil spill. What does each answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: MARPOL asks how we stop it happening - construction, equipment and discharge standards, before the event. OPRC asks whether anyone is ready and whether they can help each other - plans, authorities, equipment and response, before and during. CLC, FUND and Bunkers ask who pays - liability and compensation, afterwards. Above them all, UNCLOS article 199 obliges States to develop contingency plans against pollution.
retrieval_cards.why: Three instruments, one incident, three questions - it keeps prevention and compensation material out of an OPRC answer.

sources: AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (identity and dates): the International Convention on the Control of Harmful Anti-fouling Systems on Ships, 2001, entered into force 17 September 2008. It prohibited the application of organotin compounds acting as biocides in anti-fouling systems from 1 January 2003 and their presence on ship surfaces from 1 January 2008. Ships of 400 gross tonnage and above on international voyages carry an International Anti-fouling System Certificate; smaller ships of 24 metres or more in length carry a Declaration on Anti-fouling Systems.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (identity and date): MEPC.331(76), adopted 17 June 2021, added CYBUTRYNE to the controlled substances. The control APPLIED FROM 1 JANUARY 2023 - ten months before this sitting. Anti-fouling systems containing cybutryne may not be applied or re-applied from that date, and an existing cybutryne-containing system must be removed or over-coated with a sealer coat at the next scheduled renewal of the anti-fouling system after that date, and in any event no later than sixty months following the last application.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: the four families of tin-free anti-fouling system - controlled depletion polymer, self-polishing copolymer, tin-free hybrid, and non-biocidal foul release - and their distinguishing mechanisms of dissolution, hydrolysis-driven polishing, blended behaviour, and low-adhesion release.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: average hull roughness is the accepted measure of the physical roughness of a ship's underwater surface, obtained by traversing a stylus gauge over the hull and averaging the maximum peak-to-trough height measured over successive short intervals, and reported in micrometres.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: added surface roughness increases frictional resistance and therefore the power required at a given speed, and biological fouling causes a substantially larger penalty than physical roughness of the same nominal magnitude.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: a foul release coating works by presenting a surface of low surface energy and low elastic modulus, so that organisms adhere weakly and are removed by hydrodynamic shear once the ship exceeds a threshold speed. The force required to release an adhered organism scales with the square root of the product of elastic modulus and surface energy, which is why both must be low.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: silicone oils blended into but not chemically bound to the polydimethylsiloxane matrix migrate toward the surface and form a mobile liquid layer, which lowers the effective surface energy further, interferes with the curing and anchoring of biological adhesives, and reduces the shear stress and therefore the ship speed required to release fouling.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: incorporated oil is a finite reservoir which depletes as it leaches, so the enhancement decays across the docking interval; and unbound oil at the surface complicates repair, over-coating and adhesion of subsequent schemes.

P3 INDUSTRY GUIDANCE: coating application practice - surface preparation and blasting, airless spray at very high pressure, wet-film and dry-film thickness control, over-coating intervals, tie coats between incompatible schemes, and the containment of spent abrasive and paint residue in dry dock.

P3 INDUSTRY GUIDANCE: occupational hygiene practice for marine coating work - the hierarchy of control, solvent and isocyanate exposure control, air-fed breathing protection for spray application, confined-space atmosphere monitoring, and the management of high-pressure injection injury.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (identity only): MLC 2006 Regulation 4.3 - health and safety protection and accident prevention; the ISM Code as amended through MSC.353(92), sections 7 and 8, for shipboard operations and emergency preparedness; and the SOLAS requirement for enclosed-space entry and rescue drills. Named at identity level; nothing quoted.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT: the organisation of limb (a) around roughness BEHAVIOUR ACROSS THE DOCKING INTERVAL rather than at application, and the placing of the physical-against-biological distinction before the type comparison; and the organisation of limb (c) by the hierarchy of control rather than as a list of protective equipment.
