blocks.p: The Anti-fouling Systems Convention, 2001, in force 17 September 2008, prohibited organotin compounds acting as biocides — the application ban from 1 January 2003 and the presence ban from 1 January 2008 — and every coating discussed below exists because tributyltin was withdrawn. Ships of 400 gross tonnage and above on international voyages carry an International Anti-fouling System Certificate; smaller ships of 24 metres or more carry a Declaration.

One control is fresh at this sitting and is worth a mark. MEPC.331(76), adopted 17 June 2021, added cybutryne to the controlled substances, and the control applied from 1 January 2023 — ten months before this examination. A cybutryne-containing system may no longer be applied or re-applied, and an existing one must be removed or over-coated with a sealer coat at the next scheduled renewal of the anti-fouling system after that date and in any event no later than sixty months after its last application.
The four tin-free families, which limb (a) then compares:

rows: Controlled depletion polymer (CDP)
A soluble rosin-based matrix. Seawater dissolves the binder and releases biocide, leaving a spent leached layer behind
Self-polishing copolymer (SPC), tin-free
An acrylate binder that hydrolyses at the surface and is then removed by hydrodynamic shear, so the film polishes at a controlled rate and continuously renews itself
Tin-free hybrid
A blend of rosin and acrylate chemistries; part depletion, part polishing
Foul release (FR)
Non-biocidal. A silicone or fluoropolymer surface of low surface energy and low modulus, to which fouling adheres so weakly that it is released by the water flow once the ship is moving

blocks.h: (a) Hull roughness of the different types
2. What hull roughness is, and why it costs money

ul: Hull roughness is the texture of the underwater surface, reported as average hull roughness in micrometres: a stylus gauge is traversed over the hull and the maximum peak-to-trough height over each short interval is averaged.

It matters because it sits inside the boundary layer. A rough surface thickens the turbulent boundary layer and raises frictional resistance, which for a full-form ship is the dominant part of total resistance — so roughness is paid for directly in shaft power and fuel.

As orders of magnitude only: a newbuilding is typically in the region of 100 micrometres average hull roughness, and roughness accumulates over successive dockings as paint is applied over paint. Full removal to bare steel resets it; over-coating does not.

blocks.p: The distinction that must come first. Roughness has two entirely different sources and they behave differently:

ul: Physical roughness — the paint film's own texture, application defects such as orange peel, dry spray and runs, the porous leached layer, mechanical damage, weld seams and plate undulation. It is permanent until the surface is treated.
Biological roughness — slime, weed and shell. It is removable, and for the same nominal height it is far more expensive than physical roughness because it is compliant, irregular and thick.

blocks.p: The consequence for the comparison: the smoothest coating is not automatically the best. A very smooth foul release surface that has fouled because the ship idles is worse than a rougher self-polishing surface that is clean. Limb (a) is answered properly only by comparing roughness behaviour across the whole docking interval, not at the moment of application.

rows: CDP
Moderate — rosin systems give a relatively coarse film

Roughness increases, and increases fastest of the four — the soluble matrix dissolves unevenly, leaving a thick and porous leached layer that is itself rough; and because CDP schemes are usually over-coated rather than removed, roughness compounds from docking to docking
SPC
Good — a smooth, uniform film

Roughness is stable or improves — hydrolysis plus hydrodynamic shear removes the outermost layer continuously, so the surface is polished by service; the leached layer stays very thin and constant. This is why SPC suits long intervals and high-activity ships
Hybrid
Between the two
Between the two — some polishing, some leaching — blended chemistry gives intermediate behaviour, at intermediate cost
Foul release
The smoothest of all

Very low if the ship keeps moving; poor if she does not — the silicone film flows out to a near-glassy surface and does not leach at all, so there is no leached layer. But it is mechanically soft — tug contact, ice, groundings and hard brushing damage it, damage is difficult to repair invisibly, and biological roughness takes over on a slow or idle ship

blocks.p: Two practical points that separate a good answer. First, repair and over-coating behave differently: a self-polishing scheme can normally be over-coated with a compatible scheme, whereas a foul release surface has such low surface energy that nothing adheres to it — recoating means full removal or an approved tie coat, and that cost belongs in any roughness comparison. Second, the hull cleaning regime interacts with the coating: aggressive brushing that a hard scheme tolerates will remove the polishing film of an SPC and physically damage a foul release coating, so the cleaning method must be chosen with the coating and not against it.

blocks.h: (b) Enhancement of foul release coatings by oil incorporation

blocks.p: A foul release coating kills nothing. It works on adhesion. Two surface properties govern how firmly an organism can hold on:

ol: Low surface energy. A silicone surface is poorly wetted, so the biological adhesives that barnacles and tubeworms secrete cannot spread and key into it.
Low elastic modulus. The film is soft and flexible, so it deforms under the organism's attachment and peels away from it rather than resisting in shear.

blocks.p: The established relationship is that the force required to release an adhered organism scales with the square root of the product of the coating's elastic modulus and its surface energy — which is exactly why both have to be low, and why a hard low-energy coating is not a foul release coating. In service the release is done by hydrodynamic shear, so the coating has a threshold speed: below it, fouling stays.
That threshold is the weakness, and it is what oil incorporation is aimed at.

Silicone oils are blended into the matrix but are not chemically bound into it. Being mobile and incompatible with the cured network, they migrate steadily toward the surface and form a thin, continuously replenished liquid layer on top of the solid film. The benefits follow from that one fact:

ul: Lower effective surface energy. The organism now meets a mobile liquid rather than a solid, so the surface it is trying to bond to will not hold still.
Interference with adhesive curing. Biological glues need a stable substrate to cure against; the oil layer disrupts anchoring at the moment of settlement, which is the cheapest moment to defeat it.

A lower release threshold. Less shear stress is needed to detach what does settle, so fouling releases at a lower ship speed — the single most valuable practical gain, because it widens the range of ships and trades a non-biocidal coating can serve.
Better static performance. Idle time in port or at anchor is where a plain foul release coating is weakest; the oil layer improves resistance to settlement while the ship is stopped.
A degree of self-healing. Oil migrating into a minor scratch or abrasion partially restores the low-energy surface where the solid film has been marked.
It remains non-biocidal in mechanism. Nothing is being poisoned — the surface is simply made harder to hold on to. That is the whole commercial argument for the technology after tributyltin.

blocks.p: Related approaches attack the same threshold differently — amphiphilic surfaces combining water-loving and water-repelling segments so that no single adhesive chemistry works well, and silicone-hydrogel systems that hold a bound water layer at the interface. Oil incorporation is the simplest and the most widely used of the family.

blocks.h: 6. The limits - which is where the marks are

ul: The oil is a finite reservoir. It migrates out and is lost to the sea, so the enhancement decays across the docking interval. The coating ends its life closer to an unmodified foul release film than it began.
Depletion is not uniform. It runs faster where shear and temperature are highest, so performance varies over the hull.

Repair and over-coating are harder still. Unbound oil at the surface is exactly what prevents anything from sticking — including a repair patch. Surface preparation before any repair is critical and often imperfect in a dock.

The regulatory question is open. The Convention controls systems whose substances act as biocides. Oil-amended foul release systems are put forward as non-biocidal, and that is the mechanism; but the deliberate release of a substance into the sea to prevent settlement attracts scrutiny, and the position should be checked against the ship's approval rather than assumed. This answer takes no position on it.

The cost and the caveats survive. Oil does not make the coating mechanically tougher, does not remove the threshold speed, and does not change the fact that a foul release scheme is expensive to apply and unforgiving to damage.

blocks.p: The honest summary: oil incorporation widens the operating window of a foul release coating — lower speeds, more idle time, better early life — at the cost of a benefit that fades, and it does not cure the coating's mechanical fragility.

blocks.h: (c) Personnel and health safety during application

blocks.p: Note first that the hazard is the whole coating system, not only the tin alternatives: the primer, the tie coat and the removal of the old scheme are all in scope.

rows: Solvent vapour
Narcosis, headache, loss of co-ordination, dermatitis; and the vapour is flammable, so it is a fire and explosion hazard in any enclosed space
Isocyanates and epoxy amines in tie coats and primers
Respiratory sensitisation and occupational asthma; skin sensitisation and burns. Sensitisation is permanent - once acquired, the person cannot work with the material again
Biocides in the antifouling itself
Copper and organic biocides are irritant and toxic by skin contact, inhalation of mist and ingestion
Removal of the OLD coating
Blasting dust carrying heavy metals and, on older hulls, organotin residues - and cybutryne, which now has to come off. This is often the most toxic operation of the whole job
Airless spray
Very high pressure. High-pressure injection injury - fluid driven through the skin from a leak or a careless hand - looks like a pinprick and is a surgical emergency
Enclosed and confined spaces
Oxygen deficiency, accumulation of heavier-than-air solvent vapour, and an explosive atmosphere
Physical
Work at height on staging and cradles, noise from blasting, dust, slips on overspray, and dry-dock hazards including simultaneous operations and hot work nearby

blocks.h: 8. The controls, in the order they must be applied

ol: Eliminate or substitute. Choose a low-solvent, high-solids or water-borne scheme where the specification allows, and a non-biocidal foul release system where the trade suits it. The safest exposure is the one that never occurs.

Engineering controls. Mechanical ventilation and forced extraction in every enclosed space; wet or vacuum blasting to suppress dust; containment and screening of the dock, with collection of spent abrasive and paint residue; explosion-protected lighting and equipment; bonding and earthing.

Administrative controls. Read the safety data sheets before the work is planned, not after. Risk assessment and method statement; permit to work, with a separate enclosed-space entry permit and hot work permit; atmosphere testing for oxygen, flammable vapour and contaminants before entry and continuously during it; a standby person and a rehearsed rescue plan; exclusion zones and control of simultaneous operations; limits on exposure time; training and health surveillance for those working with sensitisers.

Personal protective equipment — last, never first. Air-fed positive-pressure hood or full-face breathing apparatus for spray application and for any work with isocyanates — a cartridge respirator is not sufficient for spraying. Chemical-resistant coveralls and gloves selected against the actual product, eye and face protection, hearing protection, safety footwear, and a harness where there is a fall risk.

Emergency arrangements. Eyewash and emergency shower at the workface; fire watch and extinguishing media; and one specific instruction that must be briefed: any suspected high-pressure injection injury goes to hospital immediately, however trivial the wound looks.

Waste and environment. Spent abrasive and paint residues containing biocides are hazardous waste. They are contained, collected and landed ashore to a licensed receiver; nothing is washed into the dock or over the side, and the dock's own runoff is contained. Removed cybutryne and organotin residues are handled on that basis without exception.

blocks.p: The regulatory frame, named rather than quoted: MLC 2006 Regulation 4.3 on health and safety protection and accident prevention; the ISM Code at sections 7 and 8, under which the procedures and the emergency arrangements are written into the safety management system; the SOLAS requirement for enclosed-space entry and rescue drills; the ship's own permit-to-work system; and the yard's occupational health regime, which for work done in dock is usually the controlling one.

The closing judgement. The three limbs of this question meet at one point: the choice of an anti-fouling system is not only an efficiency decision. It settles how rough the hull will be in three years, whether the coating works at the speed the ship actually steams, and what the people applying and later removing it will be exposed to — and the last of those is the one that is decided by whoever writes the specification, not by whoever holds the spray gun.

The marks are printed 6 + 6 + 4 against three limbs which have almost nothing to do with one another, and the biggest structural risk is spending the page on the preamble. The words “referring to various alternatives to tin-based antifouling paints” look like an invitation to write the standard CDP / SPC / hybrid / foul-release essay. They are not. That taxonomy is worth about two sentences and a four-row table here; everything else belongs to the three limbs.

Limb (a) is answered as a comparison across the docking interval, not as a list of coatings, and the physical-against-biological distinction is put before the comparison because the comparison makes no sense without it. Limb (b) has to start with the mechanism being enhanced — a candidate who has not said what a foul release coating does cannot explain what oil adds to it — and then closes on the limits, which is where the second half of the marks are. Limb (c) is organised by the hierarchy of control, which turns a shapeless list of precautions into an argument with an order.

blocks.h: The preamble does not govern limb (c)

blocks.p: The printed preamble governs limbs (a) and (b) fully. Limb (c) is different: personnel and health safety during application is about occupational exposure to the whole coating system — the primer, the tie coat, the solvents, and above all the removal of the old scheme, which is frequently the most toxic operation of the job and has nothing to do with which tin alternative is going on afterwards.
So the preamble is treated as governing (a) and (b) fully and (c) contextually. Saying that in one line shows the stem was read rather than skimmed.

blocks.h: The one relationship that makes limb (b) answerable

blocks.p: Release force scales with the square root of (modulus × surface energy).
That single statement is the whole of foul release technology and it explains everything the limb asks:

ul: It is why a foul release coating must be both low-energy and soft. A hard low-energy coating — glass, for instance — fouls badly.
It is why release needs speed: the shear has to exceed the release force, so there is a threshold below which fouling stays.
It is why oil helps: a mobile liquid layer at the surface drives the effective surface energy down further, so the release force falls and the threshold speed falls with it.
And it is why oil does not fix everything: it does nothing to the coating's mechanical toughness, and once it has leached out, the relationship returns to where it started.

blocks.h: Roughness: two kinds, and a trap

rows: What it is
Paint texture, application defects, leached layer, damage, weld seams, plate undulation
Slime, weed, shell
Reversible?
No - it stays until the surface is treated, and over-coating compounds it
Yes - it cleans off
Cost per micrometre
Lower
Much higher - compliant, irregular and thick

blocks.p: The trap: assuming the smoothest coating always wins. A foul release film is the smoothest thing available at application, but on a ship that idles it fouls, and a fouled smooth coating is worse than a clean rougher one. Roughness is a property of the ship's whole operating pattern, not of the paint tin.

ul: Writing the standard AFS Convention essay and running out of page before limb (b).
Comparing coatings only at application, when the whole question in limb (a) is what happens over three to five years.
Forgetting the leached layer, which is the reason CDP roughens and SPC does not.
Saying a foul release coating kills fouling. It does not; it is non-biocidal and works entirely on adhesion.
Explaining oil incorporation without first explaining the mechanism it enhances.
Giving the benefits of oil incorporation and stopping — the limits are half the marks: finite reservoir, decay across the interval, repair and recoating difficulty, and the open regulatory question.
Ignoring that a foul release surface cannot be over-coated without full removal or an approved tie coat, which is a real cost.
In limb (c), listing personal protective equipment first. PPE is the last line of the hierarchy, not the first.
Omitting the removal of the old coating, which is where the organotin and cybutryne exposure actually occurs.
Omitting high-pressure injection injury — the most serious acute hazard of airless spraying and the one nobody expects.
Treating spent abrasive and paint residue as ordinary waste. It is hazardous waste and it is landed ashore.
“When did the AFS Convention enter into force?” 17 September 2008 — with the organotin application ban from 1 January 2003 and the presence ban from 1 January 2008.
“What changed on 1 January 2023?” The cybutryne control under MEPC.331(76) applied — ten months before this sitting.

“Your ship has cybutryne in her existing coating. What must happen?” It must be removed or over-coated with a sealer coat at the next scheduled renewal of the anti-fouling system, and in any event no later than sixty months after its last application.
“Which certificate, and from what size?” International Anti-fouling System Certificate for 400 GT and above on international voyages; a Declaration for ships of 24 metres or more below that.
“Why does a CDP get rougher?” The soluble matrix dissolves unevenly and leaves a thick, porous leached layer — and successive over-coating compounds it.
“Why does an SPC not?” The binder hydrolyses and is sheared away, so the film polishes itself and the leached layer stays thin.
“Does a foul release coating contain biocide?” No. It works on adhesion, not toxicity.
“Why does foul release need speed?” Because release is by hydrodynamic shear, and below a threshold speed the shear is insufficient.
“What does the oil do?” Migrates to the surface as a mobile layer, lowers the effective surface energy, disrupts adhesive curing, and lowers the release threshold.
“What is the drawback of the oil?” It is a finite reservoir; as it leaches out the benefit decays, and it makes repair and over-coating harder.
“Which protection for spray application?” Air-fed positive-pressure hood or full-face breathing apparatus. A cartridge respirator is not sufficient.
“A rating has a pinprick on his hand from the spray gun and says he is fine.” Hospital immediately. High-pressure injection injury is a surgical emergency and the wound always looks trivial.
“Where does the spent grit go?” Contained, collected and landed ashore to a licensed receiver. It is hazardous waste.
What does AFS stand for? The Control of Harmful Anti-fouling Systems on Ships.
Name the four families of tin-free system. Controlled depletion polymer, self-polishing copolymer, tin-free hybrid, and foul release.
How is hull roughness measured? A stylus gauge traversed over the hull, averaging the maximum peak-to-trough height over successive short intervals, reported in micrometres.
Which costs more, physical or biological roughness? Biological, for the same nominal height.
Does over-coating reduce roughness? No - it compounds it. Only removal to bare steel resets it.
What are the two properties a foul release coating needs? Low surface energy and low elastic modulus.
Why does hard glass foul badly? Low surface energy but very high modulus - both terms have to be low.
Can you paint over a foul release coating? Not with a conventional scheme - nothing adheres to it. Full removal or an approved tie coat.
Which is the most dangerous coating operation? Usually the removal of the old scheme, because of the metal and organotin residues in the dust.
Where does PPE sit in the hierarchy of control? Last.

blocks.p: For the families, four words in order of how the film behaves: DISSOLVES, POLISHES, BLENDS, RELEASES.
For limb (a), one question asked four times: WHAT HAPPENS TO THE SURFACE OVER THREE YEARS? CDP roughens; SPC smooths; hybrid sits between; foul release is smoothest but only if the ship moves.

For limb (b), one relationship and one consequence: SOFT AND SLIPPERY — release force follows the square root of modulus times surface energy — and oil makes the surface slipperier still, but not for ever.
For limb (c), the hierarchy in five words: ELIMINATE, ENGINEER, ADMINISTER, PROTECT, DISPOSE. If you can only remember two things: air-fed hood for spraying, and injection injury goes to hospital.

ul: AFS Convention 2001 — the International Convention on the Control of Harmful Anti-fouling Systems on Ships. In force 17 September 2008; organotin application ban from 1 January 2003, presence ban from 1 January 2008. International Anti-fouling System Certificate for 400 GT and above on international voyages; Declaration for ships of 24 metres or more below that.

MEPC.331(76), adopted 17 June 2021 — added cybutryne. Applied from 1 January 2023, ten months before this sitting. Existing systems removed or over-coated at the next scheduled anti-fouling renewal after that date, and no later than sixty months after last application.
MLC 2006 Regulation 4.3 — health and safety protection and accident prevention. The 2022 amendments enter force 23 December 2024 and are future here.
ISM Code as amended through MSC.353(92) — sections 7 (shipboard operations) and 8 (emergency preparedness), under which the procedures and rescue arrangements live in the safety management system.
SOLAS — enclosed-space entry and rescue drills.
No paint manufacturer, product or formulation is named anywhere in this answer, and every numerical figure given is expressly an order of magnitude. See the uncertainty section.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of the evidence

blocks.p: The AFS Convention is not held by the True Source corpus. The corpus's IMO instrument directory contains no anti-fouling folder, and its reference resolver holds 320 entries of which every one is MARPOL Annex VI. The Convention, its entry into force, the organotin controls, the certificate and the declaration are therefore carried at authoritative-secondary level, and no annex or regulation is quoted or attributed a paragraph. MEPC.331(76) is likewise not held: its identity, adoption date and 1 January 2023 application date are stated, and the compliance arithmetic that follows is stated as the rule it is rather than quoted.

The coatings science is industry and engineering knowledge, and the numbers are deliberately thin. The four-family taxonomy and the depletion, polishing and release mechanisms are uncontroversial and consistently recorded. Every figure in the answer is expressly an order of magnitude. No service life, polishing rate, leached-layer thickness, surface energy value, elastic modulus, threshold release speed or roughness-to-power coefficient is presented as sourced, because none is held and all of them differ between products. No paint manufacturer, product, brand or formulation is named anywhere.

The release relationship is used qualitatively. That the release force scales with the square root of the product of modulus and surface energy is the established relationship, and it is used here to explain why both must be low. It is not used to compute anything and no coefficient is given.

One question is left open on purpose. Whether an oil-amended foul release coating falls to be treated as biocidal is a live regulatory question, and this answer takes no position because no held instrument or determination resolves it. Recording it as a question is more honest than resolving it by assertion.

Limb (c) carries two further limits. No exposure limit, threshold value or biological monitoring criterion is quoted for any solvent, isocyanate or biocide — those are national occupational hygiene limits, they differ between jurisdictions, and none is held. And the Organization's recommendations for entering enclosed spaces aboard ships are referred to descriptively rather than by resolution number, because the current instrument identity could not be established from a held source.

Currency. The cybutryne control is the live date in this question and it must stay framed as at this sitting: it applied from 1 January 2023, so at November 2023 it is ten months old and the sixty-month compliance arithmetic is still running for most ships. An answer written from a later sitting would treat the transition as historical, which it is not here.

notes: NOVEMBER 2023 IS BOUNDARY-FREE AT DAY LEVEL. MEPC 80 is four months past and the 33rd Assembly one month future, and neither touches this question.

THE CYBUTRYNE CONTROL IS THE LIVE TEMPORAL FACT AND IT IS FRESH AT THIS SITTING. MEPC.331(76) was adopted 17 June 2021 and the control APPLIED FROM 1 JANUARY 2023 - TEN MONTHS BEFORE THIS EXAMINATION. It is therefore operative, and it is in TRANSITION: application and re-application are already prohibited, while existing systems run to the next scheduled anti-fouling renewal after that date, and in any event to no later than sixty months after last application. An answer written from a 2025 or 2026 sitting would describe the transition as complete or historical. It is not complete here.

THE AFS CONVENTION ITSELF IS STABLE. In force 17 September 2008; organotin application ban 1 January 2003 and presence ban 1 January 2008. There is no other amendment in the window and no edition question to resolve.

THE ISM CODE POSITION AT THIS SITTING IS THE MSC.353(92) TEXT, in force 1 January 2015, which the corpus amendment register records as the latest Code amendment. Sections 7 and 8 are cited at identity level only.
MLC 2006 IS AT ITS 2018 AMENDMENT STATE. Regulation 4.3 is cited at identity level. THE 2022 MLC AMENDMENTS ENTER FORCE 23 DECEMBER 2024 - thirteen months FUTURE - and are not cited.

THE COATINGS TECHNOLOGY IS CORRECTLY DATED. Oil-amended foul release systems, amphiphilic surfaces and silicone-hydrogel systems were all in commercial or near-commercial use by 2023 and are described as established rather than as emerging. No technology is described that did not exist at the sitting.

FUTURE CONTAMINATION EXCLUDED: no instrument adopted after November 2023 is cited. The whole A.118x(33) set, the MLC 2022 amendments, the Hong Kong Convention of 26 June 2025 and the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 are all absent. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is the Indian statute at this sitting.

questions.understand_first: Everything in this question follows from one fact: the paint that used to work best was banned because it poisoned the sea, and the industry has been living with the replacements ever since. Those replacements fall into two quite different camps. One camp still uses a poison, just a gentler one, and manages how fast it is released — either by letting the paint dissolve away, or by having it wear off smoothly as the water rushes past. The other camp poisons nothing at all: it makes the hull so slippery and so soft that barnacles and weed cannot get a proper grip, and the flow of water simply peels them off once the ship is moving. Both the roughness question and the oil question fall out of that split. The dissolving paints get rougher as they age, because what is left behind after the soluble part has gone is a spent, porous crust; the self-wearing ones stay smooth because the outer skin is constantly renewed; and the slippery ones start smoothest of all but only stay clean if the ship actually goes somewhere. Their weakness is exactly that: they need a certain speed before the water can strip the growth off. Blending a light oil into the slippery paint attacks that weakness — the oil creeps to the surface and makes it slipperier still, so less water flow is needed to shed the growth — but the oil supply is finite, and when it has gone the coating is back where it started. The last part of the question is about the people. Whatever goes on the hull has to be sprayed at enormous pressure onto a surface that first has to be blasted clean of the old, often far more toxic, coating — and that job is the most dangerous part of the whole operation.
questions.memory_cue: Four families by what the film does: DISSOLVES, POLISHES, BLENDS, RELEASES (1). Limb (a) asks one thing four times: what happens over three years (2, 3). Limb (b) is one line: SOFT AND SLIPPERY, and oil makes it slipperier but not for ever (4, 5, 6). Limb (c) hierarchy: ELIMINATE, ENGINEER, ADMINISTER, PROTECT, DISPOSE (8).

steps.title: The setting, in two sentences
points: the AFS Convention 2001 entered into force 17 September 2008 and prohibited organotin compounds acting as biocides
the APPLICATION ban ran from 1 January 2003 and the PRESENCE ban from 1 January 2008 - every coating below exists because tributyltin was withdrawn
IAFS Certificate for ships of 400 GT and above on international voyages; a Declaration for ships of 24 metres or more below that
MEPC.331(76), adopted 17 June 2021, added CYBUTRYNE and the control APPLIED FROM 1 JANUARY 2023 - ten months before this examination

a cybutryne system may no longer be applied or re-applied, and an existing one must be removed or over-coated with a sealer coat at the next scheduled anti-fouling renewal after that date and no later than sixty months after last application
the four tin-free families: CONTROLLED DEPLETION POLYMER - a soluble rosin matrix that dissolves and leaves a leached layer
SELF-POLISHING COPOLYMER - an acrylate binder that hydrolyses at the surface and is sheared away, so the film polishes and renews itself
TIN-FREE HYBRID - a blend of rosin and acrylate, part depletion and part polishing
FOUL RELEASE - non-biocidal silicone or fluoropolymer of low surface energy and low modulus, from which fouling is released by the water flow

steps.title: What hull roughness is, and why it costs money
points: average hull roughness is reported in micrometres from a stylus gauge traversed over the hull, averaging the maximum peak-to-trough height over successive short intervals
it matters because it sits inside the boundary layer - roughness thickens the turbulent boundary layer and raises FRICTIONAL RESISTANCE, the dominant component for a full-form ship
as an order of magnitude only, a newbuilding is in the region of 100 micrometres, and roughness accumulates over successive dockings as paint goes over paint
FULL REMOVAL TO BARE STEEL RESETS IT; OVER-COATING DOES NOT
PHYSICAL roughness - paint texture, application defects, the porous leached layer, damage, weld seams and plate undulation - is permanent until the surface is treated
BIOLOGICAL roughness - slime, weed and shell - is removable, but for the same nominal height it costs far more because it is compliant, irregular and thick
THE CONSEQUENCE - the smoothest coating is not automatically the best, and a smooth fouled surface is worse than a clean rougher one
so limb a) must compare roughness behaviour ACROSS THE DOCKING INTERVAL, not at the moment of application

steps.title: The four families compared
points: CDP - moderate at application, and ROUGHENS FASTEST of the four: the soluble matrix dissolves unevenly leaving a thick porous leached layer, and successive over-coating compounds it

SPC - a smooth uniform film at application, and roughness STABLE OR IMPROVING: hydrolysis plus shear removes the outermost layer continuously so the surface is polished by service and the leached layer stays thin
SPC therefore suits long intervals and high-activity ships
HYBRID - between the two at application and between the two through the interval, at intermediate cost
FOUL RELEASE - THE SMOOTHEST AT APPLICATION, with no leached layer at all because it does not leach
but it is MECHANICALLY SOFT - tug contact, ice, grounding and hard brushing damage it, repair is difficult, and on a slow or idle ship biological roughness takes over

REPAIR AND OVER-COATING DIFFER - a self-polishing scheme can be over-coated with a compatible scheme, but nothing adheres to a foul release surface, so recoating means full removal or an approved tie coat
THE CLEANING REGIME INTERACTS WITH THE COATING - aggressive brushing removes an SPC's polishing film and physically damages a foul release coating

steps.title: First, the mechanism being enhanced
points: a foul release coating KILLS NOTHING - it works on adhesion
LOW SURFACE ENERGY - the silicone surface is poorly wetted, so biological adhesives cannot spread and key into it
LOW ELASTIC MODULUS - the film is soft and deforms under the attachment, peeling away from it rather than resisting in shear
the established relationship: THE FORCE REQUIRED TO RELEASE AN ADHERED ORGANISM SCALES WITH THE SQUARE ROOT OF THE PRODUCT OF ELASTIC MODULUS AND SURFACE ENERGY
which is why BOTH must be low, and why a hard low-energy surface such as glass is not a foul release coating
release in service is by HYDRODYNAMIC SHEAR, so the coating has a THRESHOLD SPEED below which fouling stays
that threshold is the weakness, and it is what oil incorporation is aimed at

steps.title: What incorporated oil does
points: silicone oils are blended into the matrix but NOT chemically bound into it, so being mobile and incompatible with the cured network they migrate steadily to the surface
they form a thin, continuously replenished LIQUID layer on top of the solid film, and every benefit follows from that
LOWER EFFECTIVE SURFACE ENERGY - the organism meets a mobile liquid rather than a solid, and the surface will not hold still
INTERFERENCE WITH ADHESIVE CURING - biological glues need a stable substrate to cure against, and the oil disrupts anchoring at the moment of settlement
A LOWER RELEASE THRESHOLD - less shear is needed to detach what does settle, so fouling releases at a LOWER SHIP SPEED, which is the most valuable practical gain
BETTER STATIC PERFORMANCE - idle time in port or at anchor is where a plain foul release coating is weakest, and the oil layer resists settlement while stopped
A DEGREE OF SELF-HEALING - oil migrating into a minor scratch partially restores the low-energy surface
IT REMAINS NON-BIOCIDAL IN MECHANISM - nothing is poisoned; the surface is simply made harder to hold on to
related approaches attack the same threshold - amphiphilic surfaces combining water-loving and water-repelling segments, and silicone-hydrogel systems holding a bound water layer

steps.title: The limits - which is where the marks are
points: THE OIL IS A FINITE RESERVOIR - it migrates out and is lost to the sea, so the enhancement DECAYS across the docking interval
the coating ends its life closer to an unmodified foul release film than it began
depletion is not uniform - it runs faster where shear and temperature are highest, so performance varies over the hull
REPAIR AND OVER-COATING ARE HARDER STILL - unbound oil at the surface is exactly what prevents anything from sticking, including a repair patch

THE REGULATORY QUESTION IS OPEN - the Convention controls systems whose substances act as BIOCIDES; oil-amended systems are put forward as non-biocidal and that is the mechanism, but deliberate release into the sea attracts scrutiny and the position should be checked against the ship's approval rather than assumed
oil does not make the coating mechanically tougher, does not remove the threshold speed, and does not change the cost of application or the difficulty of damage repair
THE HONEST SUMMARY - oil incorporation widens the operating window at the cost of a benefit that fades, and does not cure mechanical fragility

steps.title: The hazards
points: the hazard is THE WHOLE COATING SYSTEM - primer, tie coat, and the removal of the old scheme - not only the tin alternatives
SOLVENT VAPOUR - narcosis, headache, loss of co-ordination, dermatitis; and flammable, so a fire and explosion hazard in any enclosed space
ISOCYANATES AND EPOXY AMINES in tie coats and primers - respiratory sensitisation and occupational asthma, skin sensitisation and burns; sensitisation is PERMANENT
BIOCIDES in the antifouling - copper and organic biocides, irritant and toxic by skin contact, mist inhalation and ingestion
REMOVAL OF THE OLD COATING - blasting dust carrying heavy metals, organotin residues on older hulls, and now cybutryne; often the most toxic operation of the job
AIRLESS SPRAY - very high pressure, and HIGH-PRESSURE INJECTION INJURY looks like a pinprick and is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY
ENCLOSED AND CONFINED SPACES - oxygen deficiency, heavier-than-air solvent vapour, explosive atmosphere
PHYSICAL - work at height on staging, noise from blasting, dust, slips on overspray, simultaneous operations and hot work nearby

steps.title: The controls, in the order they must be applied
points: ELIMINATE OR SUBSTITUTE - low-solvent, high-solids or water-borne schemes where the specification allows, and a non-biocidal foul release system where the trade suits it

ENGINEERING CONTROLS - mechanical ventilation and forced extraction in every enclosed space, wet or vacuum blasting to suppress dust, containment and screening of the dock with collection of spent abrasive, explosion-protected lighting, bonding and earthing

ADMINISTRATIVE CONTROLS - safety data sheets read BEFORE the work is planned; risk assessment and method statement; permit to work with separate enclosed-space entry and hot work permits; atmosphere testing before and during entry; standby person and rehearsed rescue plan; exclusion zones and control of simultaneous operations; exposure time limits; training and health surveillance for sensitisers

PPE LAST, NEVER FIRST - air-fed positive-pressure hood or full-face breathing apparatus for spray application and for isocyanate work, a cartridge respirator being insufficient; chemical-resistant coveralls and gloves selected against the actual product; eye and face protection, hearing protection, safety footwear, harness where there is a fall risk

EMERGENCY ARRANGEMENTS - eyewash and emergency shower at the workface, fire watch and extinguishing media, and one briefed instruction: ANY SUSPECTED HIGH-PRESSURE INJECTION INJURY GOES TO HOSPITAL IMMEDIATELY however trivial the wound looks

WASTE AND ENVIRONMENT - spent abrasive and paint residues containing biocides are HAZARDOUS WASTE, contained, collected and landed ashore to a licensed receiver; nothing washed into the dock or over the side; removed cybutryne and organotin residues handled on that basis without exception

the regulatory frame named rather than quoted - MLC 2006 Regulation 4.3, ISM Code sections 7 and 8, the SOLAS enclosed-space entry and rescue drill requirement, the ship's permit-to-work system, and the yard's own regime which usually controls work done in dock

THE CLOSING JUDGEMENT - the choice of anti-fouling system settles how rough the hull will be in three years, whether the coating works at the speed the ship actually steams, and what the people applying and later removing it are exposed to

Roughness is average hull roughness in micrometres from a stylus gauge; it thickens the boundary layer and raises frictional resistance; over-coating compounds it, only removal to bare steel resets it. Physical roughness is permanent, biological is removable but costs far more per micrometre. quick_revision.major_trap: Answering the preamble instead of the limbs. The opening words invite the standard AFS Convention and CDP/SPC/hybrid/foul-release essay, and none of the three printed limbs asks for it — the taxonomy is worth two sentences and a table, and everything else belongs to roughness, oil incorporation and safety. The technical paired traps are assuming the smoothest coating is always best (a fouled foul release surface on an idle ship is worse than a clean self-polishing one, and biological roughness costs far more per micrometre than physical), and explaining oil incorporation without first stating the mechanism it enhances — release force follows the square root of modulus times surface energy, so both must be low, and the oil's whole function is to lower the threshold speed at which shear can strip the fouling off.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the four families of tin-free anti-fouling system and say what each does.
retrieval_cards.answer: Controlled depletion polymer - a soluble rosin matrix that dissolves to release biocide, leaving a leached layer. Self-polishing copolymer - an acrylate binder that hydrolyses at the surface and is sheared away, so the film polishes and renews itself. Tin-free hybrid - a blend of the two chemistries. Foul release - non-biocidal silicone or fluoropolymer with low surface energy and low modulus, from which fouling is released by the water flow.
retrieval_cards.why: Dissolves, polishes, blends, releases - the four verbs carry the whole taxonomy.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What changed for anti-fouling systems on 1 January 2023, and what must a ship do about it?
retrieval_cards.answer: The cybutryne control introduced by MEPC.331(76) applied. A cybutryne-containing system may no longer be applied or re-applied, and an existing one must be removed or over-coated with a sealer coat at the next scheduled renewal of the anti-fouling system after that date, and in any event no later than sixty months after its last application.
retrieval_cards.why: At a November 2023 sitting the control is ten months old and the transition is still running - a later paper would treat it as history.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish physical from biological hull roughness, and say which costs more.
retrieval_cards.answer: Physical roughness is the paint film's own texture, application defects, the porous leached layer, damage, weld seams and plate undulation - permanent until the surface is treated, and compounded by over-coating. Biological roughness is slime, weed and shell - removable, but for the same nominal height it costs substantially more because it is compliant, irregular and thick.
retrieval_cards.why: The comparison in limb (a) makes no sense until the two are separated.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does a CDP get rougher over the docking interval while an SPC does not?
retrieval_cards.answer: The CDP's soluble rosin matrix dissolves unevenly and leaves a thick, porous leached layer that is itself rough, and CDP schemes are usually over-coated rather than removed so the roughness compounds from docking to docking. The SPC's binder hydrolyses at the surface and is then sheared away, so the film is polished by service and the leached layer stays very thin and constant.
retrieval_cards.why: The leached layer is the mechanism, and an answer without it is describing rather than explaining.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the smoothest coating always the best choice?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. A foul release film is the smoothest at application, but it needs the ship to exceed a threshold speed for the flow to strip fouling off. On a slow or idle ship it fouls, and a smooth fouled surface is worse than a clean rougher one. Roughness is a property of the ship's operating pattern as much as of the paint.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the judgement the limb is really testing, and it prevents a one-dimensional answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a foul release coating work, and what two properties does it need?
retrieval_cards.answer: It kills nothing - it works on adhesion. It needs low surface energy, so biological adhesives cannot spread and key into the surface, and low elastic modulus, so the film deforms and peels away from the attachment. The force to release an adhered organism scales with the square root of the product of modulus and surface energy, which is why both must be low; release in service is by hydrodynamic shear above a threshold speed.
retrieval_cards.why: This one relationship makes the whole of limb (b) answerable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does incorporated silicone oil do to a foul release coating?
retrieval_cards.answer: Being blended in but not chemically bound, the oil migrates to the surface and forms a thin, continuously replenished mobile liquid layer. That lowers the effective surface energy, disrupts the curing and anchoring of biological adhesives at the moment of settlement, lowers the shear stress and therefore the ship speed needed for release, improves resistance to settlement while the ship is idle, and partially self-heals minor surface damage.
retrieval_cards.why: Every benefit follows from the single fact that the oil is unbound and mobile.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the limits of oil incorporation?
retrieval_cards.answer: The oil is a finite reservoir: it leaches out and the enhancement decays across the docking interval, faster where shear and temperature are highest, so the coating ends its life closer to an unmodified film. Unbound oil also makes repair and over-coating harder, because it is exactly what stops anything sticking. And whether an oil-amended system falls to be treated as biocidal is an open regulatory question. It does nothing for the coating's mechanical fragility.
retrieval_cards.why: Half the marks in limb (b) are in the limits, and most answers stop at the benefits.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Order the controls for anti-fouling application work.
retrieval_cards.answer: Eliminate or substitute - low-solvent, high-solids or water-borne schemes, or a non-biocidal system. Engineering - ventilation and extraction, wet or vacuum blasting, dock containment and residue collection, explosion-protected equipment. Administrative - safety data sheets read at planning, risk assessment and method statement, permit to work with enclosed-space and hot work permits, atmosphere testing, standby and rescue plan, exclusion zones, exposure limits, training and health surveillance. PPE last - air-fed hood for spraying, chemical-resistant clothing and gloves. Then emergency arrangements and hazardous waste disposal ashore.
retrieval_cards.why: PPE first is the classic wrong answer; the hierarchy is what turns a list into an argument.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which part of an anti-fouling job is usually the most toxic, and what is its acute hazard?
retrieval_cards.answer: Removing the OLD coating. Blasting dust carries heavy metals and, on older hulls, organotin residues, and now cybutryne which has to come off - and it is easy to plan the job around the new paint and forget the old. The acute hazard of the spraying itself is high-pressure injection injury from an airless gun: it looks like a pinprick and is a surgical emergency requiring immediate hospital treatment.
retrieval_cards.why: Both are routinely omitted, and both are the things a Chief Engineer would actually be held responsible for.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: ISM Code section 10 requires the Company to establish procedures to ensure that the ship is maintained in conformity with the relevant rules and regulations and with any additional requirements the Company establishes; and in meeting that requirement, to ensure that inspections are held at appropriate intervals, that any non-conformity is reported with its possible cause where known, that appropriate corrective action is taken, and that records of these activities are maintained.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: ISM Code section 10 further requires the Company to identify equipment and technical systems the sudden operational failure of which may result in hazardous situations, and to provide specific measures to promote their reliability, including the regular testing of stand-by arrangements and of equipment or technical systems not in continuous use; and requires those inspections and measures to be integrated into the ship's operational maintenance routine.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: ISM Code section 9 requires the safety management system to include procedures ensuring that non-conformities, accidents and hazardous situations are reported to the Company, investigated and analysed with the objective of improving safety and pollution prevention; and requires the Company to establish procedures for the implementation of corrective action, INCLUDING MEASURES INTENDED TO PREVENT RECURRENCE.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: ISM Code section 11 governs documentation and document control, and section 12 requires the Company to carry out internal safety audits on board and ashore AT INTERVALS NOT EXCEEDING TWELVE MONTHS, and to conduct periodical evaluation of the efficiency of the system.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: classification societies may approve a ship's planned maintenance scheme so that maintenance carried out under it is credited against continuous survey items, subject to periodical audit of the scheme and its records.

blocks.h: 1. The structure behind the four printed terms

blocks.p: The four terms are not a random list. Read against ISM Code section 10, they line up almost exactly with what that section requires the Company to ensure:

headers: Where it comes from in section 10
rows: (a) Corrective action process
That appropriate corrective action is taken — read with section 9, which requires reporting, investigation and analysis, and corrective action including measures to prevent recurrence
(b) Developing and improving maintenance records
That records of these activities are maintained — read with section 11 on documentation and document control
(c) Systematic approach of maintenance

The opening requirement for procedures to maintain the ship in conformity with the rules and with the Company's own additional requirements; the critical equipment obligation; and the requirement that inspections and measures be integrated into the ship's operational maintenance routine
(d) Maintenance intervals and periodicity of inspections
That inspections are held at appropriate intervals

blocks.p: One boundary before starting. The planned maintenance system is the Company's regime under the ISM Code and answers when the ship overhauls the item. The classification survey regime answers when class must see it. They meet at one point — where class approves the PMS, maintenance done under it can be credited against continuous survey items, subject to periodical audit. That link is worth one sentence here and no more; the survey side is Q1 on this paper.

blocks.h: 2. The three things that are not the same

blocks.p: Most weak answers use one word for three different acts. Section 9 requires all three and only names two:

rows: Correction
Fixes the symptom and restores the function
Renew the failed bearing
Corrective action
Removes the cause so it does not happen again on this ship
Correct the lubricating oil supply pressure and the alarm setting that let it fail
Preventive action
Stops it occurring elsewhere — sister ships, similar machinery
Fleet circular, revised PMS interval, amended procedure

blocks.p: The Code makes this explicit: the procedures for corrective action must include measures intended to prevent recurrence. A replaced bearing with no change to anything else is a correction, and closing a non-conformity on it is the commonest audit finding in this area.

ol: Detection and reporting. Non-conformities, defects, near misses, accidents and hazardous occurrences reported to the Company — with the possible cause where it is known. This only works under a no-blame reporting culture; a system that punishes reports stops receiving them and goes blind.

Immediate containment. Make safe, isolate, put an alternative arrangement in place, inform the master and the Designated Person Ashore, and notify class or flag where the item is statutory or class-credited.

Investigation and root cause analysis. Section 9 requires the occurrence to be investigated and analysed, not merely logged. Repeated questioning, cause-and-effect analysis or fault tree, run past the equipment to the system — the procedure, the training, the spare quality, the interval.
Decide corrective and preventive action, distinguishing the three acts above.
Assign it. A named owner, the resources, and a target date. Unassigned actions do not happen.
Implement and record — which is where limb (b) attaches.
Verify close-out AND effectiveness. Two separate checks: was it done, and did it work? An action that was done and did not work is reopened, not closed.
Disseminate. Lessons learned to sister ships; amend the SMS procedure, the job specification or the PMS interval where the analysis points there. This is where corrective action feeds limb (d).
Trend and review. Repeat defects analysed across the fleet; the whole loop verified by internal safety audit and by management review, and the efficiency of the system periodically evaluated.

blocks.h: 4. What a record must contain, and what makes it good

blocks.p: Content — a maintenance record that will survive an audit carries:

ul: the equipment identity and its tag; the job specification performed; the date and the running hours at execution;
as-found condition and as-left condition — the single most valuable field, and the one most often left blank;
measured values against limits — clearances, wear-down, insulation resistance, pressures, alignment — not a tick;
spares used, by part number, and the quantity, so consumption reconciles with the inventory;
who did it and how long it took; test results and photographs; and any defect found and its disposition;
for deferred jobs, the deferral record with its risk assessment and approval;
and the supporting certificates — servicing, calibration, lifting gear, and class credit records.

blocks.p: Quality — the attributes that make it evidence rather than paperwork: complete, contemporaneous, attributable, accurate, legible, retrievable, retained and controlled. The last is section 11: documents in force at the right place, obsolete versions removed, and the electronic system backed up.

blocks.h: 5. How a mediocre record system is actually improved

ol: Standardise the job card so that every occurrence of the same job asks for the same fields, and make the measurement fields mandatory — a system that accepts “OK” will be given “OK”.
Demand as-found condition, not only as-left. Without it there is no basis for changing an interval, and limb (d) becomes guesswork.
Record at the machine and at the time, not from memory at the end of the watch.
Link spares consumption to the job, so the inventory, the maintenance history and the ordering all reconcile.
Trend the data. A record system that is only ever written to is a filing cabinet; one that is read produces interval changes, repeat-defect analysis and early warning.
Review overdue and deferred jobs at a fixed point every month, with the reason and the approval visible.
Audit the records internally before anyone else does — sample them, and check that what is recorded matches the condition of the machine.
Use a computerised system properly: mandatory fields, offline capability, synchronisation with shore, backup, and access control. Digitisation without discipline simply produces bad records faster.
Hand records over formally at every crew change, so continuity survives the relief.
Feed the analysis back into the PMS — which is the point of the whole exercise.

blocks.p: Why the quality matters, beyond the audit: records are the evidence for class credit under an approved scheme; for port State control and vetting inspections; for warranty, insurance and damage claims; for on-hire, off-hire and sale disputes; for root cause analysis; and for interval optimisation. A ship with poor records does not merely fail an audit — it loses arguments it would otherwise win.
“Systematic” means the maintenance is generated by a method rather than by whoever notices something. Seven steps, and the last one closes back onto the first:

ol: Register every item. A complete equipment register with a tagging hierarchy — system, sub-system, item — so nothing exists outside the system and every record has somewhere to attach.

Assess criticality. Identify the equipment and technical systems whose sudden operational failure may result in a hazardous situation. This is an express requirement, and it is the step most often skipped or copied unread from a sister ship.
Choose a strategy per item, matched to that criticality — not one policy for the whole engine room:

rows: Preventive, calendar or running-hour
Time or hours elapsed
The bulk of machinery; simple and auditable
Condition-based
Measured condition — vibration, oil analysis, thermography, performance
High-value or hard-to-open machinery, where opening up is itself a risk
Run to failure (corrective)
Deliberate acceptance
Non-critical items with no safety or pollution consequence and a spare available
Statutory or class-fixed
The rule, not the engineer
Anything where the interval is set outside the Company. Not negotiable

ol: Write the job specification — what is done, by whom, with what tools, spares, permits and safety precautions, and what is to be measured and recorded.
Plan and schedule against reality: manning, port calls, weather, cargo operations, and the survey and docking windows. A plan that ignores the trading pattern generates deferrals.
Execute and record, under the permit-to-work and risk assessment regime.
Review and improve — feed defects, condition data and audit findings back into criticality, strategy and interval. That feedback is what makes it a system rather than a schedule.

blocks.p: Two obligations inside the loop that are routinely omitted. First, critical equipment attracts specific measures to promote reliability — and expressly the regular testing of stand-by arrangements and of equipment or technical systems not in continuous use: the emergency generator, the emergency fire pump, standby pumps, emergency steering, lifeboat engines. Equipment that is never used is exactly the equipment that fails when it is. Second, those tests and inspections must be integrated into the ship's operational maintenance routine — they belong in the PMS, not on a separate list somebody remembers.

blocks.h: (d) Maintenance intervals and periodicity of inspections

rows: Statutory — SOLAS and MARPOL inspection, testing and drill requirements
No. Fixed by the instrument
Classification — survey items and the terms of an approved maintenance scheme
Only with the society's agreement, and the credit is at risk if not
Maker's recommendation
Yes, with justification — but warranty and technical support may follow the recommendation
Company standard
Yes — this is where fleet experience and analysis are applied
Condition
The interval is set by the machine; the Company sets the monitoring regime instead

blocks.p: The four bases on which an interval is expressed: calendar time; running hours; use or cycles; and condition. Choosing the wrong basis is a real error — a standby pump maintained on running hours may never come due at all, which is precisely why the standby-testing obligation exists.

blocks.h: 8. Optimising an interval, and changing one safely

blocks.p: Both directions cost money and one of them costs more than money:

ul: Too short — unnecessary opening-up, wasted spares and manhours, and defects introduced by reassembly. Dismantling a healthy machine is a real source of failure, not a neutral act.
Too long — wear beyond limits, consequential damage, unplanned breakdown, and on a critical item a safety or pollution consequence.

blocks.p: Optimisation therefore runs on evidence: as-found condition records, defect and failure history, condition-monitoring trends, maker guidance and criticality. Extending an interval is a controlled change — justified from data, risk assessed, approved by the Company's technical management, agreed with class or the maker where the item is credited or under warranty, and recorded. Shortening one is not free either, and the same evidence should support it.

Deferral is not interval change. Where a job cannot be done when due, the SMS must have a procedure: risk assessment, compensating measures, approval at the right level ashore, agreement of class or flag if the item is statutory or credited, a new date, and a record. Silent deferral is the failure mode, and a monthly review of overdue items is what catches it.
Inspections are a distinct rhythm from maintenance jobs, and the limb names them separately:

ul: Continuous and daily — watchkeeping rounds, alarm and parameter monitoring.
Weekly and monthly — the statutory life-saving and fire-fighting appliance inspections and tests, emergency equipment tests, and the safety committee's own inspections.
Before departure — steering gear testing and the associated checks.
Periodic shipboard inspections — the master's and senior officers' inspections of accommodation, catering and working spaces, which are a seafarer welfare requirement as well as a maintenance one.

Annual and multi-annual — servicing and thorough examination of life-saving appliances, launching appliances and release gear, under the dedicated maintenance-requirements instrument in force since 1 January 2020; and the class and statutory survey cycle.
Internal safety audits — on board and ashore, at intervals not exceeding twelve months. This is the Code's own number and is worth stating exactly.
Management review — the periodical evaluation of the efficiency of the system, which is where the trends from limb (b) are supposed to arrive.

blocks.p: The closing point that ties all four limbs together. The four terms are one loop, not four subjects. Intervals generate the work; the work generates records; the records reveal non-conformities; the non-conformities drive corrective action; and corrective action changes the intervals. The systematic approach is simply the name for that loop being closed. A ship where the loop is open — where records are written but never read — has a planned maintenance system on paper and a reactive one in fact.

Four limbs, four marks each, printed as bare terms with almost no verb attached to them. That is the difficulty: the stem gives four nouns and leaves the candidate to supply the question. The structural key is that the four terms are, almost exactly, the four things ISM Code section 10 requires the Company to ensure — inspections at appropriate intervals, reporting of non-conformity, appropriate corrective action, and records of these activities.

Opening the answer with that mapping does three things at once. It shows the candidate recognised what the examiner was quoting from. It turns four disconnected essays into one loop. And it makes the closing paragraph write itself: intervals generate work, work generates records, records reveal non-conformities, non-conformities drive corrective action, and corrective action changes the intervals.

The other structural decision is to keep the class survey material to a single sentence. An approved planned maintenance scheme can be credited against continuous survey items — that is the whole link, and Q1 on this paper is where the survey side belongs. Writing it twice loses time in both.

The stem prints “...and ISM code with the following terms,” — a comma where a colon is required to introduce four lettered items. It reads as though the terms were a continuation of the sentence rather than a list. It also prints “ISM code” with a lower-case c, ends three limbs with semicolons and the fourth with a full stop, and capitalises “Inspections” mid-phrase.

All of it is preserved exactly as printed. The practical consequence is that the candidate must supply the structure the punctuation does not: four headings, four marks, four blocks, and no drift between them.

rows: Correction
The symptom
Renew the bearing
Corrective action
The cause, on this ship
Fix the oil supply pressure and the alarm setting that allowed it
Preventive action
The same cause elsewhere
Fleet circular, revised interval, amended procedure on the sister ships

blocks.p: The Code requires corrective action procedures to include measures intended to prevent recurrence, which is why a renewed bearing and a closed report is an audit finding rather than a closure. If you remember nothing else about limb (a), remember that replacing the part is not corrective action.

blocks.h: The two parts of section 10 that get left out

ul: Critical equipment. The Company must identify equipment and technical systems whose sudden operational failure may result in a hazardous situation, and provide specific measures to promote reliability — expressly including regular testing of stand-by arrangements and of equipment not in continuous use. Emergency generator, emergency fire pump, standby pumps, emergency steering, lifeboat engines. Equipment that is never used is exactly the equipment that fails when it is needed.

Integration. Those inspections and measures must be integrated into the ship's operational maintenance routine — in the PMS, not on a separate list somebody keeps in a drawer. An auditor who finds critical equipment tests outside the PMS has found a non-conformity.

blocks.p: A related trap in limb (d): a standby pump maintained on running hours may never come due at all, because it does not run. That is precisely why the standby-testing obligation exists and why the basis of an interval matters as much as its length.

ul: Writing one essay on planned maintenance and hoping it covers four limbs. Four terms, four headings, four marks each.
Never mentioning the ISM Code, when the stem names it.
Using “corrective action” to mean repairing the defect.
Omitting verification of effectiveness — an action that was done but did not work is reopened, not closed.
Describing records as a list of forms rather than as evidence, and never saying what makes a record good.
Leaving out as-found condition, which is what makes interval optimisation possible at all.
Answering limb (c) with the words “planned maintenance system” and no method — register, criticality, strategy, specification, plan, execute, review.
Omitting critical equipment and the standby-testing obligation.
In limb (d), giving intervals without their source, and so implying the Company can change a statutory one.
Treating interval extension as an engineering decision alone. It is a controlled change — justified, risk assessed, approved, and agreed with class or the maker where credited.
Confusing deferral with interval change. They are different acts with different approvals.
Forgetting the twelve-month internal audit ceiling, which is the one number the Code itself supplies.
“Which section of the ISM Code covers maintenance?” Section 10 — maintenance of the ship and equipment. Section 9 covers reports and analysis of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences.
“You renewed the failed bearing. Is the non-conformity closed?” No — that is a correction. Corrective action removes the cause and must include measures to prevent recurrence.
“What is critical equipment?” Equipment and technical systems whose sudden operational failure may result in a hazardous situation.

“Give three examples and say what the Code requires for them.” Emergency generator, emergency fire pump, standby steering. Specific measures to promote reliability, including regular testing of standby arrangements and equipment not in continuous use.
“Where must those tests live?” Integrated into the ship's operational maintenance routine — in the PMS.
“How often are internal safety audits?” At intervals not exceeding twelve months, on board and ashore.

“Who may extend a maintenance interval?” The Company for its own standards, with justification and risk assessment; not at all for a statutory interval; and only with the society's agreement where the item is class-credited.
“What is the risk of maintaining too often?” Wasted resource, and defects introduced by unnecessary dismantling and reassembly.

“A job cannot be done when due. What do you do?” Follow the deferral procedure — risk assessment, compensating measures, approval ashore, class or flag agreement if statutory or credited, a new date, and a record.

“Why does class care about your maintenance records?” Because under an approved planned maintenance scheme those records are what the credit against continuous survey items rests on, and the scheme is audited.
“What single field would you add to a poor job card?” As-found condition, with measured values against limits.

What does the ISM Code require the Company to establish for maintenance? Procedures to ensure the ship is maintained in conformity with the relevant rules and with the Company's own additional requirements.

Name the four things section 10 requires the Company to ensure. Inspections at appropriate intervals; non-conformity reported with its possible cause; appropriate corrective action taken; and records of these activities maintained.
Who is the Designated Person Ashore and what is his role here? The link between ship and highest level of management, with access to the highest level, to whom non-conformities are reported.
Name four maintenance strategies. Calendar or running-hour preventive, condition-based, run to failure, and statutory or class-fixed.
What is a criticality assessment for? To decide which items get which strategy, and to identify the critical equipment the Code requires to be identified.
Name three condition-monitoring techniques. Vibration analysis, lubricating oil analysis, and thermographic or performance monitoring.
What makes a maintenance record good evidence? Complete, contemporaneous, attributable, accurate, legible, retrievable, retained and under document control.
Where does document control sit in the Code? Section 11, documentation.

What is the difference between deferring a job and extending an interval? Deferral moves one occurrence with a risk assessment and approval; extension changes the standard and needs justification, risk assessment and, where credited, class agreement.

blocks.p: One sentence for the whole answer: section 10 wants inspections at intervals, non-conformities reported, corrective action taken, and records kept — which is limbs (d), (a), (a) and (b), with (c) as the method that holds them together.
For limb (a), nine steps but four words: REPORT, INVESTIGATE, ACT, VERIFY — and one distinction: SYMPTOM, CAUSE, ELSEWHERE.
For limb (b), the good-record test in one line: WHAT DID YOU FIND, WHAT DID YOU MEASURE, WHAT DID YOU USE, WHAT DID YOU LEAVE?
For limb (c), seven steps: REGISTER, RATE, CHOOSE, SPECIFY, PLAN, DO, REVIEW — and the review step is what makes it a system.
For limb (d), four sources and four bases: sources STATUTE, CLASS, MAKER, COMPANY; bases CALENDAR, HOURS, USE, CONDITION. And one number: TWELVE MONTHS for internal audits.

ul: ISM Code, base A.741(18) of 1993, mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX from 1 July 1998, as amended through MSC.353(92), in force 1 January 2015. That is the operative text at this sitting and is the latest Code amendment recorded.

Section 10 — maintenance of the ship and equipment: procedures, inspections at appropriate intervals, reporting, corrective action, records, critical equipment and standby testing, and integration into the operational maintenance routine. Section 11 — documentation and document control. Section 12 — internal safety audits at intervals not exceeding twelve months, and periodical evaluation of the efficiency of the system.

MSC.402(96) — maintenance, thorough examination, operational testing, overhaul and repair of lifeboats and rescue boats, launching appliances and release gear. In force 1 January 2020 through MSC.404(96). Its MSC.559(108) amendment enters force 1 January 2026 and is future here.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of the evidence

blocks.p: The primary layer here is instrument identity and status, not text, and the distinction is worth being exact about.

The ISM Code amendment chain is primary: the corpus central amendment register records the base, the mandatory route through SOLAS chapter IX, and the chain to MSC.353(92), in force 1 January 2015 and recorded as the latest Code amendment. The Code text itself is not held as an extractable corpus object, so sections 9, 10, 11 and 12 are described and not quoted, and no sub-paragraph is reproduced verbatim.

The mapping of the four printed terms onto section 10 is a structural reading derived in this session, not a statement printed in any instrument. It is offered as a reading and labelled as one, because it is the answer's spine and the reader is entitled to know where it came from.

The planned maintenance content is industry practice and engineering judgement. No company procedure, maintenance management software product, class approval scheme or society is named anywhere, and no numerical maintenance interval is asserted for any item of machinery — intervals are described by their source and their basis instead, because they are set by maker recommendation, class or statutory requirement and company standard, and none of those is held. The one number given, twelve months for internal safety audits, is the Code's own.

Currency, and one reversal. A.1188(33), the 2023 Guidelines on implementation of the ISM Code by Administrations, is a 6 December 2023 instrument — one month after this sitting. It is therefore future and is not cited, and the operative Assembly guidance here is its predecessor, referred to descriptively rather than by number because its identity could not be established from a held source. MSC.559(108) is future for the same reason, entering force 1 January 2026. Both are exactly the kind of instrument a later editor would import.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Four limbs of four marks each, printed as bare noun phrases with almost no verb attached, behind a stem that names both PMS and the ISM Code. The examiner is quoting, almost term for term, the four things ISM Code section 10 requires the Company to ensure - inspections at appropriate intervals, reporting of non-conformity, appropriate corrective action, and records of these activities - and the discriminating feature is whether the candidate recognises that and answers the four terms as ONE LOOP rather than as four disconnected essays. The second discriminating feature is the three-way distinction between correction, corrective action and preventive action, which is what section 9 actually requires.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4, all printed. Equal marks and four bare terms mean the answer must be four visibly separate blocks with no drift. An opening mapping section is written FIRST, before the limbs, because it costs a table and buys coherence across all sixteen marks. Limb a) gets a three-row distinction table and a nine-step process. Limb b) gets a content-and-quality section and a ten-step improvement list, because 'developing and improving' is an action instruction. Limb c) gets a seven-step loop with a four-row strategy table and the two commonly omitted obligations. Limb d) gets a source table, the four bases, an optimisation section and an inspection-rhythm list ending on the twelve-month audit ceiling.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate names the ISM Code and knows which sections apply; distinguishes correction from corrective action from preventive action and knows the Code demands measures to prevent recurrence; can say what makes a maintenance record evidence rather than paperwork; can describe a maintenance METHOD rather than restating the words 'planned maintenance system'; knows the critical equipment and standby-testing obligation and that it must be integrated into the operational routine; and knows where an interval comes from, so that he does not imply the Company may change a statutory one.

decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW - the Code's operative text has been stable since 1 January 2015 and no later Code amendment exists to import. Two instruments are future by narrow margins and are the live edges: A.1188(33), the 2023 ISM implementation guidelines, adopted ONE MONTH after this sitting, and MSC.559(108), in force 1 January 2026. Both are exactly what an editor working from a later paper would add. The answer is also protected structurally, because it asserts no numerical maintenance interval that could be silently updated.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The ISM Code is international and applies through SOLAS chapter IX. The Company's own standards are contractual rather than national. The domestic statute at this sitting is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958; the 2025 Act commenced 15 March 2026 and is prohibited.
technical_ambiguities: Whether the planned maintenance system and the class survey regime are the same thing - they are not; the PMS is the Company's ISM-driven overhaul regime and the survey regime is class's, and they meet only where class approves the scheme and credits maintenance against survey items
Whether replacing the failed part is corrective action - it is a CORRECTION; corrective action removes the cause, and the Code requires measures intended to prevent recurrence
Whether closing an action means checking it was done - it means checking it was done AND that it worked; an ineffective action is reopened
Whether a maintenance record is paperwork or evidence - it is the evidence for class credit, port State control, vetting, insurance, charter disputes and interval optimisation
Whether as-left condition alone is sufficient - it is not; without AS-FOUND condition there is no basis for changing an interval

Whether critical equipment is a class term - it is an ISM Code requirement: equipment whose sudden operational failure may result in a hazardous situation, attracting specific measures including regular testing of standby arrangements
Whether critical equipment tests may sit outside the PMS - they may not; the Code requires them to be integrated into the ship's operational maintenance routine
Whether running hours is always the right basis for an interval - it is not; a standby item maintained on running hours may never come due, which is why the standby-testing obligation exists
Whether deferring a job and extending an interval are the same act - they are not; they are different decisions with different approvals and different records
