Describing intervals by SOURCE and BASIS rather than by number is both honest and structurally protective, because it leaves nothing that a later editor could silently update. questions.understand_first: Underneath the four terms there is one loop, and seeing it is the whole question. Somebody has to decide how often each machine is opened, tested or looked at. That decision generates work. The work only counts if somebody writes down what they found — not that they did it, but what condition the machine was actually in and what they measured. Those written findings are what reveal that something is not as it should be. And when something is not as it should be, the response has to go further than replacing the broken part: it has to find out why it broke and stop that happening again — which very often means changing how often the job is done, and the loop closes. The systematic approach is just the name for keeping that loop closed rather than letting it run in one direction. The distinction that carries the most marks is between three different things people all call 'fixing it': putting the machine back into service, removing the reason it failed, and making sure the same reason cannot bite on the sister ship. Only the first of those is what most people actually do. And the second idea worth holding is that the equipment most likely to fail when it is finally needed is the equipment that never runs — emergency generators, standby pumps, emergency steering — which is why the rules insist those are deliberately tested on a schedule rather than left to look after themselves.
questions.memory_cue: The Code's own four: INTERVALS, REPORT, ACT, RECORD (1) - which is limbs (d), (a), (a), (b). Limb (a): SYMPTOM, CAUSE, ELSEWHERE (2). Limb (c): REGISTER, RATE, CHOOSE, SPECIFY, PLAN, DO, REVIEW (6). Limb (d) sources: STATUTE, CLASS, MAKER, COMPANY (7); bases: CALENDAR, HOURS, USE, CONDITION (7).

steps.title: The structure behind the four printed terms
points: the four terms line up almost exactly with what ISM Code section 10 requires the Company to ensure
CORRECTIVE ACTION PROCESS - that appropriate corrective action is taken, read with section 9 on reporting, investigation and analysis and measures to prevent recurrence
MAINTENANCE RECORDS - that records of these activities are maintained, read with section 11 on documentation and document control

SYSTEMATIC APPROACH - the requirement for PROCEDURES to maintain the ship in conformity with the rules and the Company's own additional requirements, the critical equipment obligation, and integration into the operational maintenance routine
MAINTENANCE INTERVALS AND PERIODICITY - that inspections are held at appropriate intervals
ONE BOUNDARY BEFORE STARTING - the PMS is the Company's regime under the ISM Code and says when the ship OVERHAULS the item; the class survey regime says when class must SEE it
they meet where class APPROVES the PMS, so maintenance can be credited against continuous survey items subject to periodical audit - one sentence, because the survey side is Q1 on this paper

steps.title: The three things that are not the same
points: CORRECTION fixes the symptom and restores the function - renew the failed bearing
CORRECTIVE ACTION removes the cause so it does not happen again on this ship - correct the lubricating oil supply pressure and the alarm setting that let it fail
PREVENTIVE ACTION stops it occurring elsewhere - fleet circular, revised PMS interval, amended procedure on sister ships
the Code makes it explicit: corrective action procedures must include MEASURES INTENDED TO PREVENT RECURRENCE
a replaced bearing with no other change is a CORRECTION, and closing a non-conformity on it is the commonest audit finding in this area

steps.title: The process, end to end
points: DETECTION AND REPORTING - non-conformities, defects, near misses, accidents and hazardous occurrences reported to the Company with the possible cause where known
this works only under a NO-BLAME REPORTING CULTURE; a system that punishes reports stops receiving them and goes blind
IMMEDIATE CONTAINMENT - make safe, isolate, alternative arrangement, inform the master and the Designated Person Ashore, notify class or flag where statutory or class-credited

INVESTIGATION AND ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS - the Code requires the occurrence to be investigated and analysed, not merely logged; repeated questioning, cause-and-effect analysis or fault tree, run PAST the equipment to the system
DECIDE CORRECTIVE AND PREVENTIVE ACTION, distinguishing the three acts
ASSIGN IT - a named owner, the resources and a target date; unassigned actions do not happen
IMPLEMENT AND RECORD - which is where limb b) attaches
VERIFY CLOSE-OUT AND EFFECTIVENESS - two separate checks: was it done, and did it work? An action that was done and did not work is REOPENED
DISSEMINATE - lessons learned to sister ships, amend the SMS procedure, the job specification or the PMS INTERVAL, which is where corrective action feeds limb d)
TREND AND REVIEW - repeat defects analysed across the fleet, the loop verified by internal safety audit and by management review

steps.title: What a record must contain, and what makes it good
points: equipment identity and tag, the job specification performed, the date and the RUNNING HOURS AT EXECUTION
AS-FOUND AND AS-LEFT CONDITION - the single most valuable field and the one most often left blank
MEASURED VALUES AGAINST LIMITS - clearances, wear-down, insulation resistance, pressures, alignment - NOT A TICK
spares used by part number and quantity, so consumption reconciles with the inventory
who did it and how long it took; test results and photographs; any defect found and its disposition
for deferred jobs, the deferral record with its risk assessment and approval
supporting certificates - servicing, calibration, lifting gear, and class credit records
QUALITY ATTRIBUTES - complete, contemporaneous, attributable, accurate, legible, retrievable, retained and CONTROLLED
control is section 11 - documents in force at the right place, obsolete versions removed, the electronic system backed up

steps.title: How a mediocre record system is actually improved
points: STANDARDISE THE JOB CARD so every occurrence asks the same fields, and make measurement fields MANDATORY - a system that accepts 'OK' will be given 'OK'
DEMAND AS-FOUND CONDITION, not only as-left; without it there is no basis for changing an interval
RECORD AT THE MACHINE AND AT THE TIME, not from memory at the end of the watch
LINK SPARES CONSUMPTION TO THE JOB so inventory, history and ordering reconcile
TREND THE DATA - a record system only ever written to is a filing cabinet; one that is read produces interval changes and early warning
REVIEW OVERDUE AND DEFERRED JOBS at a fixed monthly point, with reason and approval visible
AUDIT THE RECORDS INTERNALLY BEFORE ANYONE ELSE DOES, and check that what is recorded matches the condition of the machine
USE A COMPUTERISED SYSTEM PROPERLY - mandatory fields, offline capability, shore synchronisation, backup, access control; digitisation without discipline produces bad records faster
HAND RECORDS OVER FORMALLY AT EVERY CREW CHANGE so continuity survives the relief
FEED THE ANALYSIS BACK INTO THE PMS - which is the point of the whole exercise

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE AUDIT - class credit under an approved scheme, port State control, vetting, warranty and insurance claims, on-hire and off-hire and sale disputes, root cause analysis and interval optimisation

steps.title: The closed loop
points: 'systematic' means maintenance generated by a METHOD rather than by whoever notices something
REGISTER EVERY ITEM - a complete equipment register with a tagging hierarchy so nothing exists outside the system
ASSESS CRITICALITY - identify equipment and technical systems whose SUDDEN OPERATIONAL FAILURE MAY RESULT IN A HAZARDOUS SITUATION; the step most often skipped or copied unread from a sister ship

CHOOSE A STRATEGY PER ITEM matched to criticality - preventive on calendar or running hours, condition-based, run to failure for non-critical items, and statutory or class-fixed where the interval is set outside the Company
WRITE THE JOB SPECIFICATION - what is done, by whom, with what tools, spares, permits and precautions, and what is measured and recorded
PLAN AND SCHEDULE against reality - manning, port calls, weather, cargo operations, survey and docking windows; a plan that ignores the trading pattern generates deferrals
EXECUTE AND RECORD under the permit-to-work and risk assessment regime
REVIEW AND IMPROVE - feed defects, condition data and audit findings back into criticality, strategy and interval; THAT FEEDBACK IS WHAT MAKES IT A SYSTEM RATHER THAN A SCHEDULE

CRITICAL EQUIPMENT attracts specific measures to promote reliability, expressly including REGULAR TESTING OF STANDBY ARRANGEMENTS AND EQUIPMENT NOT IN CONTINUOUS USE - emergency generator, emergency fire pump, standby pumps, emergency steering, lifeboat engines
EQUIPMENT THAT IS NEVER USED IS EXACTLY THE EQUIPMENT THAT FAILS WHEN IT IS NEEDED
and those tests must be INTEGRATED INTO THE SHIP'S OPERATIONAL MAINTENANCE ROUTINE - in the PMS, not on a separate list

steps.title: Where an interval comes from
points: STATUTORY - SOLAS and MARPOL inspection, testing and drill requirements; the Company CANNOT change them
CLASSIFICATION - survey items and the terms of an approved maintenance scheme; changeable only with the society's agreement, and the credit is at risk if not
MAKER'S RECOMMENDATION - changeable with justification, but warranty and technical support may follow the recommendation
COMPANY STANDARD - changeable, and this is where fleet experience and analysis are applied
CONDITION - the interval is set by the MACHINE, and the Company sets the monitoring regime instead
THE FOUR BASES on which an interval is expressed - CALENDAR time, RUNNING HOURS, USE or cycles, and CONDITION
choosing the wrong basis is a real error - a standby pump maintained on running hours may never come due at all, which is why the standby-testing obligation exists

steps.title: Optimising an interval, and changing one safely
points: TOO SHORT - unnecessary opening-up, wasted spares and manhours, and DEFECTS INTRODUCED BY REASSEMBLY; dismantling a healthy machine is a real source of failure
TOO LONG - wear beyond limits, consequential damage, unplanned breakdown, and on a critical item a safety or pollution consequence
OPTIMISATION RUNS ON EVIDENCE - as-found condition records, defect and failure history, condition-monitoring trends, maker guidance and criticality

EXTENDING AN INTERVAL IS A CONTROLLED CHANGE - justified from data, risk assessed, approved by the Company's technical management, agreed with class or the maker where credited or under warranty, and recorded
shortening one is not free either, and the same evidence should support it
DEFERRAL IS NOT INTERVAL CHANGE - it needs a procedure: risk assessment, compensating measures, approval ashore, class or flag agreement if statutory or credited, a new date and a record
SILENT DEFERRAL IS THE FAILURE MODE, and a monthly review of overdue items is what catches it

steps.title: Periodicity of inspections
points: CONTINUOUS AND DAILY - watchkeeping rounds, alarm and parameter monitoring
WEEKLY AND MONTHLY - statutory life-saving and fire-fighting appliance inspections and tests, emergency equipment tests, and safety committee inspections
BEFORE DEPARTURE - steering gear testing and the associated checks
PERIODIC SHIPBOARD INSPECTIONS - the master's and senior officers' inspections of accommodation, catering and working spaces, a seafarer welfare requirement as well as a maintenance one

ANNUAL AND MULTI-ANNUAL - servicing and thorough examination of life-saving appliances, launching appliances and release gear under the dedicated maintenance-requirements instrument in force since 1 January 2020, and the class and statutory survey cycle
INTERNAL SAFETY AUDITS on board and ashore AT INTERVALS NOT EXCEEDING TWELVE MONTHS - the Code's own number
MANAGEMENT REVIEW - the periodical evaluation of the efficiency of the system, where the trends from limb b) are supposed to arrive

THE CLOSING POINT - the four terms are one loop: intervals generate work, work generates records, records reveal non-conformities, non-conformities drive corrective action, and corrective action changes the intervals
a ship where the loop is open, where records are written but never read, has a planned maintenance system on paper and a reactive one in fact

quick_revision.recall_15s: The four printed terms ARE ISM Code section 10: inspections at appropriate intervals (d), non-conformity reported with possible cause, appropriate corrective action taken (a), and records of these activities maintained (b) — with the procedures, critical equipment and integration requirements making up the systematic approach (c). Section 9 requires reporting, investigation and analysis, and corrective action including measures to prevent recurrence. Correction fixes the symptom; corrective action removes the cause; preventive action stops it elsewhere. Process: report → contain → investigate root cause → decide corrective and preventive → assign owner and date → implement and record → verify close-out AND effectiveness → disseminate → trend and audit. Records must carry as-found and as-left condition, measured values against limits, running hours, spares by part number, and who did it — complete, contemporaneous, attributable, accurate, retrievable, retained and under document control (section 11). Improve them by standardising job cards, making measurement fields mandatory, recording at the machine, trending, monthly overdue review, internal audit and feedback into the PMS. Systematic approach: register → criticality → strategy per item → job specification → plan against the trading pattern → execute → review. Critical equipment — sudden failure may cause a hazardous situation — gets specific reliability measures including regular testing of standby arrangements and equipment not in continuous use, and those tests must be integrated into the operational maintenance routine. Intervals come from statute (unchangeable), class (society's agreement), maker and Company; bases are calendar, running hours, use and condition. Too short introduces defects; too long risks failure. Extension is a controlled change; deferral is a different act with its own approval. Internal safety audits at intervals not exceeding twelve months.
critical_numbers: Internal safety audits on board and ashore at intervals NOT EXCEEDING TWELVE MONTHS - ISM Code section 12
ISM Code base A.741(18) 1993; mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX from 1 July 1998
The operative Code text at this sitting is the MSC.353(92) amendment, in force 1 January 2015
MSC.428(98) cyber risk in the SMS - effective at the first Document of Compliance verification after 1 January 2021
The dedicated life-saving appliance maintenance framework, MSC.402(96), in force 1 January 2020 through MSC.404(96)
Four bases for an interval: calendar, running hours, use or cycles, and condition
quick_revision.critical_regulation: ISM Code section 10 is the whole question. It requires the Company to establish procedures to ensure the ship is maintained in conformity with the relevant rules and regulations and with any additional requirements the Company establishes; and, in meeting that, to ensure that inspections are held at appropriate intervals, that any non-conformity is reported with its possible cause where known, that appropriate corrective action is taken, and that records of these activities are maintained. It further requires critical equipment to be identified and given specific reliability measures including regular testing of standby arrangements and equipment not in continuous use, and requires those inspections and measures to be integrated into the ship's operational maintenance routine. Read it with section 9 for corrective action including measures to prevent recurrence, section 11 for document control, and section 12 for internal audits at intervals not exceeding twelve months.
quick_revision.major_trap: Using “corrective action” to mean repairing the defect. Replacing the failed component is a correction; corrective action removes the cause, and the Code expressly requires the procedures to include measures intended to prevent recurrence, which reaches beyond this ship to the sister vessels. A non-conformity closed on a replaced part with nothing else changed is the commonest audit finding in this area. The paired traps are omitting critical equipment and the standby-testing obligation — equipment that never runs is exactly what fails when it is needed — and implying in limb (d) that the Company may change a statutory interval, when it may change only its own standards and, with the society's agreement, class-credited ones.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What four things does ISM Code section 10 require the Company to ensure?
retrieval_cards.answer: That inspections are held at appropriate intervals; that any non-conformity is reported, with its possible cause if known; that appropriate corrective action is taken; and that records of these activities are maintained. All four sit under the opening requirement to establish procedures ensuring the ship is maintained in conformity with the relevant rules and with the Company's own additional requirements.
retrieval_cards.why: These four are, almost term for term, the four limbs the paper prints - recognising that is the answer's spine.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish correction, corrective action and preventive action.
retrieval_cards.answer: Correction fixes the symptom and restores function - renew the failed bearing. Corrective action removes the cause so it does not recur on this ship - correct the oil supply pressure and the alarm setting that allowed the failure. Preventive action stops the same cause biting elsewhere - a fleet circular, a revised interval, an amended procedure on the sister ships. The Code requires corrective action procedures to include measures intended to prevent recurrence.
retrieval_cards.why: One word is routinely used for three different acts, and only one of them is what the Code asks for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Run the corrective action process from detection to closure.
retrieval_cards.answer: Report the non-conformity with its possible cause; contain it and make safe, informing the master and the DPA and notifying class or flag where statutory or credited; investigate and analyse the root cause past the equipment to the system; decide corrective and preventive action; assign an owner, resources and a date; implement and record; verify both that it was done and that it worked, reopening it if not; disseminate to sister ships and amend the procedure or the interval; then trend and verify through internal audit and management review.
retrieval_cards.why: Report, investigate, act, verify - and the verification of EFFECTIVENESS is what most systems omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is critical equipment under the ISM Code, and what does the Code require for it?
retrieval_cards.answer: Equipment and technical systems the sudden operational failure of which may result in a hazardous situation. The Company must identify them and provide specific measures to promote their reliability, including the regular testing of standby arrangements and of equipment or technical systems not in continuous use - and those measures must be integrated into the ship's operational maintenance routine rather than kept on a separate list.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the part of section 10 most often omitted, and the integration requirement is a standing audit finding.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What single field would you add to a poor maintenance job card, and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: As-found condition, with measured values against limits rather than a tick. Without as-found condition there is no evidence of how the machine actually was when it was opened, and therefore no basis on which to lengthen or shorten the interval - which means the whole feedback loop that makes a planned maintenance system 'planned' cannot run.
retrieval_cards.why: It connects limb (b) to limb (d) in one sentence and is the highest-value practical point in the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What makes a maintenance record evidence rather than paperwork?
retrieval_cards.answer: That it is complete, contemporaneous, attributable to a named person, accurate with measured values, legible, retrievable, retained for the required period, and under document control with obsolete versions removed and the electronic system backed up. Records in that state support class credit under an approved scheme, port State control, vetting, warranty and insurance claims, charter disputes, root cause analysis and interval optimisation.
retrieval_cards.why: The commercial consequences are what turn a bureaucratic answer into a Chief Engineer's answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Describe the systematic approach to maintenance in seven steps.
retrieval_cards.answer: Register every item with a tagging hierarchy so nothing sits outside the system; assess criticality and identify the critical equipment; choose a maintenance strategy per item - calendar or running-hour preventive, condition-based, run to failure, or statutory and class-fixed; write the job specification with tools, spares, permits and what is to be measured; plan and schedule against manning, port calls and the survey and docking windows; execute and record under permit to work; and review, feeding defects, condition data and audit findings back into criticality, strategy and interval.
retrieval_cards.why: The seventh step is what makes it a system rather than a schedule.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where do maintenance intervals come from, and which of them may the Company change?
retrieval_cards.answer: Statutory intervals from SOLAS and MARPOL - the Company cannot change them. Classification intervals, including the terms of an approved maintenance scheme - only with the society's agreement, and the survey credit is at risk if not. Maker's recommendations - changeable with justification, though warranty and technical support may follow them. Company standards - changeable, and this is where fleet experience is applied. Condition-based intervals are set by the machine, the Company setting the monitoring regime instead.
retrieval_cards.why: Implying that the Company may vary a statutory interval is the structural error in limb (d).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why can maintaining too often be as damaging as maintaining too seldom?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because unnecessary dismantling introduces defects - assembly error, contamination, gasket and fastener failure - in addition to wasting spares and manhours. Too seldom risks wear beyond limits, consequential damage and unplanned breakdown, and on a critical item a safety or pollution consequence. Both directions are errors, which is why interval optimisation runs on as-found records, failure history and condition trends.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the judgement behind condition-based maintenance and it links limb (d) back to limb (b).

retrieval_cards.prompt: A due job cannot be carried out. What is the correct action, and how does it differ from extending the interval?
retrieval_cards.answer: Follow the deferral procedure: risk assess it, put compensating measures in place, obtain approval at the right level ashore, obtain class or flag agreement if the item is statutory or class-credited, set a new date and record all of it. Extending the interval is a different act - a controlled change to the standard, justified from data, risk assessed, approved by technical management and agreed with class or the maker where credited. Silent deferral is the failure mode and a monthly overdue review is what catches it.
retrieval_cards.why: Confusing a one-off deferral with a permanent interval change is how a PMS quietly stops being planned.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How often must internal safety audits be carried out, and where does the requirement sit?
retrieval_cards.answer: On board and ashore at intervals not exceeding twelve months, under ISM Code section 12, which also requires the Company to conduct a periodical evaluation of the efficiency of the safety management system.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the one number the Code itself supplies in this area, and it is the mechanism by which the whole loop is checked.

questions.short_title: ISO 8217 Marine Fuel Standards, the Fuel Oil Analysis Report and Corrective Action
questions.text_verbatim: Name the present ISO standards for Marine Fuel and explain the salient features of it. With reference to fuel oil analysis report, explain the content of such a report and discuss corrective action that would be required to be initiated against each of the undesirable observations in it. (16)
questions.subpart_marks_note: Printed as a single unlimbed block of 16 marks, but it sets THREE distinct tasks in two sentences: name the standards and give their salient features; state the content of a fuel oil analysis report; and give the corrective action for each adverse observation. The last of the three is the largest and the paper gives it no separate mark, so the candidate must allocate the page himself.
questions.recurrence_adjudication: The host prints a single self-referential annotation and claims no earlier sitting. MIW's canonical position is that QP2408-Q6 sets substantially the same first task nine months later, which the host does not and could not know.
decomposition: Which ISO standard is THE marine fuel specification, and which edition is current AT THIS SITTING - the whole question turns on that date
The supporting ISO standards that a complete answer names, in particular the one that governs how a disputed result is interpreted
The salient features of the specification: its structure into distillate and residual tables, the general requirements clause, and the deference of sulphur to statutory law
The parameters the specification controls, grouped by what they actually threaten - handling, combustion, wear, corrosion, safety, statutory compliance
The content of a fuel oil analysis report, section by section, including the parts candidates omit - sample identity, method and the precision statement
The governance step that must come before any corrective action: sample identity, ISO 4259 precision, segregation and the contractual notice period
Corrective action parameter by parameter, which is the largest of the three tasks and gets a table
The three findings where the correct action is NOT to burn the fuel, which is where the judgement mark sits
reuse_evidence: NEAR RECURRENCE ON THE FIRST TASK ONLY. QP2408-Q6 (August 2024, +9 months) prints as limb a): 'Name the present ISO standards for Marine Fuel and explain the salient features of it. With reference to fuel oil analysis report, explain the relevant corrective action which can be initiated against various adverse observations in it. (12)'. blocks.h: 1. The present standards - and which edition is present

blocks.p: The marine fuel specification is ISO 8217, “Petroleum products — Fuels (class F) — Specifications of marine fuels”. It is the standard against which a bunker is bought, delivered and disputed.

The edition matters and must be stated. The specification has been revised several times — 2005, 2010, 2012 and 2017 — and the present edition is the sixth, ISO 8217:2017. A purchase is made against a named edition, because the parameters and their limits differ between them, and a bunker meeting one edition may be off-specification against another. Naming the standard without naming the edition is an incomplete answer.
A complete answer names the supporting standards as well, because the specification does not work alone:

rows: The specification. Grades, parameters and limits for marine distillate and residual fuels
Classification and designation — the system by which a grade such as a residual marine grade of a given viscosity gets its name
Precision of test methods and interpretation of results. The most important of the supporting standards in practice, because it is what decides whether a marginal result is genuinely off-spec
Guidance on fuels meeting the 0.50% sulphur limit — compatibility, stability and the handling of blended low-sulphur fuels
The individual test methods
Density, kinematic viscosity, sulphur, water, ash, carbon residue, total sediment, flash point, pour point and metals — each parameter is defined by the method used to measure it

ol: Two tables. One for distillate grades and one for residual grades, the residual grades ordered principally by kinematic viscosity. The grade name is the shorthand by which the fuel is ordered.

The general requirements clause is the most important sentence in the standard. It requires the fuel to be a homogeneous blend of hydrocarbons and to be free from any material at a concentration that causes harm to personnel, jeopardises the safety of the ship, or adversely affects the performance of the machinery. That clause catches contamination the numerical table never anticipated — chemical waste, used lubricating oil, styrene, phenols — and it is what a claim is founded on when a fuel damages an engine while meeting every tabulated limit.

Sulphur defers to statute. The standard requires the purchaser to specify the maximum sulphur content in accordance with the relevant statutory requirements. So the operative sulphur limit is MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14 — 0.50% m/m globally since 1 January 2020 and 0.10% m/m in emission control areas — and not a number in the specification.

Bio-content is now explicit. The 2017 edition introduced distillate grades that permit a defined proportion of fatty acid methyl ester, distinguished by an F in the grade designation, alongside grades that must be substantially free of it. That matters operationally because FAME brings oxidation stability, microbial growth and filter-blocking questions with it.

The specification is a delivery specification, not an engine-inlet specification. A residual fuel may be perfectly on-spec at the manifold and still unfit to burn until it has been settled and purified. The clearest example is abrasive particulate: the concentration permitted at delivery is substantially higher than the concentration engine makers accept at the engine inlet. The gap between those two is the fuel treatment plant's whole job.

Flash point is a statutory matter, not a commercial one. The minimum of 60 degrees Celsius for fuel oil used in machinery spaces is a SOLAS requirement. A fuel below it is not a quality dispute; it is a safety breach.

Precision is built in. Because every parameter is a measurement, the standard is read with ISO 4259: a result that differs from the limit by less than the method's reproducibility is not proof of an off-spec fuel. This is what decides most marginal disputes.

blocks.p: Grouping the parameters by the failure they threaten is how the specification becomes usable rather than memorised:

rows: Handling and treatment
Kinematic viscosity, density, pour point, water
Combustion and ignition
Calculated carbon aromaticity index, micro carbon residue, viscosity at injection
Abrasive wear
Aluminium plus silicon — the catalytic fines
High-temperature corrosion
Vanadium, sodium, and the ratio between them; ash
Stability and compatibility
Total sediment, potential and aged; FAME content; oxidation stability
Safety and health
Flash point, hydrogen sulphide
Contamination
Used lubricating oil markers — calcium with zinc, calcium with phosphorus; acid number
Statutory
Sulphur

blocks.h: 3. The content of a fuel oil analysis report

blocks.p: A report has six parts. Candidates normally give the second and omit the rest, and the omitted parts are where the marks are:

ol: Sample and delivery identity. Ship, port, date, supplier and barge, the bunker delivery note reference, the grade and quantity ordered, the sample seal number, the sampling point and method, and the type of sample — the MARPOL delivered sample, the ship's own sample, or a commercial sample. This section is what makes the rest admissible: an analysis of a sample that cannot be tied to the delivery proves nothing.

The results table. For every parameter: the result, the unit, the specification limit for the grade ordered, the test method used, and a pass or fail indication. The test method must be stated because the limit only means anything against the method.

Derived and calculated values. The calculated carbon aromaticity index as an indication of ignition quality; the estimated net specific energy, which is what the fuel is actually worth per tonne; and often a recommended purifier temperature and throughput.
Comments and recommendations. The laboratory's narrative on the marginal or adverse results, the handling and treatment advice, and any warning about commingling with the fuel already on board.

The verdict. An overall statement — on specification, off specification, or on specification with cautions — and, where a result is marginal, a statement of the precision of the method under ISO 4259 so that the reader can see whether the deviation is real.
Laboratory identity and traceability. The laboratory, its accreditation, the date of receipt and of testing, and the report reference — without which the report is not usable in a claim.

blocks.h: 4. Before any corrective action - four steps that come first

blocks.p: This is the part a Chief Engineer is actually marked on, and it is almost always missing:

ol: Verify the identity of the sample. Seal number against the bunker delivery note, grade against what was ordered. A report on the wrong sample has caused a debunkering that was never needed.

Apply the precision. A result marginally outside a limit may be within the reproducibility of the test method. Under ISO 4259, that is not a proven off-specification fuel — and treating it as one starts a claim that will fail.
Segregate and do not consume. Keep the bunker in its own tanks, do not commingle it, and do not put it into service until it is cleared. Once it is burnt, the evidence and the claim are gone.

Notify inside the contractual window. Owners, charterers, the supplier and the club as appropriate, with a letter of protest. Supply contracts commonly impose a short period for a quality claim — the applicable period is read from the contract, not assumed — and a joint analysis of the MARPOL delivered sample is usually the next step.

blocks.p: The regulatory scaffolding behind those steps is MARPOL Annex VI regulation 18: the bunker delivery note with the information the Annex prescribes, retained on board for three years; the MARPOL delivered sample, sealed, signed and retained for at least twelve months, to be analysed by the prescribed method; the port State's right to inspect the note and take certified copies; and the port State's follow-up duties where non-compliant fuel is found.

rows: Viscosity higher than the grade ordered
Cannot reach injection viscosity; poor atomisation, afterburning, fouling

Check heater capacity and trace heating; raise settling, service and injection temperatures within limits and control on a viscometer; if injection viscosity still cannot be reached, segregate and blend down or land the fuel
Viscosity lower than expected
Leakage past fuel pump plungers, loss of injection pressure, poor lubrication of the pump elements
Reduce heating; where a cooler is fitted, control to the minimum injection viscosity; watch for pump leakage and sticking
Density high
Separation efficiency falls; water and solids may not be removed

Confirm the separator's rated capability for the density; select the correct gravity disc or set the clean-oil interface; reduce throughput and raise separation temperature to the recommended figure; use two separators where fitted
High calculated carbon aromaticity index
Poor ignition quality — long ignition delay, rapid pressure rise, knock, high peak pressure, liner and bearing damage

Raise fuel and jacket cooling water temperatures; maintain scavenge air temperature; retard injection timing where the engine permits; reduce load and avoid rapid load changes; ensure injector condition and correct opening pressure; blend with a better-igniting fuel
Water high
Loss of energy, sludge, filter blocking, corrosion; if seawater, sodium-driven high-temperature corrosion

Drain settling and service tanks frequently; settle at temperature; purify at reduced throughput; test for chlorides to establish whether it is seawater; if seawater in quantity, treat as a serious contamination and consider debunkering
Aluminium plus silicon high — catalytic fines
Severe abrasive wear of liners, rings, fuel pumps and injectors — the single most destructive fuel fault

Settle for as long as possible with frequent tank draining; run separators at the recommended temperature and reduced throughput, in series or parallel as fitted; sample at the engine inlet, not just at the manifold, and verify the removal actually achieved; reduce load; blend down; and where the delivered concentration is extreme, debunker
Total sediment high (potential or aged)
Instability or incompatibility; sludging, separator overload, filter and purifier blocking

Keep the fuel segregated and do not commingle; carry out a compatibility spot test before any mixing becomes unavoidable; increase purification and filter and tank cleaning frequency; use the fuel promptly; if severe, debunker
Vanadium and sodium high, or an adverse sodium-to-vanadium ratio
High-temperature corrosion of exhaust valves, seats and turbocharger nozzle rings

Purify thoroughly — sodium is largely water-borne and is removed with the water; maintain valve rotation and correct valve temperatures; monitor exhaust valve condition and shorten inspection intervals; use an approved fuel additive only where the maker permits
Ash, micro carbon residue high
Deposits on rings, liner, exhaust valves and turbine; fouling and gas-way deposits
Optimise combustion — injection condition, air supply, load; increase turbocharger and gas-way cleaning; review cylinder oil feed rate and base number
Pour point high
Wax; blocked lines, filters and suction strainers, especially in cold weather
Keep tanks, lines and filters heated and traced above the pour point with a margin; avoid cold spots and dead legs; plan tank changeovers so cold fuel is never drawn
Used lubricating oil contamination — calcium with zinc or phosphorus
Abrasive and corrosive damage; and a breach of the specification's general requirements clause however the numbers read
Do not use; segregate; notify supplier, owners and club at once; obtain joint analysis of the MARPOL delivered sample; debunker
Acid number high
Corrosion of fuel pumps, injectors and the fuel system
Segregate; monitor fuel system components closely; take advice; consider blending down or landing the fuel
Hydrogen sulphide high
Toxic to personnel in tank atmospheres and around sounding pipes and vents
Treat as a personnel hazard first: gas monitoring, no tank entry without full enclosed-space procedure, ventilation, restricted sounding and ullaging, and a briefing to all concerned
FAME above the grade, or present in a grade that should be free of it
Oxidation, microbial growth, sludge and filter blocking; poor storage life
Keep water out — drain tanks frequently; use the fuel promptly; monitor filters; treat only with an approved biocide and only where the maker permits
Flash point below 60 degrees Celsius
Fire and explosion. A SOLAS breach, not a commercial dispute
Do not use. Segregate, inform master, owners, flag and supplier immediately, and land the fuel. It is never corrected by blending
Sulphur above the applicable statutory limit
Non-compliance with MARPOL Annex VI — detention, fine, and a port State record

Do not burn it where the limit applies; change over to compliant fuel; notify flag, port State and supplier and record the sequence; retain the MARPOL delivered sample for verification. A non-availability report is a record of a supply failure, not a defence for burning a fuel you already know is non-compliant
Low net specific energy
Higher consumption for the same work — a commercial loss rather than a technical fault
Adjust consumption expectations and performance monitoring baselines; raise a commercial claim on the quantity-energy shortfall

blocks.p: Three findings are not treatable and the correct action is not to burn the fuel: a flash point below the statutory minimum, sulphur above the applicable limit where that limit applies, and chemical or used-lubricating-oil contamination. Everything else in the table is a question of treatment, load and monitoring. Knowing which class a finding falls into — treat it, or refuse it — is the whole of the engineering judgement this question is testing.

And one closing structural point: the specification governs the fuel as delivered, while the engine is protected by the fuel treatment plant and the way it is run. A perfectly on-specification bunker will still destroy liners if the separators are run at full throughput and the tanks are never drained. The analysis report tells you what you have been given; it does not tell you what will arrive at the injector.

The paper prints 16 marks in one unlimbed block, and hides three tasks inside two sentences: name the standards and give their salient features; state the content of an analysis report; and give the corrective action for each adverse observation. Because no marks are apportioned, the candidate must apportion them, and the apportionment is the first decision of the answer.

The third task is the largest — the word is “each” — and it goes in a three-column table: observation, what it threatens, what you do. A table is not decoration here; it is the only format in which fifteen or more findings can be delivered inside an examination and still be read. The first task gets a table of standards and a numbered list of features. The second gets six numbered parts.

The highest-value section is the one nobody writes: what happens before any corrective action — check the sample identity, apply the precision, segregate and do not burn, notify inside the contractual window. That is the difference between an engineer's answer and a textbook's.
The standard is ISO 8217. The present edition at this sitting is the sixth, ISO 8217:2017.

This matters more than it looks. A bunker is bought against a named edition, and the parameters and limits differ between editions — a fuel that is on-spec against one may be off-spec against another. Naming the standard without its edition answers half the first task.

It also matters for a reason peculiar to this paper: the seventh edition was published in 2024, eight months after this examination. Every later paper in the corpus that sets this question is entitled to call the 2024 edition current. Here it does not exist. That is the single most dangerous inherited error available on this paper, and it is the reason the uncertainty section below exists.

blocks.h: The three sentences that carry the first task

ul: The general requirements clause — the fuel shall be a homogeneous blend of hydrocarbons, free from any material at a concentration that causes harm to personnel, jeopardises the safety of the ship or adversely affects machinery performance. It catches what the numerical table cannot, and it is what a damage claim is built on when every tabulated limit was met.

Sulphur defers to statute. The purchaser specifies it in accordance with the relevant statutory requirements, so the operative limits are MARPOL's — 0.50% globally, 0.10% in emission control areas — not the standard's.

The specification is a DELIVERY specification. What is acceptable at the manifold is not what is acceptable at the injector, and the gap between the two is precisely what the settling tanks and separators exist to close.

blocks.h: ISO 4259: the standard that decides disputes

blocks.p: Every parameter is a measurement, and every measurement has a reproducibility. A result that lies outside a limit by less than the method's reproducibility is not proof that the fuel is off-specification.

The practical consequences are two. A Chief Engineer who declares a fuel off-spec on a marginal result starts a claim that will fail and may have segregated a perfectly usable bunker. And on the other side, a marginal sulphur result close to a statutory limit is exactly where the argument between ship, supplier and port State is conducted. Naming ISO 4259 and saying what it does is worth a mark on its own.

rows: Refuse
Flash point below 60 °C; sulphur above the applicable statutory limit; chemical or used-lubricating-oil contamination
Do not burn. Segregate, notify, land the fuel. Never blend to correct a flash point
Treat
Viscosity, density, water, catalytic fines, sediment, vanadium and sodium, ash, pour point, FAME
Settling, purification, temperature and throughput control, load management, monitoring and shortened inspection intervals
Absorb
Low net specific energy
A commercial loss. Adjust consumption baselines and claim

blocks.p: Being able to place a finding in the right row is the judgement the question is testing. Most candidates put everything in the middle row.

ul: Naming ISO 8217 without its edition.
Naming only ISO 8217 and omitting ISO 4259, which is the one that decides disputes.
Reciting grade tables and limit values instead of explaining the features of the specification.
Omitting the general requirements clause, which is the most important sentence in the standard.
Saying the standard sets the sulphur limit. It defers to MARPOL.
Skipping the content of the report altogether — this paper asks for it and the later member of this family does not, so an answer inherited from that sitting omits it.
Giving the results table as the whole report and omitting sample identity, method, precision and laboratory traceability.
Jumping straight to corrective action without verifying sample identity, applying precision, segregating and notifying.
Burning the fuel while the dispute is open, which destroys both the evidence and the claim.
Treating a low flash point as a quality problem to be blended away. It is a safety breach and the fuel is landed.
Treating a non-availability report as a licence to burn non-compliant fuel. It records a supply failure; it is not a defence for burning fuel you already know is non-compliant.
Giving catalytic fines only a delivery limit and never mentioning engine-inlet monitoring, which is where the damage is actually prevented.
“Name the marine fuel standard and its edition.” ISO 8217 — the sixth edition, of 2017, at this sitting.
“Which standard tells you whether a marginal result is really off-spec?” ISO 4259 — precision of test methods and interpretation of results.
“Where does the sulphur limit come from?” MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14, not ISO 8217. 0.50% globally, 0.10% in emission control areas.
“What is the minimum flash point and whose rule is it?” 60 degrees Celsius for fuel oil used in machinery spaces — a SOLAS requirement.
“How long do you keep the MARPOL delivered sample and the bunker delivery note?” The sample for at least twelve months; the note for three years.

“Your analysis shows high aluminium plus silicon. What is the risk and what do you do first?” Abrasive wear of liners, rings, pumps and injectors. Settle, drain, purify at reduced throughput and correct temperature — and sample at the engine inlet to prove the removal.
“High CCAI — what is it telling you?” Poor ignition quality: long ignition delay, rapid pressure rise, knock.
“High sodium with high vanadium?” High-temperature corrosion of exhaust valves and turbine nozzle rings — and sodium is often seawater, so purify.
“Total sediment high. May you mix it with the fuel already on board?” No — segregate, and do a compatibility spot test before any unavoidable mixing.
“The fuel is off-spec. Can you burn it while you argue?” No — burning it destroys the evidence and usually the claim.
“Flash point 55 degrees. What do you do?” Do not use, segregate, notify master, owners, flag and supplier, and land it. It is never blended up.
What does ISO 8217 stand for? Petroleum products - fuels (class F) - specifications of marine fuels.
Which standard classifies and designates the grades? ISO 8216-1.

Name four things on a fuel oil analysis report other than the results. Sample and delivery identity with the seal number, the test method for each parameter, the laboratory's comments and recommendations, and the overall verdict with the laboratory's accreditation.
What is CCAI and what does it tell you? The calculated carbon aromaticity index, derived from density and viscosity, indicating ignition quality.

Why does density matter for purification? Because separation depends on the density difference between oil and water, and a high-density fuel needs the correct gravity disc or interface setting and reduced throughput.

What temperature do you purify heavy fuel at, and why not higher? At the recommended separation temperature - high enough for low viscosity, not so high that water flashes off and disturbs the interface.
Why sample at the engine inlet? Because the delivery limit for catalytic fines is far above what the engine will tolerate, and only an inlet sample proves the treatment plant is actually working.
What is a letter of protest for? To put the supplier on notice within the contractual window and preserve the claim.
Who else gets a copy of an off-spec report? Owners, charterers where relevant, the supplier, and the club.

What is the difference between the MARPOL sample and the commercial sample? The MARPOL delivered sample is sealed and signed at delivery for statutory verification and retained for at least twelve months; commercial samples are for the ship's own testing.

blocks.p: For the standards, four names and one qualifier: 8217 SPECIFIES, 8216 CLASSIFIES, 4259 DECIDES, 23263 GUIDES — and always say the edition.
For the features, three sentences: GENERAL REQUIREMENTS CLAUSE, SULPHUR DEFERS TO STATUTE, DELIVERY NOT ENGINE INLET.
For the report, six words: WHO, WHAT, DERIVED, COMMENT, VERDICT, LAB.
Before acting, four: IDENTIFY, PRECISION, SEGREGATE, NOTIFY.

For the corrective actions, group them by what they attack: HANDLING (viscosity, density, pour point, water), COMBUSTION (CCAI, carbon residue), WEAR (catalytic fines), CORROSION (vanadium, sodium, acid), STABILITY (sediment, FAME), SAFETY (flash point, hydrogen sulphide), LAW (sulphur). And close on TREAT IT OR REFUSE IT.

ul: ISO 8217 — the marine fuel specification. Sixth edition, 2017, is the present edition at this sitting. ISO 8216-1 classification and designation; ISO 4259 precision and interpretation of results; ISO/PAS 23263:2019 guidance on 0.50% sulphur fuels; and the individual test method standards.

MARPOL Annex VI regulation 18 — fuel oil availability and quality. The bunker delivery note with the information the Annex prescribes and its three-year retention; the MARPOL delivered sample, sealed and signed, retained for at least twelve months and analysed by the prescribed method; port State inspection of the note and certified copies; and port State follow-up on non-compliant fuel. Cited at identity level; no paragraph is quoted.
MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14 — 0.50% m/m sulphur globally from 1 January 2020, 0.10% m/m in emission control areas.
MARPOL Annex VI as revised by MEPC.328(76) — in force 1 November 2022. See the uncertainty section on the corpus register's date.
SOLAS — the 60 degree Celsius minimum flash point for fuel oil used in machinery spaces. A statutory requirement, not an ISO one.
No laboratory, testing service, fuel additive, treatment product or engine maker is named anywhere in this answer, and no limit value is quoted from the specification.

blocks.p: This question has the sharpest evidence split on the paper: the regulation is well held and the standard cannot be held at all.

MARPOL Annex VI regulation 18 is the best-evidenced provision in this paper. The True Source corpus holds its complete paragraph tree as canonical objects — the availability duty, the whole non-availability evidence regime, the fuel oil quality requirements, the bunker delivery note and its appendix information, the three-year retention, port State inspection, the MARPOL delivered sample and its twelve-month retention and prescribed analysis, and the port State follow-up duties. The standing corpus position is that MARPOL Annex VI resolves to identity and provenance and never to text, so every reference here is made at identity level and no paragraph is quoted.

Two directional corrections were applied to the corpus record. First, the register records the entry into force of the 2021 revised Annex VI a year late; the correct date, 1 November 2022, is used, and an existing correction request is carried rather than re-raised. Second, the resolver annotates the fuel oil quality paragraphs as replaced by an MEPC 81 resolution — that resolution is a 2024 output and is future at this sitting, so the paragraphs are taken in their pre-replacement form and the annotation is not consumed.

No ISO standard is held and none can be. ISO standards are commercially licensed documents. The edition identity, the structure of the specification and the identity of the supporting standards are carried at authoritative-secondary level, and no limit value is presented as a quotation from the specification. Where a figure appears in this answer it is either fixed by statute or convention — the 0.50% and 0.10% sulphur limits, the 60 degree Celsius flash point — or is expressly flagged as engine-maker guidance, as with the engine-inlet limit for abrasive particulate, which is substantially lower than the delivery limit and differs between makers. No grade table is reproduced and no laboratory, additive or treatment product is named.

Currency — and this is the paper's most dangerous single line. The present edition of the marine fuel specification at this sitting is the sixth, of 2017. The seventh edition was published in 2024 and is eight months future. The later member of this family sits at August 2024, after that publication, and is entitled to call the newer edition current. Importing that statement here would put into a candidate's hands an edition that did not exist when he sat the paper. The statement must remain framed as at November 2023.

One further limit: no contractual notice period is stated as a legal requirement. Supply contracts commonly impose a short window for a quality claim, and the answer says the applicable period must be read from the contract rather than assumed, because no supply contract or standard term is held.

notes: THIS IS THE HIGHEST-RISK QUESTION ON THE PAPER AND THE RISK IS AN EDITION DATE. The marine fuel specification's SIXTH edition, of 2017, is the present edition at this sitting. The SEVENTH edition was published in 2024 and is EIGHT MONTHS FUTURE. The donor question, QP2408-Q6, sits at August 2024 - AFTER that publication - and is entitled to treat the newer edition as current. Inheriting that statement would hand a candidate an edition that did not exist when he sat the paper. The first task was therefore re-derived from scratch rather than carried across.
NOVEMBER 2023 IS BOUNDARY-FREE AT DAY LEVEL. MEPC 80 is four months past and the 33rd Assembly one month future; neither touches this question.

MARPOL ANNEX VI AT THIS SITTING IS THE MEPC.328(76) REVISION, IN FORCE 1 NOVEMBER 2022 - twelve months before the examination. THE CORPUS REGISTER RECORDS THAT ENTRY INTO FORCE A YEAR LATE. TSCR-3 is open on exactly that point and is CARRIED, not re-raised. The correct date is used and the register's date is not consumed.

THE SECOND DIRECTIONAL CORRECTION IS IN THE RESOLVER ITSELF. The corpus reference resolver annotates regulation 18.3 and 18.4 as 'as replaced by MEPC.385(81)'. MEPC.385(81) is an MEPC 81 output of 2024 and is FUTURE at this sitting, so those paragraphs are taken in their MEPC.328(76) form and the annotation is not consumed. This is the register-inversion trap the 2023 allocation predicted, met a second time on this paper.

THE SULPHUR REGIME IS CORRECTLY DATED. The 0.50% m/m global limit applied from 1 January 2020 and the 0.10% m/m emission control area limit is longstanding; both are operative and nearly four years old at this sitting. The carriage ban on non-compliant fuel oil for ships without an approved equivalent applied from 1 March 2020 and is likewise operative.
ISO/PAS 23263:2019 IS OPERATIVE AND CORRECTLY PLACED. It was issued to support the 2020 sulphur transition and is four years old at this sitting.

FUTURE CONTAMINATION EXCLUDED: no instrument or standard published after November 2023 is cited. The 2024 edition of the marine fuel specification, MEPC.385(81), MEPC.392(82), the whole A.118x(33) set, the EU Emissions Trading System extension to shipping of 1 January 2024 and the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 are all absent.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Sixteen marks printed as one unlimbed block concealing THREE tasks: name the present ISO standards for marine fuel and give their salient features; state the CONTENT of a fuel oil analysis report; and give corrective action against EACH adverse observation. The word 'each' makes the third task the largest. The discriminating features are naming the correct EDITION of the specification at this sitting, naming ISO 4259 and knowing what it does, giving the report's structure rather than only its results table, and knowing which findings are treatable and which mean the fuel is not burnt at all.

The corrective action task is delivered as a three-column table - observation, what it threatens, what you do - because seventeen findings cannot be delivered as prose inside an examination. A separate short section is placed BEFORE the corrective action table covering sample identity, precision, segregation and notification, because that is the sequence a Chief Engineer is actually judged on and no donor supplies it.

Importing it would hand a candidate an edition that did not exist. technical_ambiguities: Which edition of the specification is current at this sitting - the sixth, of 2017; the seventh is eight months future
Whether the specification sets the sulphur limit - it does not; it requires the purchaser to specify sulphur in accordance with the relevant statutory requirements, so MARPOL governs
Whether the flash point minimum is an ISO requirement - it is a SOLAS requirement, which is why a low flash point is a safety breach and not a commercial dispute
Whether an on-specification fuel is safe to burn as delivered - not necessarily; the specification is a DELIVERY specification and the engine-inlet requirement for abrasive particulate is far lower
Whether a marginal result proves an off-specification fuel - it does not, once the method's reproducibility under ISO 4259 is applied
Whether the fuel may be burnt while a claim is being pursued - it should not be; burning it destroys the evidence and usually the claim
Whether a low flash point can be corrected by blending - it cannot, and attempting it is a safety breach
Whether a non-availability report permits burning non-compliant fuel - it does not; it records a supply failure and is not a defence for burning fuel already known to be non-compliant
Whether high sodium is a fuel quality problem or a water problem - very often it is seawater, which is why purification and a chloride test come before any additive
