questions.understand_first: There is one idea holding this whole question together: a fuel is bought against a written description, and everything else follows from whether it matches. The description is an international specification — a list of properties with limits, plus a catch-all sentence saying the fuel must not contain anything that harms people, endangers the ship or damages the machinery. That catch-all matters more than it looks, because it is what you rely on when a fuel wrecks an engine while passing every number in the table. Two things about that description are easy to get wrong. It is tied to a particular version, and versions differ, so a fuel can pass against one and fail against another. And it describes the fuel as it arrives at the ship's side — not as it should be by the time it reaches the injector. Closing that gap is exactly what the settling tanks and separators are for, which is why a perfectly acceptable delivery can still ruin liners if the treatment plant is run badly. When the laboratory report comes back, the instinct is to start fixing things. The better instinct is to stop: confirm the sample really is the fuel you were given, check whether the failing number is outside the limit by more than the test's own margin of error, keep the fuel in its own tanks and unburnt, and tell the supplier inside whatever time the contract allows. Burning the fuel while arguing about it destroys both the evidence and the argument. Only then does the question of what to do with it arise — and the sorting that matters is between the faults you can manage by heating, cleaning and easing the load, and the three you cannot: a fuel that will catch fire too easily, a fuel that breaks the law on sulphur, and a fuel that has something in it that should never have been there.
questions.memory_cue: Standards: 8217 SPECIFIES, 8216 CLASSIFIES, 4259 DECIDES (1) - and always the EDITION (1). Features: GENERAL CLAUSE, SULPHUR DEFERS, DELIVERY NOT INLET (2). Report: WHO, WHAT, DERIVED, COMMENT, VERDICT, LAB (3). Before acting: IDENTIFY, PRECISION, SEGREGATE, NOTIFY (4). Then TREAT IT OR REFUSE IT (6).

steps.title: The present standards - and which edition is present
points: the marine fuel specification is ISO 8217, Petroleum products - Fuels (class F) - Specifications of marine fuels
THE EDITION MATTERS AND MUST BE STATED - the specification has been revised in 2005, 2010, 2012 and 2017
THE PRESENT EDITION AT THIS SITTING IS THE SIXTH, ISO 8217:2017
a purchase is made against a NAMED EDITION, because parameters and limits differ between editions and a fuel on-spec against one may be off-spec against another
ISO 8216-1 - classification and designation of marine fuels
ISO 4259 - precision of test methods and interpretation of results; the most important supporting standard in practice because it decides whether a marginal result is genuinely off-spec
ISO/PAS 23263:2019 - guidance on fuels meeting the 0.50% sulphur limit, their compatibility and stability
and the individual test method standards for density, viscosity, sulphur, water, ash, carbon residue, sediment, flash point, pour point and metals

steps.title: Salient features of the specification
points: TWO TABLES - one for distillate grades and one for residual grades, the residual grades ordered principally by kinematic viscosity

THE GENERAL REQUIREMENTS CLAUSE IS THE MOST IMPORTANT SENTENCE IN THE STANDARD - the fuel shall be a homogeneous blend of hydrocarbons free from any material at a concentration that causes harm to personnel, jeopardises the safety of the ship or adversely affects machinery performance
that clause catches contamination the numerical table never anticipated, and it is what a damage claim is founded on when every tabulated limit was met

SULPHUR DEFERS TO STATUTE - the purchaser specifies it in accordance with the relevant statutory requirements, so MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14 governs: 0.50% m/m globally since 1 January 2020 and 0.10% m/m in emission control areas

BIO-CONTENT IS EXPLICIT - the 2017 edition introduced distillate grades permitting a defined proportion of fatty acid methyl ester, distinguished by an F in the designation, alongside grades that must be substantially free of it

THE SPECIFICATION IS A DELIVERY SPECIFICATION, NOT AN ENGINE-INLET SPECIFICATION - the abrasive particulate permitted at delivery is substantially higher than engine makers accept at the inlet, and closing that gap is the fuel treatment plant's whole job
FLASH POINT IS STATUTORY, NOT COMMERCIAL - the 60 degree Celsius minimum for fuel oil in machinery spaces is a SOLAS requirement, so a low result is a safety breach
PRECISION IS BUILT IN - read with ISO 4259, a result outside a limit by less than the method's reproducibility is not proof of an off-spec fuel
GROUP THE PARAMETERS BY THE FAILURE THEY THREATEN - handling, combustion, wear, corrosion, stability, safety, contamination, statutory

steps.title: The content of a fuel oil analysis report
points: SAMPLE AND DELIVERY IDENTITY - ship, port, date, supplier and barge, the bunker delivery note reference, the grade and quantity ordered, the SAMPLE SEAL NUMBER, the sampling point and method, and the type of sample
this section is what makes the rest admissible - an analysis of a sample that cannot be tied to the delivery proves nothing
THE RESULTS TABLE - for every parameter the result, the unit, the specification limit for the grade ordered, THE TEST METHOD, and a pass or fail indication
the method must be stated because the limit only means anything against the method

DERIVED AND CALCULATED VALUES - the calculated carbon aromaticity index as an indication of ignition quality, the estimated net specific energy, and often a recommended purifier temperature and throughput
COMMENTS AND RECOMMENDATIONS - the laboratory's narrative on marginal or adverse results, handling and treatment advice, and any warning about commingling

THE VERDICT - on specification, off specification, or on specification with cautions - and for a marginal result a statement of the METHOD PRECISION so the reader can see whether the deviation is real
LABORATORY IDENTITY AND TRACEABILITY - the laboratory, its accreditation, dates of receipt and testing, and the report reference, without which the report is not usable in a claim

steps.title: Before any corrective action - four steps that come first
points: VERIFY THE IDENTITY OF THE SAMPLE - seal number against the bunker delivery note, grade against what was ordered; a report on the wrong sample has caused an unnecessary debunkering
APPLY THE PRECISION - a result marginally outside a limit may be within the reproducibility of the method, and under ISO 4259 that is not a proven off-specification fuel
SEGREGATE AND DO NOT CONSUME - keep the bunker in its own tanks, do not commingle, do not put it into service until cleared; ONCE IT IS BURNT THE EVIDENCE AND THE CLAIM ARE GONE
NOTIFY INSIDE THE CONTRACTUAL WINDOW - owners, charterers, supplier and club as appropriate, with a letter of protest; the applicable period is read from the contract, not assumed
and usually a joint analysis of the MARPOL delivered sample is the next step

the regulatory scaffolding is MARPOL Annex VI regulation 18 - the bunker delivery note with the prescribed information retained three years, the MARPOL delivered sample sealed and signed and retained at least twelve months and analysed by the prescribed method, port State inspection and certified copies, and port State follow-up where non-compliant fuel is found

steps.title: Corrective action, observation by observation
points: VISCOSITY HIGH - check heater capacity and trace heating, raise temperatures within limits under viscometer control; if injection viscosity cannot be reached, segregate and blend down or land the fuel
VISCOSITY LOW - reduce heating and cool where a cooler is fitted, control to the minimum injection viscosity, watch for fuel pump leakage
DENSITY HIGH - confirm the separator's rated capability, select the correct gravity disc or interface, reduce throughput and raise separation temperature, use two separators where fitted

HIGH CCAI - poor ignition quality; raise fuel and jacket temperatures, maintain scavenge air temperature, retard timing where permitted, reduce load, ensure injector condition, blend with a better-igniting fuel
WATER HIGH - drain tanks frequently, settle at temperature, purify at reduced throughput, TEST FOR CHLORIDES to establish whether it is seawater, and if seawater in quantity consider debunkering

CATALYTIC FINES HIGH - the most destructive fuel fault; settle and drain, purify at recommended temperature and reduced throughput in series or parallel, SAMPLE AT THE ENGINE INLET to prove removal, reduce load, blend down, and debunker if extreme
TOTAL SEDIMENT HIGH - segregate and do not commingle, compatibility spot test before any unavoidable mixing, increase purification and filter and tank cleaning, use promptly, debunker if severe

VANADIUM AND SODIUM HIGH - high-temperature corrosion of valves and nozzle rings; purify thoroughly since sodium is largely water-borne, maintain valve rotation and temperatures, shorten inspection intervals, additive only where the maker permits
ASH AND CARBON RESIDUE HIGH - deposits and fouling; optimise combustion, increase turbocharger and gas-way cleaning, review cylinder oil feed rate and base number
POUR POINT HIGH - keep tanks, lines and filters heated above the pour point with a margin, avoid cold spots and dead legs, plan changeovers so cold fuel is never drawn
USED LUBRICATING OIL CONTAMINATION - do not use, segregate, notify supplier owners and club at once, joint analysis of the MARPOL sample, DEBUNKER
ACID NUMBER HIGH - segregate, monitor fuel system components, consider blending down or landing
HYDROGEN SULPHIDE HIGH - treat as a PERSONNEL HAZARD first: gas monitoring, no tank entry without full enclosed-space procedure, ventilation, restricted sounding and ullaging
FAME ABOVE GRADE - keep water out and drain tanks frequently, use promptly, monitor filters, biocide only where the maker permits
FLASH POINT BELOW 60 DEGREES CELSIUS - DO NOT USE; segregate, inform master, owners, flag and supplier, land the fuel; NEVER corrected by blending

SULPHUR ABOVE THE APPLICABLE LIMIT - do not burn where the limit applies, change over to compliant fuel, notify flag, port State and supplier and record the sequence, retain the MARPOL sample; a non-availability report is a record of a supply failure and NOT a defence for burning fuel already known to be non-compliant
LOW NET SPECIFIC ENERGY - a commercial loss; adjust consumption baselines and performance monitoring, and raise a commercial claim

steps.title: The judgement to close on
points: THREE FINDINGS ARE NOT TREATABLE AND THE FUEL IS NOT BURNT - flash point below the statutory minimum, sulphur above the applicable limit where it applies, and chemical or used-lubricating-oil contamination
everything else is a question of treatment, load and monitoring
knowing which class a finding falls into - TREAT IT OR REFUSE IT - is the whole of the engineering judgement this question tests
and one closing structural point - the specification governs the fuel AS DELIVERED, while the engine is protected by the treatment plant and how it is run
a perfectly on-specification bunker will still destroy liners if the separators run at full throughput and the tanks are never drained
THE ANALYSIS REPORT TELLS YOU WHAT YOU HAVE BEEN GIVEN; IT DOES NOT TELL YOU WHAT WILL ARRIVE AT THE INJECTOR

quick_revision.recall_15s: ISO 8217 — Petroleum products, fuels (class F), specifications of marine fuels. The present edition at this sitting is the SIXTH, of 2017. Supporting: ISO 8216-1 classification, ISO 4259 precision and interpretation (the one that decides marginal disputes), ISO/PAS 23263:2019 on 0.50% sulphur fuels, and the individual test methods. Features: two tables, distillate and residual; the general requirements clause — homogeneous hydrocarbons, free from any material harming personnel, endangering the ship or damaging machinery; sulphur defers to MARPOL (0.50% global, 0.10% ECA); FAME-permitting distillate grades marked with an F; a delivery specification, not an engine-inlet one; flash point 60 °C is SOLAS, not ISO. Report content: sample and delivery identity with seal number; results with limit and test method; derived values — CCAI, net specific energy; comments; verdict with precision; laboratory accreditation. Before acting: identify the sample, apply ISO 4259 precision, segregate and do not burn, notify inside the contractual window — regulation 18 gives the BDN (3 years) and the MARPOL delivered sample (12 months minimum). Corrective action by group: handling — heat or cool to injection viscosity, gravity disc and reduced throughput for high density, drain and settle for water, heat above pour point; combustion — high CCAI means raise temperatures, retard timing, reduce load, blend; wear — catalytic fines: settle, drain, purify at temperature and low throughput, sample at the engine inlet; corrosion — vanadium and sodium: purify, valve rotation, shorter intervals; stability — sediment: segregate, compatibility test, no commingling; safety — H2S is a personnel hazard. Refuse, do not treat: flash point below 60 °C, sulphur above the limit, used-lube or chemical contamination.
critical_numbers: ISO 8217 - the SIXTH edition, of 2017, is the present edition at this November 2023 sitting
MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14 - 0.50% m/m sulphur globally from 1 January 2020; 0.10% m/m in emission control areas
Minimum flash point 60 degrees Celsius for fuel oil used in machinery spaces - a SOLAS requirement
Bunker delivery note retained on board for THREE YEARS
MARPOL delivered sample retained for at least TWELVE MONTHS
MARPOL Annex VI as revised by MEPC.328(76) - in force 1 November 2022
The abrasive particulate concentration permitted at DELIVERY is substantially higher than engine makers accept at the ENGINE INLET - maker guidance, not specification
quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 18 is the regulatory scaffolding behind every step of the response to an adverse report: it prescribes the bunker delivery note and the information it must carry, requires it to be retained on board for three years, requires the MARPOL delivered sample to be sealed and signed and retained for at least twelve months and analysed by the prescribed method, gives the port State the right to inspect the note and take certified copies, and imposes follow-up duties where non-compliant fuel oil is found. Read with regulation 14, which supplies the sulphur limits the specification itself defers to. Annex VI at this sitting is the MEPC.328(76) revision, in force 1 November 2022.
quick_revision.major_trap: Naming the standard without its edition — and, worse on this paper, naming the wrong one. At November 2023 the present edition is the sixth, of 2017; the seventh edition was published in 2024 and did not exist when this paper was sat. The second trap is starting corrective action before the governance steps: verify the sample identity, apply the ISO 4259 precision, segregate and do not burn the fuel, and notify inside the contractual window. Burning a disputed bunker destroys both the evidence and the claim. The third is failing to separate the findings that are treated from the three that are refused — a flash point below 60 °C, sulphur above the applicable statutory limit, and used-lubricating-oil or chemical contamination.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the marine fuel specification, its present edition at this sitting, and three supporting standards.
retrieval_cards.answer: ISO 8217, Petroleum products - Fuels (class F) - Specifications of marine fuels, in its sixth edition of 2017. Supporting: ISO 8216-1 for classification and designation; ISO 4259 for the precision of test methods and interpretation of results; and ISO/PAS 23263:2019 for guidance on fuels meeting the 0.50% sulphur limit, together with the individual test method standards.
retrieval_cards.why: The edition is half the mark, and ISO 4259 is the standard candidates most often omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the general requirements clause of the specification, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: That the fuel shall be a homogeneous blend of hydrocarbons, free from any material at a concentration that causes harm to personnel, jeopardises the safety of the ship, or adversely affects the performance of the machinery. It matters because it catches contamination the numerical table never anticipated - chemical waste, used lubricating oil - and it is the clause a damage claim rests on when the fuel met every tabulated limit.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the most important sentence in the standard and the one most often left out of an answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does ISO 8217 set the sulphur limit?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It requires the purchaser to define the maximum sulphur content in accordance with the relevant statutory requirements. The operative limits are MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14 - 0.50% m/m globally since 1 January 2020 and 0.10% m/m in emission control areas.
retrieval_cards.why: The deferral is a feature of the standard and shows the candidate understands how specification and regulation interlock.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The fuel is on specification. Is it safe to burn as delivered?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not necessarily. ISO 8217 is a DELIVERY specification. The abrasive particulate concentration permitted at the manifold is substantially higher than engine makers accept at the engine inlet, so the fuel must be settled and purified before it reaches the injector. Closing that gap is the fuel treatment plant's whole purpose.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the single most useful structural idea in the question and it explains why the report never tells the whole story.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does a fuel oil analysis report contain, beyond the results?
retrieval_cards.answer: Sample and delivery identity - ship, port, date, supplier and barge, bunker delivery note reference, grade and quantity ordered, sample seal number, sampling point and sample type. The test method for each parameter alongside the result and the limit. Derived values such as the calculated carbon aromaticity index and estimated net specific energy. The laboratory's comments and treatment recommendations. An overall verdict with a precision statement for marginal results. And laboratory identity, accreditation and dates.
retrieval_cards.why: This paper asks for report CONTENT and the later member of this family does not, so an answer inherited from that sitting omits it entirely.

retrieval_cards.prompt: An adverse analysis report arrives. What do you do BEFORE any treatment decision?
retrieval_cards.answer: Verify the sample identity - seal number against the bunker delivery note, grade against what was ordered. Apply the ISO 4259 precision, since a result outside a limit by less than the method's reproducibility does not prove an off-specification fuel. Segregate the bunker and do not consume or commingle it. And notify owners, charterers, the supplier and the club inside the contractual window, with a letter of protest, usually leading to joint analysis of the MARPOL delivered sample.
retrieval_cards.why: Burning the fuel while the dispute is open destroys both the evidence and the claim - it is the Chief Engineer's judgement mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does MARPOL Annex VI regulation 18 require of the bunker delivery note and the sample?
retrieval_cards.answer: The bunker delivery note must carry the information the Annex prescribes and be retained on board for three years. The MARPOL delivered sample must be sealed and signed and retained for at least twelve months, and analysed by the prescribed method. The port State may inspect the note and take certified copies, and has follow-up duties where non-compliant fuel oil is found.
retrieval_cards.why: Three years and twelve months are the two retention numbers examiners ask for, and they are the evidence chain behind any dispute.

retrieval_cards.prompt: High aluminium plus silicon. What is the risk, and what proves your response worked?
retrieval_cards.answer: Catalytic fines - severe abrasive wear of liners, rings, fuel pumps and injectors, the most destructive fuel fault there is. Settle for as long as possible with frequent tank draining, run the separators at the recommended temperature and reduced throughput in series or parallel, blend down and reduce load. What proves it worked is SAMPLING AT THE ENGINE INLET, not at the manifold - the delivery limit is far above what the engine tolerates.
retrieval_cards.why: Engine-inlet monitoring is what separates a real answer from a recital of the delivery limit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which analysis findings mean the fuel must NOT be burnt at all?
retrieval_cards.answer: Three. A flash point below the statutory minimum of 60 degrees Celsius - a SOLAS breach and never corrected by blending. Sulphur above the applicable statutory limit where that limit applies. And chemical or used-lubricating-oil contamination, shown by calcium with zinc or phosphorus, which breaches the general requirements clause however the rest of the numbers read. Everything else is a question of treatment, load and monitoring.
retrieval_cards.why: Sorting findings into 'treat it' and 'refuse it' is the judgement the whole question is testing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You are short of compliant fuel. Does a non-availability report let you burn what you have?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It records a supply failure - that compliant fuel could not be obtained despite best efforts, with the evidence the Party may require. It is not a defence for burning a fuel you already know to be non-compliant. Change over to compliant fuel where the limit applies, notify flag, port State and supplier, record the sequence, and retain the MARPOL delivered sample for verification.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the standard misconception about the non-availability regime and it has real detention consequences.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The result is marginally outside the limit. Is the fuel off specification?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not necessarily. Every parameter is a measurement and every method has a reproducibility. Under ISO 4259, a result lying outside a limit by less than the method's reproducibility is not proof of an off-specification fuel. Declaring off-spec on a marginal result starts a claim that will fail and may segregate a usable bunker unnecessarily.
retrieval_cards.why: ISO 4259 is what actually decides marginal disputes, and naming it is worth a mark on its own.

blocks.h: 1. Why the question exists - and why it is regulatory by this sitting

blocks.p: Slow steaming began as a commercial response: with a fixed-pitch propeller in unchanged conditions, delivered power varies roughly as the cube of shaft speed, so a modest speed reduction removes a large amount of fuel. Ships built for one speed were then run for years at another.

By this sitting it is no longer only commercial. MARPOL Annex VI as revised is in force since 1 November 2022, and the EEXI requirement and the CII rating regime have applied since 1 January 2023 — eleven months. EEXI compliance is verified at the first annual, intermediate or renewal survey of the air pollution prevention certificate on or after that date, and for a large part of the existing fleet the practical route to compliance was to limit the installed power. The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, adopted four months before this examination, sets the direction beyond that.
So the engineering question is precise: an engine designed to run near its rated duty is now required to spend its life a long way below it. Everything below is an answer to that.

rows: Geometry
Long-stroke and ultra-long-stroke designs at high stroke-to-bore ratio
The design mechanical duty is reached at lower shaft speed, which permits a larger, slower, more efficient propeller and gives more time per cycle for combustion
Control
Electronically controlled, camshaft-less engines — common rail or servo-actuated injection and electronically actuated exhaust valves

The single most important development for this question. Injection timing, rate and profile and valve timing become software, so the engine can be re-optimised for a different operating range without new hardware
Air side
High-efficiency and two-stage turbocharging, variable turbine area, exhaust bypass, power turbines and waste heat recovery
Air supply stops being fixed at one matched point and becomes adjustable across the load range
Emissions
Primary measures — injection and valve timing, scavenge air moisturising, exhaust gas recirculation; and secondary — selective catalytic reduction for Tier III
Kept short here: it is a large subject of its own. It matters because after-treatment has its own minimum temperature, and very low load can take an engine outside it
Lubrication
Electronically controlled timed cylinder lubrication, feed proportional to load and fuel sulphur; anti-polishing rings
Directly enables low load: feed rate can be cut with load without losing the neutralising and film-forming duty
Fuels
Dual-fuel operation on gas and on methanol, in service; ammonia and hydrogen under development and not in commercial service at this sitting

Changes the combustion problem rather than solving the low-load one — and ammonia is not zero-emission at the funnel: unburnt ammonia slip and nitrous oxide, a far more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide, both require after-treatment
Digital
Continuous performance monitoring, electronic indication, remote diagnostics and predictive maintenance
Makes the effect of a retrofit measurable, which is what allows an interval or a setting to be changed on evidence

blocks.p: The development that changed retrofitting. On a mechanically controlled engine, timing lives in a camshaft and changing it means cams, links and hardware. On an electronically controlled engine it lives in a control system. That is why modern low-load work is often a tuning package rather than a shipyard job, and why the retrofit menu below divides sharply by which kind of engine is in the ship.

blocks.h: 3. What actually goes wrong at prolonged low load

blocks.p: Every retrofit that follows answers one of these, so it is worth stating them first:

ul: Not enough air. The turbocharger is off its matched point, so scavenge pressure and air-fuel ratio fall and the auxiliary blowers run for long periods. This is the root failure and most retrofits attack it.
Low compression pressure and temperature, which lengthens ignition delay and worsens combustion.
Poor atomisation at low injection pressure, giving incomplete combustion, smoke and unburnt fuel.

Deposits — on rings and ring grooves, in the scavenge spaces, in the gas ways, on the turbine and in the exhaust gas economiser. Hence scavenge fires and economiser soot fires, which are the real safety consequence.

Cold corrosion. Where metal temperatures fall, sulphuric acid condenses on the liner surface; if the cylinder oil base number and feed rate are not matched to the load and the fuel, corrosive wear follows.
Turbocharger surging, and unstable running near the barred speed range.

Falling waste heat. Exhaust temperature and mass flow drop, so the economiser makes less steam and the auxiliary boiler has to fire — burning fuel to replace the heat the main engine is no longer wasting.
Propeller mismatch. The propeller was designed for a speed the ship no longer runs at, so it is now working off its best efficiency point.
Rising SFOC. The engine burns more fuel per kilowatt precisely when the point of the exercise was to burn less.

ol: Turbocharger cut-out. On an engine with two or more turbochargers, one is blanked off so that the remaining units work near their design point and scavenge pressure is restored at low load. It is the cheapest effective measure on a multi-turbocharger engine, requiring a cut-out kit with blanking and isolating arrangements, and it is reversible for high-load running.

Variable turbine area. An adjustable nozzle ring changes the turbine's effective area with load, so the turbocharger stays near its match across a wide range instead of at one point. It converts a fixed match into a variable one.

Nozzle ring exchange, or turbocharger re-matching. Where the low-load duty is permanent, a smaller nozzle ring or a smaller or higher-efficiency turbocharger is fitted, permanently re-matching the air side.
Exhaust gas bypass and waste-gate re-setting. Adjusted so that the bypass no longer robs the turbine of energy it now needs.

Auxiliary blower control. Revised cut-in and cut-out logic and, where fitted, frequency-controlled blowers that run continuously at reduced speed rather than cycling. Continuous cycling is hard on the machinery and on the electrical plant.

Low-load or part-load tuning. On an electronically controlled engine, a software package re-optimises injection timing, rate and profile and exhaust valve timing for the load range actually used. No hardware changes, and it is normally reversible — the least disruptive retrofit available.
Variable injection timing adjustment. On a mechanically controlled engine, the equivalent is re-setting the variable injection timing and, where necessary, re-timing the fuel cams.

Compression ratio increase. Raising the compression ratio — by shims or by a modified piston crown — restores compression pressure and temperature at low load, shortening ignition delay and improving combustion. This is real hardware and has to be checked against the maximum pressure limit.
Slide-type fuel valves in place of conventional valves. Eliminating the sac volume removes after-dripping, which is a principal source of smoke and deposits at low load.

Full de-rating. The permanent option: the engine is re-tuned to a lower rated output, typically combining new injection timing, a compression ratio change, a new turbocharger nozzle ring and sometimes new fuel valve nozzles. The engine is then genuinely designed for the duty it performs, and its specific consumption at the new operating point improves. It is the most thorough answer and the least reversible.

ul: Electronically controlled timed cylinder lubrication, replacing mechanical lubricators. Feed rate becomes proportional to load and to fuel sulphur, and injection is timed to the ring pack, so feed can be reduced with load without losing the neutralising duty. On a slow-steaming ship this is what stands between low load and corrosive liner wear.
Cylinder oil base number matched to the fuel and the load — too low invites cold corrosion, too high leaves deposits.
Anti-polishing rings at the top of the liner, to scrape the deposit collar off the piston crown and control bore polishing.

Revised scavenge space inspection and drain monitoring, and drain oil analysis to see wear and residual base number before they become damage. This is a PMS change and belongs in the maintenance system, not in somebody's notebook.

blocks.p: The engine is not the only thing matched to the old speed:

ul: Propeller re-pitching or replacement — a new propeller optimised for the speed and power the ship now uses, often of larger diameter and lower revolutions, which is the largest single efficiency gain available on a genuinely re-purposed ship.
Energy-saving devices — pre-swirl ducts and stators, boss cap fins, rudder bulbs and twisted rudders, all of which recover swirl energy and matter more at the lower wake speeds of slow steaming.
Hull coating and cleaning regime — a slower ship gives a foul release coating less shear to work with, so the coating and cleaning policy must be revisited with the speed.

Torsional vibration re-assessment. Changing propeller, pitch or engine rating moves the barred speed range, and the new range must be established and observed. This is a safety item, not an optimisation.

blocks.p: And the heat balance changes with the speed — the most commonly forgotten consequence of all:

ul: Exhaust gas economiser. Lower exhaust mass flow and temperature mean less steam and more soot. Retrofits are soot blowers, water-washing arrangements, dry-running protection and revised circulation control — and the economiser fire risk rises sharply, so the cleaning regime changes with the operating profile.
Auxiliary boiler. It now fires much more often, so its burner control, maintenance and fuel consumption all move — and part of the main engine saving is quietly given back here.
Waste heat recovery. Systems sized for full load produce much less at low load; bypass and control changes may be needed, and a power turbine may cease to be usable at all below a certain output.

blocks.h: 8. The regulatory retrofit unique to this period

blocks.p: Engine power limitation and shaft power limitation. For a large part of the existing fleet, the practical EEXI compliance route was not to change the ship but to limit the power that may be delivered, so that the attained index falls to the required value.

ul: Engine power limitation is applied to the engine's own control or fuel index; shaft power limitation is applied through shaft power measurement and a limiting control.
The limitation must be verifiable and sealed or otherwise secured, and its arrangement and setting recorded in the ship's technical file and onboard management manual.

It must be capable of being overridden to release a power reserve where the safety of the ship or the saving of life at sea requires it — with the override recorded and reported. A limitation that could not be overridden would itself be a hazard.
The arrangements follow the Organization's guidelines on power limitation systems and the use of a power reserve.

blocks.p: The engineering consequence is the whole point of this question: a power-limited ship is a ship that will spend its remaining life at a load its engine was not designed for. Power limitation makes the low-load retrofits necessary rather than optional.
No retrofit works on its own. The supporting practice is part of the answer:

ul: Periodic load-up runs to burn off deposits and dry out gas ways.
Increased turbocharger, gas-way and economiser cleaning, with soot blowing and water washing on a revised schedule.
Raised jacket cooling water temperature where the maker permits, to keep liner metal temperatures up and cold corrosion down.
More frequent scavenge space inspection, and drain oil analysis trended rather than filed.
Performance monitoring against a re-established baseline after every change, because a retrofit whose effect is not measured cannot be defended.
Revised PMS intervals recorded in the maintenance system, and the whole envelope recorded in the SEEMP.

blocks.p: The judgement to close on. There is no single answer, and the mark is for saying which ship needs what:

ol: An electronically controlled engine with more than one turbocharger is the easy case: low-load tuning plus turbocharger cut-out, both reversible, both cheap, both quick.
A mechanically controlled engine needs hardware — timing changes, compression ratio, slide fuel valves, nozzle ring — and the case has to be made on the remaining life of the ship.
A ship whose speed reduction is permanent, or which is power-limited for EEXI, should be de-rated properly and the propeller re-matched, because half-measures leave it running badly for years.
Every case needs the lubrication and inspection regime changed, whatever else is or is not done. That is the cheapest measure and the one that decides whether the liners survive.

blocks.p: “Hassle free” slow steaming, in the phrase the paper uses, is therefore not a single product. It is an engine given enough air, a combustion process given back its compression and timing, a cylinder oil regime matched to the new duty, a propeller matched to the new speed, and a heat balance that has been re-thought — and the ships that got it wrong are the ones that found out through scavenge fires, economiser fires and liner wear.

Sixteen marks in one unlimbed block, with the word “including” doing the apportioning: developments in marine diesel engines generally, including the retrofits for slow and ultra-slow steaming. That makes the retrofits the larger task, and roughly a third of the page belongs to the developments.

The structural decision that earns the most is to insert a section on what actually goes wrong at low load between the two. Without it, the retrofit list is a catalogue and reads like one. With it, every retrofit is visibly an answer to a named failure — not enough air, lost compression, deposits, cold corrosion, lost waste heat, propeller mismatch — and the answer acquires an argument.

The second decision is to keep the emissions material short. Tier III, SCR, EGR and scavenge air moisturising are a whole question of their own and appear elsewhere in the corpus; here they are one row of a table, mentioned only because after-treatment has a minimum temperature that very low load can fall below.

blocks.h: The one development that explains the whole retrofit menu

blocks.p: Electronic control. On a mechanically controlled engine, injection and valve timing live in a camshaft, so changing them is a hardware job. On an electronically controlled engine they live in software.

That single difference splits the retrofit menu in two and is the basis of the judgement at the end of the answer. An electronically controlled engine can often be re-optimised for a new load range with a tuning package and a turbocharger cut-out — reversible, cheap, quick. A mechanically controlled engine needs timing changes, a compression ratio change, slide fuel valves and a nozzle ring, and the business case has to be made against the ship's remaining life.

blocks.h: The failures, and which retrofit answers which

rows: Not enough air - turbocharger off its match, blowers running continuously
Turbocharger cut-out; variable turbine area; nozzle ring exchange or turbocharger re-match; bypass re-setting; blower control
Low compression pressure and temperature
Compression ratio increase; raised jacket water temperature
Poor atomisation, smoke, deposits
Low-load tuning or variable injection timing adjustment; slide-type fuel valves
Cold corrosion and liner wear
Electronically controlled timed cylinder lubrication; base number matching; anti-polishing rings
Scavenge and economiser fires
Cleaning regime, soot blowing and water washing; load-up runs; inspection frequency
Propeller off its design point
Re-pitch or replace the propeller; energy-saving devices; re-assess the barred speed range
Lost waste heat
Economiser control and protection; auxiliary boiler; waste heat recovery bypass
Permanent mismatch
Full de-rating to a lower rated output

blocks.h: What is unique about a 2023 answer

blocks.p: This question would have been answered differently in 2015. By November 2023, slow steaming has become regulatory, and three dates carry the change:

ul: MARPOL Annex VI as revised is in force from 1 November 2022 — twelve months before the sitting.

EEXI and CII apply from 1 January 2023 — eleven months. EEXI is verified at the first annual, intermediate or renewal survey of the air pollution prevention certificate on or after that date, and for much of the existing fleet the compliance route was power limitation. 2023 is the first CII data year and it is still running at this sitting.
The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy was adopted on 7 July 2023 — four months before, so it is operative here and sets the direction beyond EEXI.

blocks.p: The connecting sentence is the one worth learning: power limitation makes the low-load retrofits necessary rather than optional, because a power-limited ship will spend its remaining life at a load its engine was not designed for.

ul: Writing a catalogue of retrofits with no statement of what problem each solves.
Spending the page on emissions technology — SCR, EGR, Tier III — which is a different question.
Ignoring the word “developments” and answering only on retrofits, or the reverse.
Treating slow steaming as purely commercial in 2023 and never mentioning EEXI, CII or power limitation.
Forgetting the air side is the root failure. Most low-load trouble is insufficient scavenge air.
Omitting cylinder lubrication, which is what actually decides whether the liners survive years of low load.
Omitting cold corrosion, or confusing it with hot corrosion from vanadium and sodium.
Forgetting the heat balance — less waste heat, more auxiliary boiler firing, and part of the saving quietly given back.
Forgetting the propeller, which was matched to a speed the ship no longer uses.
Not mentioning that changing propeller, pitch or rating moves the barred speed range.
Naming maker products and tuning packages. Describe the mechanism — it is what earns the mark and it does not date.
Quoting percentage savings and de-rating figures. They are ship-specific and unsupportable.
“What is the first thing that goes wrong at low load?” Insufficient scavenge air — the turbocharger is off its matched point.

“What is turbocharger cut-out and when can you use it?” Blanking off one turbocharger on a multi-turbocharger engine so the rest work near their design point. Only where there is more than one, and it is reversible.
“What does variable turbine area do?” Changes the turbine's effective area with load, so the match follows the load instead of being fixed at one point.
“Why fit slide fuel valves?” They eliminate the sac volume and so the after-dripping that causes smoke and deposits at low load.
“Why raise the compression ratio?” To restore compression pressure and temperature at low load, shortening ignition delay — and it must be checked against the maximum pressure limit.

“What is cold corrosion and what do you do about it?” Sulphuric acid condensing on the liner when metal temperatures are low. Match cylinder oil base number and feed rate to load and fuel, raise jacket water temperature where permitted, and monitor drain oil.
“Why do economiser fires become more likely?” Lower exhaust temperature and mass flow mean soot deposits and dry surfaces — hence soot blowing, water washing and dry-running protection.
“What happens to your steam?” Less of it. The auxiliary boiler fires more, and part of the main engine saving is given back.

“What is EPL and can it be overridden?” Engine power limitation for EEXI compliance — verifiable, secured, and yes: it must be capable of override to release a power reserve where safety or saving life at sea requires, with the override recorded and reported.
“You re-pitch the propeller. What must be re-checked?” The barred speed range, because it moves.
“Which is the cheapest measure of all?” Changing the cylinder lubrication and inspection regime — and it is the one that decides whether the liners survive.
Why does slow steaming save so much fuel? Because with a fixed-pitch propeller in unchanged conditions, power varies roughly as the cube of shaft speed.
Then why not go slower still? Because specific fuel consumption rises off the matched point, and deposits, fouling and maintenance costs rise with it.
What is de-rating? Permanently re-tuning the engine to a lower rated output, usually with new injection timing, a compression ratio change and a new turbocharger nozzle ring.

What is the difference between de-rating and power limitation? De-rating changes the engine; power limitation restricts the power that may be delivered, for EEXI compliance, and can be overridden for safety.
Which retrofit needs no hardware? Low-load tuning on an electronically controlled engine.
Why do auxiliary blowers matter? Because at low load they run for long periods, and continuous cycling is hard on the machinery and the electrical plant.
What does an anti-polishing ring do? Scrapes the deposit collar from the piston crown and controls bore polishing.
What do you monitor to see whether the lubrication regime is right? Drain oil analysis - wear metals and residual base number - and scavenge space condition.
Are ammonia or hydrogen engines in service? Not at this time; they are under development.
Where is the whole operating envelope recorded? In the SEEMP.

blocks.p: Two halves: DEVELOPMENTS then RETROFITS, with WHAT GOES WRONG between them as the hinge.
For the developments, six words: STROKE, ELECTRONICS, AIR, EMISSIONS, LUBRICATION, FUELS — and one sentence: electronics turned timing from a camshaft into software.
For what goes wrong, five words in the order they bite: AIR, COMPRESSION, DEPOSITS, CORROSION, HEAT.

For the retrofits, the same five plus two: AIR (cut-out, variable turbine area, nozzle ring, blowers), COMBUSTION (tuning, timing, compression ratio, slide valves, de-rating), WEAR (timed lubrication, base number, anti-polishing ring), PROPELLER (re-pitch, energy-saving devices, barred range), HEAT (economiser, boiler, waste heat recovery) — and LAW (engine or shaft power limitation).

ul: MARPOL Annex VI as revised by MEPC.328(76) — in force 1 November 2022. See the uncertainty section on the corpus register's date.

EEXI and the CII rating regime — applicable from 1 January 2023. EEXI verified at the first annual, intermediate or renewal survey of the air pollution prevention certificate on or after that date. 2023 is the first CII data year and it is still running at this sitting.

SEEMP with Part III mandatory from 1 January 2023 — where the operating envelope and improvement measures are recorded. The operative guidance is the 2022 SEEMP Guidelines, MEPC.346(78); the 2024 successor is future and is not cited.
MEPC.377(80), the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, adopted 7 July 2023 — four months before this sitting, therefore operative. A strategy, not law.

Engine or shaft power limitation for EEXI compliance, with override to release a power reserve, following the Organization's guidelines. The guidelines are referred to descriptively and not by resolution number; see the uncertainty section.

No engine maker, engine type, tuning package, retrofit kit, turbocharger model or proprietary device is named anywhere, and no numerical de-rating percentage, load threshold or fuel saving is asserted.

blocks.p: This is an engineering answer with a thin but real regulatory layer, and the two are kept apart deliberately.

The regulatory frame is primary by identity and status: the revised Annex VI in force 1 November 2022, EEXI and CII applicable from 1 January 2023, SEEMP Part III mandatory from the same date, and the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy adopted 7 July 2023 and therefore operative here. The corpus register records the entry into force of the revised Annex VI a year late; an existing correction request covers exactly that point and is carried rather than re-raised, with the correct date used. The register also marks the 2022 SEEMP Guidelines as superseded — a 2024 event, reversed for this sitting.

The engineering is authoritative secondary and engineering judgement throughout, and it is deliberately anonymous. No engine maker, engine type, tuning package, retrofit kit, turbocharger model, lubricator system or proprietary energy-saving device is named anywhere in this answer. Every retrofit is described by its mechanism — which is what the examiner is testing, and which also means the answer cannot be dated by a product that has since been renamed or withdrawn.

No numerical value is asserted for a low-load threshold, a de-rating percentage, an SFOC gain, a compression ratio, a blower cut-in load, a fuel saving or a payback period. All are ship-specific and no held source records any of them. For the same reason no ranking of the retrofit families is offered: their merits depend on engine type, age, control system and trading pattern.

Two identity limits are recorded rather than guessed. The Organization's guidelines on the shaft or engine power limitation arrangement and the use of a power reserve are referred to descriptively and not by resolution number, because the instrument identity could not be established from a held source. And the EEXI verification trigger is described rather than quoted, the standing corpus position being that MARPOL Annex VI resolves to identity and provenance and never to text.

Currency. Two statements are pinned to this sitting and must not drift. Ammonia and hydrogen are described as under development and not in commercial service, which is correct at November 2023 and would be wrong of a later paper. And 2023 is the first CII data year and it is still running — no ship has yet been issued a rating, so an inherited sentence about ships already holding ratings would be false here.

notes: NOVEMBER 2023 IS BOUNDARY-FREE AT DAY LEVEL. MEPC 80 is four months past and the 33rd Assembly one month future; neither falls inside the sitting month.

THE 2023 IMO GHG STRATEGY IS OPERATIVE AND THAT IS THE DEFINING TEMPORAL FACT FOR THIS QUESTION. MEPC.377(80) was adopted on 7 July 2023, four months before this sitting. A June or earlier 2023 paper would carry the Initial Strategy of 2018 instead; this one does not.

EEXI AND CII ARE ELEVEN MONTHS OLD AND IN TRANSITION. Both applied from 1 January 2023. EEXI compliance is verified at the first annual, intermediate or renewal survey of the air pollution prevention certificate on or after that date, so at November 2023 a substantial part of the fleet has been through that survey and a substantial part has not. Power limitation retrofits were therefore live work at this sitting, which is precisely why the question is set.
2023 IS THE FIRST CII DATA YEAR AND AT THIS SITTING IT IS STILL RUNNING. No ship has yet been issued a CII rating. Any inherited sentence about ships holding ratings would be false here.

MARPOL ANNEX VI AT THIS SITTING IS THE MEPC.328(76) REVISION, IN FORCE 1 NOVEMBER 2022. The corpus register records that entry into force a year late; TSCR-3 is open on exactly that point and is CARRIED, not re-raised.

MEPC.346(78), THE 2022 SEEMP GUIDELINES, ARE OPERATIVE. The corpus register marks them superseded by a 2024 successor and says not to cite them as current; that is correct today and wrong here, and the register's direction is reversed. This is the second occurrence of the register-inversion trap on this paper.

THE TECHNOLOGY MATURITY DATES ARE STATED AS AT THIS SITTING AND ARE A REAL RISK. Dual-fuel gas and methanol operation is in service. AMMONIA AND HYDROGEN ARE UNDER DEVELOPMENT AND NOT IN COMMERCIAL SERVICE at November 2023, and are described that way. A later editor working from a 2025 or 2026 standpoint would upgrade both and falsify the paper.

FUTURE CONTAMINATION EXCLUDED: no instrument adopted after November 2023 is cited. The 2024 SEEMP guidelines, MEPC.385(81), the whole A.118x(33) set, the EU Emissions Trading System extension to shipping of 1 January 2024, the Hong Kong Convention of 26 June 2025, the IMO Net-Zero Framework of October 2025 and the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 are all absent.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Sixteen marks in one unlimbed block setting two tasks joined by 'including': the developments in marine diesel engines generally, and the retrofit methods adopted to enable slow and ultra-slow steaming. The word 'including' makes the retrofits the larger task. The discriminating feature is whether the candidate can explain WHAT GOES WRONG at prolonged low load and present each retrofit as an answer to a named failure, rather than reciting a catalogue. A 2023 answer must additionally know that slow steaming has become a regulatory matter - EEXI, CII and power limitation - and not only a commercial one.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 in a single block with no printed apportionment. Roughly a third to the developments, delivered as a seven-row table so it cannot sprawl, and the balance to the retrofits. A section on the failure modes of prolonged low load is inserted BETWEEN the two halves, because it is what converts the retrofit list from a catalogue into an argument and it costs only a bulleted list. The retrofits are then grouped by the failure they answer - air, combustion, wear, propulsion, heat - with the regulatory power limitation retrofit as a separate section and a closing judgement on which ship needs which.

The regulatory content is recent rather than absent: EEXI and CII are eleven months old and in transition at this sitting, and the 2023 GHG Strategy is four months old, so a paper from earlier in 2023 would answer differently. The other direction is technology maturity: ammonia and hydrogen are under development and NOT in commercial service at November 2023, and a later editor would upgrade them. Both are pinned to the sitting.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The subject is engineering and the regulation is MARPOL. No Indian instrument is engaged; the domestic statute at this sitting is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and nothing in the answer needs it.
technical_ambiguities: Whether the first failure at low load is combustion or air supply - it is AIR: the turbocharger is off its matched point, and most retrofits attack that
Whether turbocharger cut-out is available on any engine - only on an engine with two or more turbochargers
Whether low-load tuning is a hardware change - not on an electronically controlled engine, where timing lives in software; on a mechanically controlled engine the equivalent requires hardware

Whether de-rating and power limitation are the same - they are not; de-rating permanently re-tunes the engine to a lower rated output, while power limitation restricts the power that may be delivered and must be capable of override
Whether power limitation may be irreversible - it may not; it must be capable of being overridden to release a power reserve where safety or saving life at sea requires, with the override recorded

Whether cold corrosion and high-temperature corrosion are the same - they are not; cold corrosion is sulphuric acid condensing on a cool liner, while vanadium and sodium corrosion attacks hot exhaust valves and turbine parts
Whether slow steaming reduces the boiler load - it INCREASES it, because less waste heat means the auxiliary boiler fires more and part of the saving is given back
Whether the propeller is unaffected - it is not; it was matched to a speed the ship no longer runs at, and re-pitching or replacement moves the barred speed range
Whether ammonia and hydrogen engines are in service at this sitting - they are not; they are under development

Then five retrofit sections grouped by the failure they answer - air, combustion, lubrication and wear, propulsion train, heat balance. One section on engine and shaft power limitation as the regulatory retrofit unique to this period. And a closing section pairing operational measures with a four-part judgement on which ship needs which retrofit.

questions.understand_first: The idea behind this question is a mismatch that lasted for years. Ships were designed and their engines built to run at one speed, and then the industry decided — first to save money, later because the rules demanded it — to run them much slower. Slowing down saves a great deal of fuel, because the water resists a propeller far harder the faster it turns. But an engine is a matched set of parts: the turbocharger, the injection timing, the compression, the lubrication and the propeller were all chosen together for one duty, and taking the speed away without changing anything else breaks the match. The first thing to fail is the air supply, because the turbocharger is driven by exhaust the engine is no longer producing enough of, and everything else follows from that — poor burning, soot everywhere, cold surfaces that let acid form and eat the liners, fires in the scavenge spaces and in the exhaust boiler. So the retrofits are not a list of clever products; each one is an answer to one of those failures, and they group naturally: get the air back, get the compression and timing back, protect the liners, re-match the propeller, and deal with the heat that is no longer there. The last of those catches people out — a slower ship makes less waste steam, so the auxiliary boiler starts burning fuel and quietly gives back part of the saving. What makes this a question of its moment rather than a general one is that by now the slow speed is often not a choice: the ship's installed power has been deliberately capped to meet an efficiency requirement, which means she will spend the rest of her life at a load her engine was never designed for.
questions.memory_cue: Two halves with a hinge: DEVELOPMENTS (2), WHAT GOES WRONG (3), RETROFITS (4-7). Failures in order: AIR, COMPRESSION, DEPOSITS, CORROSION, HEAT (3). Retrofit families: AIR, COMBUSTION, WEAR, PROPELLER AND HEAT (4, 5, 6, 7) - plus LAW (8).

steps.title: Why the question exists - and why it is regulatory by this sitting
points: slow steaming began as a COMMERCIAL response - with a fixed-pitch propeller in unchanged conditions, delivered power varies roughly as the CUBE of shaft speed
so a modest speed reduction removes a large amount of fuel, and ships built for one speed were run for years at another
by this sitting it is no longer only commercial
MARPOL Annex VI as revised is IN FORCE SINCE 1 NOVEMBER 2022
EEXI and the CII rating regime have applied since 1 JANUARY 2023 - eleven months
EEXI compliance is verified at the first annual, intermediate or renewal survey of the air pollution prevention certificate on or after that date
for much of the existing fleet the practical route to compliance was to LIMIT THE INSTALLED POWER
the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy was adopted 7 July 2023, four months before this examination, and sets the direction beyond EEXI
so the engineering question is precise - AN ENGINE DESIGNED TO RUN NEAR ITS RATED DUTY IS NOW REQUIRED TO SPEND ITS LIFE A LONG WAY BELOW IT

steps.title: Developments in marine diesel engines
points: GEOMETRY - long-stroke and ultra-long-stroke designs at high stroke-to-bore ratio, reaching the design mechanical duty at lower shaft speed and permitting a larger, slower, more efficient propeller
CONTROL - electronically controlled, camshaft-less engines with common rail or servo-actuated injection and electronically actuated exhaust valves
THIS IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT DEVELOPMENT FOR THIS QUESTION - injection timing, rate and profile and valve timing become SOFTWARE, so the engine can be re-optimised without new hardware
AIR SIDE - high-efficiency and two-stage turbocharging, variable turbine area, exhaust bypass, power turbines and waste heat recovery; air supply becomes adjustable rather than fixed at one match
EMISSIONS - primary measures including injection and valve timing, scavenge air moisturising and exhaust gas recirculation, and secondary measures including selective catalytic reduction for Tier III
kept SHORT here because it is a large subject of its own; it matters only because after-treatment has a minimum temperature that very low load can fall below
LUBRICATION - electronically controlled timed cylinder lubrication with feed proportional to load and fuel sulphur, and anti-polishing rings

FUELS - dual-fuel operation on gas and methanol in service; AMMONIA AND HYDROGEN UNDER DEVELOPMENT AND NOT IN COMMERCIAL SERVICE at this sitting, and AMMONIA IS NOT ZERO-EMISSION AT THE FUNNEL - unburnt ammonia slip and nitrous oxide, a far more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide, both require after-treatment
DIGITAL - continuous performance monitoring, electronic indication, remote diagnostics and predictive maintenance, which make a retrofit's effect measurable
THE DEVELOPMENT THAT CHANGED RETROFITTING - on a mechanical engine timing lives in a camshaft and changing it is a hardware job; on an electronic engine it lives in a control system

steps.title: What actually goes wrong at prolonged low load
points: NOT ENOUGH AIR - the turbocharger is off its matched point, scavenge pressure and air-fuel ratio fall, and auxiliary blowers run for long periods; THIS IS THE ROOT FAILURE
LOW COMPRESSION PRESSURE AND TEMPERATURE, lengthening ignition delay and worsening combustion
POOR ATOMISATION at low injection pressure, giving incomplete combustion, smoke and unburnt fuel
DEPOSITS on rings and ring grooves, in scavenge spaces, gas ways, turbine and exhaust gas economiser - hence SCAVENGE FIRES AND ECONOMISER SOOT FIRES, the real safety consequence
COLD CORROSION - sulphuric acid condensing on the liner where metal temperatures fall, if cylinder oil base number and feed rate are not matched to load and fuel
TURBOCHARGER SURGING and unstable running near the barred speed range
FALLING WASTE HEAT - lower exhaust temperature and mass flow, less steam, and the auxiliary boiler firing to replace the heat the main engine is no longer wasting
PROPELLER MISMATCH - the propeller was designed for a speed the ship no longer runs at
RISING SFOC - more fuel per kilowatt precisely when the point was to burn less

steps.title: Air-side retrofits - the first resort
points: TURBOCHARGER CUT-OUT - on an engine with two or more turbochargers, one is blanked off so the rest work near their design point and scavenge pressure is restored
the cheapest effective measure on a multi-turbocharger engine; needs a cut-out kit with blanking and isolating arrangements, and is reversible for high-load running
VARIABLE TURBINE AREA - an adjustable nozzle ring changes the turbine's effective area with load, converting a fixed match into a variable one
NOZZLE RING EXCHANGE OR TURBOCHARGER RE-MATCHING - where the low-load duty is permanent, a smaller nozzle ring or a smaller or higher-efficiency turbocharger permanently re-matches the air side
EXHAUST GAS BYPASS AND WASTE-GATE RE-SETTING, so the bypass no longer robs the turbine of energy it now needs
AUXILIARY BLOWER CONTROL - revised cut-in and cut-out logic and, where fitted, frequency-controlled blowers running continuously at reduced speed rather than cycling

steps.title: Combustion-side retrofits
points: LOW-LOAD OR PART-LOAD TUNING - on an electronically controlled engine, a software package re-optimises injection timing, rate and profile and exhaust valve timing for the load range actually used
no hardware changes, normally reversible - the least disruptive retrofit available
VARIABLE INJECTION TIMING ADJUSTMENT - on a mechanically controlled engine, re-setting the VIT and where necessary re-timing the fuel cams

COMPRESSION RATIO INCREASE - by shims or a modified piston crown, restoring compression pressure and temperature at low load and shortening ignition delay; must be checked against the maximum pressure limit
SLIDE-TYPE FUEL VALVES in place of conventional valves, eliminating the sac volume and the after-dripping that causes smoke and deposits at low load

FULL DE-RATING - the permanent option: re-tuning to a LOWER RATED OUTPUT, typically combining new injection timing, a compression ratio change, a new turbocharger nozzle ring and sometimes new fuel valve nozzles
the engine is then genuinely designed for the duty it performs and its specific consumption at the new operating point improves; the most thorough answer and the least reversible

steps.title: Lubrication and wear retrofits
points: ELECTRONICALLY CONTROLLED TIMED CYLINDER LUBRICATION replacing mechanical lubricators - feed proportional to load and fuel sulphur, injection timed to the ring pack
feed can therefore be reduced with load WITHOUT LOSING THE NEUTRALISING DUTY; on a slow-steaming ship this is what stands between low load and corrosive liner wear
CYLINDER OIL BASE NUMBER MATCHED to the fuel and the load - too low invites cold corrosion, too high leaves deposits
ANTI-POLISHING RINGS at the top of the liner, to scrape the deposit collar off the piston crown and control bore polishing
REVISED SCAVENGE SPACE INSPECTION AND DRAIN MONITORING, with drain oil analysis to see wear and residual base number before they become damage
this is a PMS CHANGE and belongs in the maintenance system, not in somebody's notebook

steps.title: Propulsion-train and heat-balance retrofits
points: the engine is not the only thing matched to the old speed

PROPELLER RE-PITCHING OR REPLACEMENT - a new propeller optimised for the speed and power now used, often larger in diameter and lower in revolutions; the largest single efficiency gain on a genuinely re-purposed ship
ENERGY-SAVING DEVICES - pre-swirl ducts and stators, boss cap fins, rudder bulbs and twisted rudders, recovering swirl energy and mattering more at the lower wake speeds of slow steaming
HULL COATING AND CLEANING REGIME - a slower ship gives a foul release coating less shear to work with, so the coating and cleaning policy must be revisited with the speed
TORSIONAL VIBRATION RE-ASSESSMENT - changing propeller, pitch or engine rating MOVES THE BARRED SPEED RANGE, and the new range must be established and observed; a safety item, not an optimisation
EXHAUST GAS ECONOMISER - lower exhaust mass flow and temperature mean less steam and more soot
retrofits are soot blowers, water-washing arrangements, dry-running protection and revised circulation control, and the economiser fire risk rises sharply
AUXILIARY BOILER - it now fires much more often, so burner control, maintenance and fuel consumption all move, and PART OF THE MAIN ENGINE SAVING IS QUIETLY GIVEN BACK
WASTE HEAT RECOVERY - systems sized for full load produce much less at low load; bypass and control changes may be needed and a power turbine may cease to be usable below a certain output

steps.title: The regulatory retrofit unique to this period
points: ENGINE POWER LIMITATION AND SHAFT POWER LIMITATION - for much of the existing fleet the practical EEXI compliance route was not to change the ship but to LIMIT THE POWER THAT MAY BE DELIVERED
engine power limitation is applied to the engine's own control or fuel index; shaft power limitation through shaft power measurement and a limiting control
the limitation must be VERIFIABLE and sealed or otherwise secured, with its arrangement and setting recorded in the ship's technical file and onboard management manual
it must be capable of being OVERRIDDEN TO RELEASE A POWER RESERVE where the safety of the ship or the saving of life at sea requires, with the override recorded and reported
a limitation that could not be overridden would itself be a hazard
the arrangements follow the Organization's guidelines on power limitation systems and the use of a power reserve

THE ENGINEERING CONSEQUENCE IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THIS QUESTION - a power-limited ship will spend her remaining life at a load her engine was not designed for, so POWER LIMITATION MAKES THE LOW-LOAD RETROFITS NECESSARY RATHER THAN OPTIONAL

steps.title: Operational measures, and the judgement
points: PERIODIC LOAD-UP RUNS to burn off deposits and dry out gas ways
INCREASED TURBOCHARGER, GAS-WAY AND ECONOMISER CLEANING, with soot blowing and water washing on a revised schedule
RAISED JACKET COOLING WATER TEMPERATURE where the maker permits, to keep liner metal temperatures up and cold corrosion down
MORE FREQUENT SCAVENGE SPACE INSPECTION, and drain oil analysis trended rather than filed
PERFORMANCE MONITORING AGAINST A RE-ESTABLISHED BASELINE after every change, because a retrofit whose effect is not measured cannot be defended
REVISED PMS INTERVALS recorded in the maintenance system, and the whole envelope recorded in the SEEMP
THE JUDGEMENT - an electronically controlled engine with more than one turbocharger is the easy case: low-load tuning plus turbocharger cut-out, both reversible, cheap and quick
a mechanically controlled engine needs hardware, and the case must be made on the remaining life of the ship
a ship whose speed reduction is permanent, or which is power-limited for EEXI, should be DE-RATED PROPERLY AND THE PROPELLER RE-MATCHED, because half-measures leave it running badly for years
EVERY CASE NEEDS THE LUBRICATION AND INSPECTION REGIME CHANGED, whatever else is done - the cheapest measure and the one that decides whether the liners survive

quick_revision.recall_15s: Why: power varies roughly as the cube of shaft speed, so slowing saves heavily — and by this sitting it is regulatory as well as commercial: revised Annex VI in force 1 November 2022, EEXI and CII from 1 January 2023, 2023 GHG Strategy adopted 7 July 2023. Developments: long-stroke geometry; electronically controlled camshaft-less engines (timing becomes software — the key one); high-efficiency and two-stage turbocharging with variable turbine area; primary and secondary emission control; electronically controlled timed cylinder lubrication; dual-fuel gas and methanol in service, ammonia and hydrogen under development only — and ammonia is not a zero-emission fuel at the funnel: unburnt ammonia slip and N2O, a very potent greenhouse gas, both have to be controlled; digital performance monitoring. What goes wrong at low load: air (turbocharger off its match) → compression → deposits (scavenge and economiser fires) → cold corrosion → lost waste heat → propeller mismatch → rising SFOC. Retrofits by family. AIR: turbocharger cut-out, variable turbine area, nozzle ring exchange or re-match, bypass re-setting, blower control. COMBUSTION: low-load tuning (software, reversible), VIT adjustment and cam re-timing, compression ratio increase, slide fuel valves, full de-rating. WEAR: timed electronic cylinder lubrication, base number matching, anti-polishing rings, revised inspection and drain analysis. PROPELLER: re-pitch or replace, energy-saving devices, re-check the barred speed range. HEAT: economiser soot blowing, water washing and dry-running protection; auxiliary boiler fires more; waste heat recovery bypass. LAW: engine or shaft power limitation for EEXI — verifiable, secured, and overridable to release a power reserve with the override recorded. Judgement: electronic engine with multiple turbochargers → tuning plus cut-out; mechanical engine → hardware; permanent or power-limited → de-rate and re-match the propeller; every case needs the lubrication regime changed.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 is what makes this a 2023 question rather than a general one. The EEXI requirement and the CII rating regime apply from 1 January 2023, EEXI being verified at the first annual, intermediate or renewal survey of the air pollution prevention certificate on or after that date; the SEEMP with Part III mandatory from the same date is where the operating envelope and its improvement measures are recorded. Annex VI at this sitting is the MEPC.328(76) revision, in force 1 November 2022, and the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy was adopted 7 July 2023 and is therefore operative. Engine or shaft power limitation is the EEXI compliance route that made these retrofits necessary, and it must be capable of override to release a power reserve where safety or the saving of life at sea requires.
quick_revision.major_trap: Presenting the retrofits as a catalogue of products instead of as answers to named failures. The examiner is testing whether the candidate knows what actually goes wrong at prolonged low load — and the root failure is insufficient scavenge air, because the turbocharger is off its matched point, with lost compression, deposits, cold corrosion and lost waste heat following from it. The three most commonly omitted items are cylinder lubrication (which decides whether the liners survive), the heat balance (less waste steam means the auxiliary boiler fires more and quietly gives back part of the saving), and the propeller, which was matched to a speed the ship no longer runs at — and re-pitching it moves the barred speed range.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the ROOT failure when an engine is held at low load for years?
retrieval_cards.answer: Insufficient scavenge air. The turbocharger is driven by exhaust energy the engine is no longer producing, so it falls off its matched point, scavenge pressure and air-fuel ratio drop and the auxiliary blowers run continuously. Lost compression, poor atomisation, deposits, scavenge and economiser fires and cold corrosion all follow from it - which is why most retrofits attack the air side first.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming the root failure is what turns a catalogue of retrofits into an argument.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is turbocharger cut-out, and when can it be used?
retrieval_cards.answer: Blanking off one turbocharger on an engine fitted with two or more, so that the remaining units operate near their design point and scavenge pressure is restored at low load. It requires a cut-out kit with blanking and isolating arrangements, is reversible for high-load running, and is the cheapest effective measure available on a multi-turbocharger engine. It is not available on a single-turbocharger engine.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the most commonly fitted low-load retrofit and its one precondition is easy to forget.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does electronic control change what a retrofit can be?
retrieval_cards.answer: On a mechanically controlled engine, injection and exhaust valve timing live in a camshaft, so changing them means cams, links and hardware. On an electronically controlled engine they live in the control system, so a low-load or part-load tuning package re-optimises timing, injection rate and profile in software - no hardware change, and normally reversible.
retrieval_cards.why: It splits the whole retrofit menu in two and is the basis of the judgement that closes the answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish de-rating from power limitation.
retrieval_cards.answer: De-rating permanently re-tunes the engine to a lower rated output - new injection timing, a compression ratio change, a new turbocharger nozzle ring and sometimes new fuel valve nozzles - so the engine is genuinely designed for the duty it now performs. Power limitation does not change the engine: it restricts the power that may be delivered, as an EEXI compliance route, is verifiable and secured, and must be capable of being overridden to release a power reserve where safety or the saving of life at sea requires.
retrieval_cards.why: They are routinely confused, and the override requirement is a standard oral question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is slow steaming a regulatory question by November 2023?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the revised Annex VI has been in force since 1 November 2022, and EEXI and the CII rating regime have applied since 1 January 2023. EEXI is verified at the first annual, intermediate or renewal survey of the air pollution prevention certificate on or after that date, and for much of the existing fleet the compliance route was power limitation. The 2023 GHG Strategy, adopted 7 July 2023, sets the direction beyond it.
retrieval_cards.why: It is what makes this a 2023 answer rather than a 2015 one, and the dates are exactly what a later editor would drift.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is cold corrosion, and what retrofit answers it?
retrieval_cards.answer: Sulphuric acid condensing on the cylinder liner where metal temperatures are low, attacking the liner surface. The answer is electronically controlled timed cylinder lubrication, which makes feed rate proportional to load and fuel sulphur so it can be reduced with load without losing the neutralising duty; with cylinder oil base number matched to the fuel and load, anti-polishing rings to control bore polishing, raised jacket water temperature where permitted, and drain oil analysis trended rather than filed.
retrieval_cards.why: It is distinct from vanadium and sodium high-temperature corrosion, and it is what decides whether liners survive years of low load.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What happens to the ship's heat balance when she slows down?
retrieval_cards.answer: Exhaust temperature and mass flow fall, so the exhaust gas economiser makes less steam and collects more soot, raising the economiser fire risk. The auxiliary boiler therefore fires much more often, burning fuel to replace the heat the main engine is no longer wasting - so part of the saving is quietly given back. Waste heat recovery sized for full load produces much less, and a power turbine may cease to be usable below a certain output.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the most commonly omitted consequence of slow steaming and it has a real safety component.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why fit slide-type fuel valves and raise the compression ratio?
retrieval_cards.answer: Slide valves eliminate the sac volume of a conventional valve, removing the after-dripping that causes smoke and deposits at low load. Raising the compression ratio - by shims or a modified piston crown - restores compression pressure and temperature at low load, shortening ignition delay and improving combustion; it is real hardware and must be checked against the engine's maximum pressure limit.
retrieval_cards.why: They are the two combustion-side hardware measures available on a mechanically controlled engine.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You re-pitch the propeller for the new service speed. What else must be done?
retrieval_cards.answer: Re-assess the torsional vibration characteristics, because changing propeller, pitch or engine rating MOVES the barred speed range, and the new range must be established and observed. It is a safety item and not an optimisation. The hull coating and cleaning policy should also be revisited, since a slower ship gives a foul release coating less shear to work with.
retrieval_cards.why: The barred speed range is the safety consequence of a propulsion retrofit and is almost always forgotten.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which retrofit for which ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: An electronically controlled engine with more than one turbocharger: low-load tuning plus turbocharger cut-out - both reversible, cheap and quick. A mechanically controlled engine: hardware - timing changes, compression ratio, slide fuel valves, nozzle ring - and the case must be made on the ship's remaining life. A ship whose speed reduction is permanent or which is power-limited for EEXI: de-rate properly and re-match the propeller. And every case needs the cylinder lubrication and inspection regime changed, whatever else is done.
retrieval_cards.why: The question says 'discuss', and a judgement about which ship needs what is what discussion means.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which alternative-fuel engines are in service at this sitting, and which are not?
retrieval_cards.answer: Dual-fuel operation on gas and on methanol is in service. Ammonia and hydrogen are under development and NOT in commercial service at this time. And ammonia is not a zero-emission fuel at the funnel: unburnt ammonia slip and nitrous oxide, a far more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide, both have to be controlled by after-treatment.
retrieval_cards.why: Technology maturity is a date, and it is exactly what a later reader would silently update.
