questions.verification_status: AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY THROUGHOUT, DECLARED, AND STRUCTURALLY SO. P&I clubs are private mutual associations governed by their own Rules, which are contractual documents between a club and its members. They are not corpus candidates and the True Source corpus holds none of them - its reference resolver contains 320 entries, every one MARPOL Annex VI, and it holds no marine insurance instrument of any kind. The nature of a P&I club, the call system, the division of risks into protection and indemnity heads, and the conditions of entry and continuation of cover are uncontroversial and consistently recorded across the industry, and are carried at authoritative-secondary level. NO CLUB IS NAMED, NO CLUB RULE IS CITED OR NUMBERED, AND NO CLUB RULE IS QUOTED. NO MONETARY FIGURE IS ASSERTED - no individual club retention, no pool layer, no reinsurance limit, no call rate and no deductible - and no number of clubs in the group is stated, because all of those change and none is held. The statutory instruments that make certain P&I certification compulsory - the civil liability, bunkers, wreck removal and maritime labour regimes - are named at IDENTITY level with their in-force status taken from the corpus central amendment register, and NO ARTICLE OR REGULATION OF ANY OF THEM IS QUOTED. The Indian statutes are likewise named at identity level for this sitting.
sources: AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: a protection and indemnity club is a MUTUAL, non-profit association of shipowners, operators, managers and demise charterers which provides its members with cover against third-party liabilities arising out of the operation of their ships. Its members are simultaneously the insured and the insurers, it is governed by its own Rules, and its board is drawn from the membership.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: the principal clubs act together through a group arrangement under which claims above each club's own retention are POOLED between them, and above the pool the group buys a common excess-loss reinsurance programme in the commercial market, with a further layer of member liability above that.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: funds are raised by CALLS rather than by a fixed premium - an advance call paid at the beginning of the policy year, often in instalments and sometimes with a deferred portion; a supplementary or additional call where the year's claims exceed the estimate; a release call payable by a member leaving the club to buy out his exposure to future calls on open years; and an overspill call where a claim exceeds the top of the reinsurance programme.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: a member's contribution is assessed on entered tonnage, ship type and trade, the member's claims record, the deductibles chosen, and any general increase applied by the club across its membership; laid-up returns may be allowed for extended lay-up.
AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: the policy year for protection and indemnity cover conventionally runs from noon on 20 February to noon on 20 February.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: the PROTECTION side of the cover derives from the mutual hull clubs and covers the owner's liabilities as operator of the ship - crew and other personal injury, illness, death and repatriation, passenger and third-party injury, the proportion of collision liability not recoverable under the hull policy and excess collision liability, damage to fixed and floating objects, wreck removal, pollution liability and clean-up, life salvage, stowaways and persons rescued at sea, quarantine and diversion expenses, certain fines, and the legal costs of all of these.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: the INDEMNITY side arose to cover liabilities the hull clubs would not, and covers cargo and contractual liabilities - loss, shortage, damage, delay, contamination and mis-delivery of cargo carried, liability arising under the contract of carriage, cargo's proportion of general average not recoverable because of a breach of the contract of carriage, damage to property on board other than cargo, and liabilities under towage and other contracts approved by the club.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: modern club rules do not divide their cover into two formally separate classes labelled protection and indemnity; the terms are historical and describe the origin of the two groups of risk rather than a present-day boundary in the rules.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: principal exclusions - damage to the entered ship herself and her machinery, which is the hull and machinery underwriter's subject; war risks, for which separate cover is arranged; freight, demurrage and defence, which is a separate class of cover; liabilities arising from unapproved contracts or from carriage on terms less favourable than the applicable carriage regime; and wilful misconduct.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: the conditions on which cover is granted and continued - application with full disclosure, issue of a certificate of entry recording the terms, maintenance of class with an approved classification society and prompt reporting of conditions or withdrawal of class, maintenance of statutory certification, submission to condition survey where required, payment of calls, compliance with the club's rules and any trading or other warranties, notification of material changes, and prompt notice and co-operation after a casualty.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: the 'pay to be paid' principle, under which a member must first discharge the liability before recovering from the club, subject to the statutory rights of direct action that certain compulsory-insurance regimes confer on claimants.

PRIMARY (identity and status, from the corpus central amendment register): the civil liability and fund regimes and the bunkers convention are in force; the wreck removal convention has been in force since 14 April 2015; and the maritime labour convention financial security provisions introduced by the 2014 amendments are in force, the 2022 amendments entering into force on 23 December 2024 and therefore being FUTURE at this sitting.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (identity only): the Indian statutory frame at this sitting - the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958; the Marine Insurance Act, 1963; and the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993, giving effect to the Hague-Visby Rules.

blocks.h: (a) What P&I clubs are, and how they raise their funds

blocks.p: A protection and indemnity club is a mutual, non-profit association of shipowners, operators, managers and demise charterers, formed to provide its members with cover against the third-party liabilities that arise out of operating their ships.
Two features distinguish it from a commercial insurer, and both are worth stating explicitly:

ol: Mutuality. The members are simultaneously the insured and the insurers. There is no external shareholder and no profit motive; the members share each other's losses, and a member's contribution is therefore not capped at what he paid in advance. The club is governed by its own Rules, and its board is drawn from the membership rather than from an insurance market.

It insures liabilities, not the ship. The hull and machinery underwriter covers damage to the ship herself. The club covers what the owner owes to other people — the crew, the passengers, the cargo, the harbour authority, the coastal State. The two are complementary, and the classic illustration is a collision: the hull policy pays for the owner's own ship, and the club picks up the part of the collision liability the hull policy does not.

blocks.p: Above the individual club there is a structure that matters. The principal clubs act together: claims above each club's own retention are pooled between them; above the pool the group buys a common excess-loss reinsurance programme in the commercial market; and above that sits a residual layer of member liability. The effect is that a single club of modest size can carry a catastrophic pollution or passenger claim — which is precisely why compulsory-insurance regimes are content to accept a club certificate.

blocks.h: 2. How the money is collected - the call system

blocks.p: A club does not charge a fixed premium. It levies calls, and the difference is the whole of mutuality:

rows: Advance call
Levied at the start of the policy year on an estimated total call, normally payable in instalments. It is the working capital for the year, sometimes with a deferred portion payable later
Supplementary (additional) call
Levied where the year's claims and reinsurance costs exceed the estimate. This is the defining feature of a mutual - the member's liability is not limited to what he has already paid
Release call
Payable by a member leaving the club, to buy out his continuing exposure to future supplementary calls on the policy years still open
Overspill call
Levied across the membership where a single claim exceeds the top of the reinsurance programme - the ultimate expression of mutuality and, in practice, extremely rare
Laid-up returns
A credit rather than a call - an allowance where a ship is laid up for an extended period and the exposure falls

blocks.p: Calls are supported by the club's free reserves and its investment income, which is why a well-reserved club can hold its calls steady through a poor claims year.
The basis of assessment — what decides how much a particular owner pays:

ul: Entered tonnage, which is the primary measure;
ship type and trade — a passenger ship, a chemical tanker and a bulk carrier carry very different liability exposures;
the member's own claims record, which is what makes the system reward good operators;
the deductibles the member accepts; and
any general increase the club applies across its whole membership for the coming year.

blocks.p: The policy year conventionally runs from noon on 20 February to noon on 20 February, which is why renewal negotiations and general increases are an annual February event across the industry.

blocks.h: (b) The risks covered under "protection" and under "indemnity"
3. Where the two words came from

blocks.p: The split is historical, not contractual, and saying so earns the mark that a list alone does not. The clubs grew out of the nineteenth-century mutual hull clubs. When the hull policy left owners exposed to a proportion of collision liability and to a growing body of personal injury liability, owners formed protecting associations to carry it. When they later needed cover for cargo claims, which the protecting associations would not take, indemnity associations were formed, and the two merged.

Modern club rules do not divide their cover into two formally separate classes. The words describe the origin of two groups of risk, not a present-day boundary — and a candidate who says that has understood the question rather than memorised a table.

blocks.h: 4. Protection risks - the owner's liabilities as operator of the ship

ul: Crew — personal injury, illness and death; medical, hospital and funeral expenses; repatriation and substitute crew; loss of personal effects; unrecoverable wages; and shipwreck unemployment indemnity.
Other people — injury or death of passengers, stevedores, pilots, visitors and shore personnel.
Collision liability — the proportion not recoverable under the hull policy, and liability in excess of the hull value.
Damage to fixed and floating objects — berths, quays, buoys, cranes, submarine cables and pipelines.
Wreck removal — the cost of raising, removing, destroying, lighting or marking the wreck where that is compulsory, which is very often the largest single claim a club will see.
Pollution — liability for escape or discharge of oil and other substances, clean-up costs, the cost of preventive measures, and consequential third-party loss.
Persons — stowaways, refugees and persons saved at sea, with the associated diversion and maintenance costs; and life salvage.

Public health and administration — quarantine and disinfection expenses, and certain fines: customs and immigration penalties, pollution fines, and fines for short or over-delivery of cargo, subject to the club's discretion.
Legal and investigation costs of all of the above, and the expense of attending official inquiries.

blocks.h: 5. Indemnity risks - cargo and contractual liabilities

ul: Cargo claims — loss, shortage, damage, delay, contamination and mis-delivery of the cargo carried.
Liability under the contract of carriage — the bill of lading and the carriage regime it incorporates.
Cargo's proportion of general average where it cannot be recovered from the cargo interests because of a breach of the contract of carriage by the owner.
Property on board other than cargo — containers, equipment and property belonging to others.
Contractual liabilities — under towage, indemnity and similar contracts, but only where the club has approved the terms. This is where owners most often lose cover.
Sue and labour — the costs of measures reasonably taken to avert or minimise a liability that would otherwise fall on the club.

blocks.h: 6. What is NOT covered - and the limb is only half answered without it

ul: Damage to the entered ship herself and her machinery — that is the hull and machinery underwriter's subject.
War risks — separately insured, through a war risks association or the market.
Freight, demurrage and defence — the cost of pursuing and defending commercial disputes is a separate class of cover, not part of ordinary P&I.

Liabilities under unapproved contracts, and liabilities assumed by carrying on terms less favourable than the applicable carriage regime — which is exactly why a bill of lading must not be signed on wider terms than the charter permits.
Wilful misconduct, and the consequences of the member's own default in the conditions of cover.

blocks.h: (c) The minimum an owner must do for the ship to have cover

ol: Be eligible. Cover is for the owner, operator, manager or demise charterer — a person with a real interest in operating the ship.

Apply, and disclose fully. Marine insurance is a contract of utmost good faith. Every material fact — age, type, trade, class, management, claims record, ownership structure — must be disclosed. Non-disclosure is the cheapest way to lose a claim years later.

Obtain the Certificate of Entry. It records the ship, the member, the terms and limits, the deductibles and any special terms or warranties. It is the contract document and its terms must actually be read.

Submit to a condition survey where the club requires one — commonly for older ships, on entry, or on a change of class or management — and rectify the surveyor's recommendations within the time allowed.

blocks.h: 8. Keeping the cover - the continuing conditions

ol: Maintain class. The ship must be, and remain, classed with a classification society approved by the club. Any condition of class or recommendation must be reported to the club and complied with by its date, and any change or withdrawal of class reported at once. This is the single most commonly breached condition, and it is why the survey regime in Q1 of this paper is an insurance matter as well as a technical one.

Maintain statutory certification and flag State compliance — the full statutory suite, the Document of Compliance and Safety Management Certificate under the ISM Code, the International Ship Security Certificate, and the maritime labour certification.
Keep the ship seaworthy and exercise due diligence. The club does not insure the consequences of an unseaworthy ship knowingly sent to sea; want of due diligence is a defence available to it.
Pay the calls. Advance, deferred and supplementary calls, on their due dates. Non-payment can suspend or terminate cover, and it is the simplest way to be uninsured without noticing.

Comply with the Rules and the warranties — trading limits and trading warranties, crewing warranties, and the requirement not to enter unapproved contracts or to carry on terms less favourable than the applicable carriage regime.
Notify material changes — ownership, management, flag, class, trade or lay-up. Cover is written on a described risk and a changed risk must be re-agreed.
Bear the deductible on each claim.

Maintain the compulsory certificates the club issues on the strength of the entry — the blue cards and certificates required by the civil liability, bunkers, wreck removal and maritime labour financial-security regimes. Without these the ship cannot lawfully trade, and they are the most visible practical product of the entry.

blocks.h: 9. Using the cover - conduct after a casualty

ol: Give prompt notice of any casualty, incident or claim likely to give rise to a liability. Late notice prejudices the club's ability to defend and can prejudice the cover.
Preserve the evidence — logs, records, charts, printouts, photographs, samples and statements — and take them while they exist.
Do not admit liability and do not settle without the club. The club has the conduct of the claim.
Use the club correspondent at the port and follow the club's instructions on surveyors, lawyers and security.
Mitigate — take reasonable steps to minimise the loss, which is itself a recoverable head.
Co-operate fully with the club's investigation, and produce the ship's records — which is where the maintenance and survey records discussed elsewhere on this paper are actually tested.

Be aware of “pay to be paid”: the general rule is that the member must first discharge the liability before recovering from the club. Certain compulsory-insurance regimes give the claimant a direct right of action against the insurer and displace that rule; ordinary cargo and crew claims do not.

blocks.p: The minimum, reduced to one sentence: enter the ship with full disclosure; keep her in class and in statutory certification; keep her seaworthy; pay the calls; obey the Rules and the warranties; notify changes and casualties promptly; and let the club run the claim. Every one of those is a condition, and each of them has been the reason a claim failed.

The marks are printed 5 + 5 + 6. Limb (a) contains two questions and both must be answered — what a club is, and how it collects funds — and the second is the one that gets dropped. The calls therefore go in a table, because five named calls are a countable, scannable deliverable.

Limb (b) names two words and gets two lists, prefaced by one short paragraph explaining where the words came from. That paragraph earns more than another six bullet points would, because it shows the split is understood rather than memorised. A third short list of exclusions closes it: a limb about what is covered is only half answered without what is not.

Limb (c) carries the most marks and is the one that differs from every other version of this question in circulation. It is written in three stages — getting the cover, keeping it, and using it — because that ordering is what makes a list of conditions into a chronology a candidate can reconstruct under pressure.

“Average” is a hull and machinery word, not a P&I one. In marine insurance it means loss or damage, and its two familiar compounds — general average and particular average — belong to the world of the hull policy, the ship, the cargo and the adjuster. A P&I club does not pay “averages”; it indemnifies third-party liabilities.

The stem is preserved as printed and not corrected. The examiner's meaning is nonetheless plain: what must the owner minimally do for his ship to have effective P&I cover and to be able to recover on it? Say the terminological point once, in a single sentence, and then answer the question that was asked. A candidate who spends a paragraph correcting the examiner has spent six marks' worth of time on grammar.

One genuine connection is worth making, because it shows the point was understood rather than merely spotted: a club does meet cargo's proportion of general average where that proportion cannot be recovered from the cargo interests because of a breach of the contract of carriage. That is the one place where average and P&I really do meet.
The members are both the insured and the insurers. Everything else about a club follows from that:

ul: there is no fixed premium, because there is no underwriter taking a risk for profit — there are calls;
a member's liability is not capped at what he has paid, which is why supplementary calls exist and why a departing member owes a release call;
the club is governed by Rules the members themselves set, and by a board drawn from the membership; and
a bad claims record raises his call, because he is spending his fellow members' money.

blocks.h: Hull and machinery against P&I - the collision illustration

rows: Insures
The ship herself
What the owner owes to others
Basis
Commercial market, fixed premium
Mutual, calls
In a collision
Damage to the member's own ship, and the greater part of the collision liability to the other ship
The balance of the collision liability not recoverable under the hull policy, and liability in excess of hull value
Also
Crew, passengers, cargo, wreck removal, pollution, fixed and floating objects, fines, legal costs

ul: Describing a club as an insurance company. It is a mutual association owned by its members.
Answering limb (a) on what a club is and never describing how it collects funds. The limb asks both.
Giving only the advance call. Supplementary, release and overspill calls are what distinguish a mutual from a premium insurer.
Presenting protection and indemnity as a formal division in the rules. It is historical, and modern rules do not draw the line.
Putting cargo claims under protection or crew claims under indemnity.
Claiming the club covers damage to the entered ship. It does not — that is hull and machinery.
Forgetting the exclusions, and in particular that war risks and freight, demurrage and defence are separately covered.
In limb (c), listing what the club does rather than what the owner must do. This paper asks the owner's side; the versions in circulation ask the club's.
Omitting maintenance of class, which is the single most commonly breached condition of cover.
Omitting payment of calls, which is the simplest way to become uninsured without noticing.
Omitting the compulsory certificates - the blue cards - which are the most visible practical product of the entry.
Correcting the examiner's use of “averages” at length instead of noting it once and answering.
“Is a P&I club an insurance company?” No — a mutual, non-profit association whose members are both the insured and the insurers.
“What is a supplementary call?” An additional levy where the year's claims exceed the estimate. It is why a member's liability is not capped at the advance call.
“You are leaving your club. What do you owe?” A release call, buying out your exposure to future calls on the open policy years.
“When does the policy year begin?” Conventionally at noon on 20 February.
“What decides how much you pay?” Entered tonnage, ship type and trade, claims record, deductibles chosen, and the club's general increase.
“Who pays for the hole in your own bow after a collision?” The hull and machinery underwriter. The club pays the part of the liability to the other ship that the hull policy does not.

“Name three protection risks and three indemnity risks.” Protection: crew injury, wreck removal, pollution. Indemnity: cargo damage, cargo's proportion of general average unrecoverable through breach of the contract of carriage, approved towage contract liabilities.
“Is FD&D part of P&I?” No — freight, demurrage and defence is a separate class of cover.
“What is a blue card?” The club's evidence of insurance supporting the compulsory certificates required by the civil liability, bunkers, wreck removal and maritime labour financial-security regimes.
“Your ship loses class. What happens to your cover?” Class must be maintained and any change or withdrawal reported at once; cover may cease automatically under the rules.
“What is 'pay to be paid'?” The member must first discharge the liability before recovering from the club — subject to the direct rights of action certain compulsory-insurance regimes give claimants.
“A stevedore is injured and asks you to sign an admission.” Do not admit liability; notify the club at once, preserve the evidence, and let the club and its correspondent handle it.
What does P&I stand for? Protection and indemnity.
Who can enter a ship in a club? The owner, operator, manager or demise charterer.
What document evidences the cover? The certificate of entry.
What is an overspill call? A levy across the membership where a single claim exceeds the top of the group reinsurance programme.
Why do clubs pool claims? So that a club of modest size can carry a catastrophic pollution or passenger claim.
Name two things the club will want after a casualty. Prompt notice, and the preserved evidence - logs, records, photographs and statements.
Who is the club correspondent? The club's local representative at the port, who arranges surveyors, lawyers and security.
What is a condition survey? A survey the club requires - typically for older ships or on entry or change of management - whose recommendations must be rectified within the time allowed.
Name a liability the club will not cover under a towage contract. Any liability under terms the club has not approved.
Which Indian statutes frame this at present? The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, and the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993.

blocks.p: For limb (a), two sentences and five words. MUTUAL, NOT COMMERCIAL. LIABILITIES, NOT THE SHIP. Then the calls: ADVANCE, SUPPLEMENTARY, RELEASE, OVERSPILL — and LAID-UP RETURN as the one that goes the other way.

For limb (b), one question each: PROTECTION is about PEOPLE AND THINGS OUTSIDE THE SHIP — crew, passengers, the other ship, the quay, the wreck, the sea. INDEMNITY is about WHAT SHE WAS CARRYING AND WHAT SHE PROMISED — cargo and contracts. Then three exclusions: HER OWN HULL, WAR, AND DEFENCE COSTS.

For limb (c), three stages: GET IT, KEEP IT, USE IT. Get it — disclose, enter, survey. Keep it — CLASS, CERTIFICATES, SEAWORTHY, CALLS, RULES, CHANGES. Use it — NOTIFY, PRESERVE, ADMIT NOTHING, CO-OPERATE.

ul: The club's own Rules are the governing document of the relationship. They are private contractual documents. No club is named and no rule is cited or quoted in this answer; see the uncertainty section.

The compulsory-insurance regimes behind the certificates a club issues — the civil liability and fund regime for oil pollution from tankers; the bunkers convention for bunker oil pollution; the wreck removal convention, in force since 14 April 2015; and the maritime labour financial-security provisions introduced by the 2014 amendments and in force since 2017. Named at identity level; nothing quoted.
MLC 2006 is at its 2018 amendment state at this sitting. The 2022 amendments enter into force on 23 December 2024 and are future here.
Hague-Visby Rules, through the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993, which is the carriage regime the indemnity side responds to.
Marine Insurance Act, 1963 (India) — the general law of marine insurance, including the duty of utmost good faith.
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 — the governing Indian shipping statute at this sitting. The 2025 Act commenced 15 March 2026 and is prohibited here.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of the evidence

blocks.p: This question is answered out of documents the corpus does not hold and could not hold.

A P&I club is a private mutual association governed by its own Rules, and those Rules are contractual documents between a club and its members. They are not corpus candidates. The True Source corpus holds no marine insurance instrument of any kind — its reference resolver contains 320 entries and every one is MARPOL Annex VI. The nature of a club, the call system, the two groups of risk and the conditions of entry and continuation are uncontroversial and consistently recorded across the industry, and are carried at authoritative-secondary level.

The consequences are deliberate and they are the reason this answer contains almost no numbers. No club is named. No club rule is cited, numbered or quoted. No monetary figure is asserted anywhere — no individual club retention, no pooling layer, no reinsurance limit, no overspill threshold, no call rate, no deductible and no premium — because all of them change annually and none is held. The number of clubs in the group is not stated for the same reason; the structure is described instead. And no time limit is given for notifying a claim, because that is set by the individual club's rules.

One boundary is left deliberately soft. The precise line between the protection heads and the indemnity heads is not asserted as a rule-based division, because modern club rules do not draw one. The answer says so in its own text and treats the terms as historical, which is more honest than presenting a tidy table as though it were the rules.

The compulsory-insurance regimes behind the certificates are named at identity level with their in-force status taken from the corpus amendment register; no article or regulation of any of them is quoted and no limitation or fund limit is given. The “pay to be paid” rule and the statutory direct-action exception are stated in outline with no case, rule or provision cited, because none is held.

Currency. Two dates are pinned to this sitting. MLC 2006 is at its 2018 amendment state here; the 2022 amendments enter into force on 23 December 2024, thirteen months after this examination, and are not cited. And the Indian statutory frame is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 with the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 — the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026, twenty-eight months after this examination, and is the single easiest anachronism to import into a 2023 answer.

notes: NOVEMBER 2023 IS BOUNDARY-FREE AT DAY LEVEL. MEPC 80 is four months past and the 33rd Assembly one month future; neither touches this question.

THE INSTITUTION ITSELF IS NOT DATE-SENSITIVE. The mutual structure, the call system and the two groups of risk have been stable for over a century, and the answer asserts no monetary figure, call rate, retention or reinsurance limit that could go stale.

MLC 2006 IS AT ITS 2018 AMENDMENT STATE AT THIS SITTING. The financial security provisions relied on for abandonment and for crew liability certification are those introduced by the 2014 amendments, in force since 2017. THE 2022 MLC AMENDMENTS ENTER INTO FORCE 23 DECEMBER 2024 - thirteen months FUTURE - and are not cited. This is the live reversal in this question, because every later paper in the corpus may properly rely on them.

THE OTHER COMPULSORY-INSURANCE REGIMES ARE ALL IN FORCE AND STABLE AT THIS SITTING. The civil liability and fund regime and the bunkers convention are long in force, and the wreck removal convention has been in force since 14 April 2015. Their identity and status are taken from the corpus central amendment register.

THE INDIAN STATUTORY FRAME IS THE PRE-RECODIFICATION ONE AND IS STATED AS AT THE SITTING. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 governs - the 2025 Act commenced 15 March 2026, twenty-eight months future. The Marine Insurance Act, 1963 and the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993 are likewise the instruments in force.
NO IMO ASSEMBLY INSTRUMENT IS ENGAGED, so the A.1155(32) and A.1156(32) reversals that govern Q1 and Q6 on this paper do not arise here.

FUTURE CONTAMINATION EXCLUDED: no instrument in force after November 2023 is cited. The MLC 2022 amendments, the Hong Kong Convention of 26 June 2025, the whole A.118x(33) set and the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 are all absent.

Limb c) is the limb that differs from every other version of this question in the corpus: the donors ask how a club HANDLES a claim, and this paper asks what the OWNER must minimally do for the ship to have effective cover. It also prints the word 'averages', which is a hull and machinery term rather than a P&I one, and that has to be adjudicated once rather than either ignored or laboured.

questions.understand_first: Two different kinds of insurance sit behind every ship and it helps to keep them apart from the first line. One covers the ship herself — the hole in her own bow after a collision. The other covers what her owner owes to everybody else: the injured crew member, the passenger, the cargo that arrived wet, the quay she hit, the wreck somebody now has to lift, the oil somebody now has to clean up. The second of those is what these clubs do, and the reason they are called clubs rather than companies is that the shipowners insure each other. There is no outside company taking a risk for profit; the members put money in, the money pays each other's claims, and if the year turns out worse than expected they are asked for more. That single fact explains almost everything about how they work — why the payments are called calls rather than premiums, why a member leaving has to buy his way out of the years still open, and why a bad claims record raises his own contribution: he has been spending his fellow members' money. The two old words in the name are just history. Protection was the part that grew up to cover injury to people and damage to things outside the ship; indemnity was added later to cover claims about the cargo and the promises made in the contract to carry it. Modern rules no longer separate them, and saying so is worth more than reciting a tidy list. The last idea is the practical one: cover is not something an owner simply buys. It is conditional, continuously — the ship must stay in class, keep her certificates, stay seaworthy, and the owner must pay when asked, tell the club when anything material changes, and after an accident say nothing and let the club run it.
questions.memory_cue: Limb (a): MUTUAL, NOT COMMERCIAL; LIABILITIES, NOT THE SHIP (1) - then ADVANCE, SUPPLEMENTARY, RELEASE, OVERSPILL (2). Limb (b): PROTECTION IS PEOPLE AND THINGS; INDEMNITY IS CARGO AND CONTRACTS (4, 5), and three exclusions - OWN HULL, WAR, DEFENCE (6). Limb (c): GET IT, KEEP IT, USE IT (7, 8, 9).

steps.title: What a club is
points: a MUTUAL, non-profit association of shipowners, operators, managers and demise charterers
formed to cover the THIRD-PARTY LIABILITIES arising out of operating their ships
MUTUALITY - the members are simultaneously the insured and the insurers; no external shareholder and no profit motive
a member's contribution is therefore NOT CAPPED at what he paid in advance
governed by its own RULES, with a board drawn from the membership rather than from an insurance market
IT INSURES LIABILITIES, NOT THE SHIP - the hull and machinery underwriter covers damage to the ship herself, the club covers what the owner OWES TO OTHER PEOPLE
the classic illustration is a collision: the hull policy pays for the owner's own ship, the club picks up the part of the collision liability the hull policy does not

ABOVE THE INDIVIDUAL CLUB - claims above each club's retention are POOLED between the principal clubs, above the pool the group buys common EXCESS-LOSS REINSURANCE, and above that sits a residual layer of member liability
the effect is that a club of modest size can carry a catastrophic pollution or passenger claim, which is why compulsory-insurance regimes accept a club certificate

steps.title: How the money is collected - the call system
points: a club does not charge a fixed premium; it levies CALLS, and the difference is the whole of mutuality
ADVANCE CALL - levied at the start of the policy year on an estimated total call, normally in instalments, sometimes with a DEFERRED portion
SUPPLEMENTARY OR ADDITIONAL CALL - where the year's claims and reinsurance costs exceed the estimate; THE DEFINING FEATURE OF A MUTUAL
RELEASE CALL - payable by a member leaving the club, buying out his continuing exposure to future calls on the policy years still open
OVERSPILL CALL - levied across the membership where a single claim exceeds the top of the reinsurance programme; the ultimate expression of mutuality and extremely rare
LAID-UP RETURNS - a credit rather than a call, where a ship is laid up for an extended period
calls are supported by the club's FREE RESERVES and INVESTMENT INCOME, which is why a well-reserved club can hold calls steady through a poor year
BASIS OF ASSESSMENT - entered tonnage as the primary measure; ship type and trade; the member's own claims record; the deductibles accepted; and any general increase applied across the membership
the policy year conventionally runs from noon on 20 February to noon on 20 February

steps.title: Where the two words came from
points: THE SPLIT IS HISTORICAL, NOT CONTRACTUAL, and saying so earns the mark a list alone does not
the clubs grew out of the nineteenth-century mutual HULL clubs
when the hull policy left owners exposed to a proportion of collision liability and to growing personal injury liability, owners formed PROTECTING associations to carry it
when they later needed cover for CARGO claims, which the protecting associations would not take, INDEMNITY associations were formed, and the two merged
MODERN CLUB RULES DO NOT DIVIDE THEIR COVER INTO TWO FORMALLY SEPARATE CLASSES - the words describe the ORIGIN of two groups of risk, not a present-day boundary

steps.title: Protection risks - the owner's liabilities as operator of the ship
points: CREW - personal injury, illness and death; medical, hospital and funeral expenses; repatriation and substitute crew; loss of personal effects; unrecoverable wages; shipwreck unemployment indemnity
OTHER PEOPLE - injury or death of passengers, stevedores, pilots, visitors and shore personnel
COLLISION LIABILITY - the proportion not recoverable under the hull policy, and liability in excess of the hull value
DAMAGE TO FIXED AND FLOATING OBJECTS - berths, quays, buoys, cranes, submarine cables and pipelines
WRECK REMOVAL - raising, removing, destroying, lighting or marking the wreck where compulsory; very often the largest single claim a club will see
POLLUTION - liability for escape or discharge, clean-up costs, preventive measures and consequential third-party loss
PERSONS - stowaways, refugees and persons saved at sea with their diversion and maintenance costs; and life salvage
PUBLIC HEALTH AND ADMINISTRATION - quarantine and disinfection expenses, and certain FINES including customs, immigration, pollution and cargo shortage, subject to the club's discretion
LEGAL AND INVESTIGATION COSTS of all of the above, and the expense of attending official inquiries

steps.title: Indemnity risks - cargo and contractual liabilities
points: CARGO CLAIMS - loss, shortage, damage, delay, contamination and MIS-DELIVERY of the cargo carried
LIABILITY UNDER THE CONTRACT OF CARRIAGE - the bill of lading and the carriage regime it incorporates
CARGO'S PROPORTION OF GENERAL AVERAGE where it cannot be recovered from cargo interests because of a BREACH of the contract of carriage by the owner
PROPERTY ON BOARD OTHER THAN CARGO - containers, equipment and property belonging to others
CONTRACTUAL LIABILITIES under towage, indemnity and similar contracts, BUT ONLY WHERE THE CLUB HAS APPROVED THE TERMS - this is where owners most often lose cover
SUE AND LABOUR - the costs of measures reasonably taken to avert or minimise a liability that would otherwise fall on the club

steps.title: What is NOT covered - and the limb is only half answered without it
points: DAMAGE TO THE ENTERED SHIP HERSELF AND HER MACHINERY - the hull and machinery underwriter's subject
WAR RISKS - separately insured through a war risks association or the market
FREIGHT, DEMURRAGE AND DEFENCE - the cost of pursuing and defending commercial disputes is a SEPARATE CLASS of cover

LIABILITIES UNDER UNAPPROVED CONTRACTS, and liabilities assumed by carrying on terms LESS FAVOURABLE than the applicable carriage regime - which is why a bill of lading must not be signed on wider terms than the charter permits
WILFUL MISCONDUCT, and the consequences of the member's own default in the conditions of cover

steps.title: Getting the cover - entry
points: BE ELIGIBLE - cover is for the owner, operator, manager or demise charterer, a person with a real interest in operating the ship
APPLY AND DISCLOSE FULLY - marine insurance is a contract of UTMOST GOOD FAITH, and every material fact must be disclosed: age, type, trade, class, management, claims record, ownership structure
NON-DISCLOSURE IS THE CHEAPEST WAY TO LOSE A CLAIM YEARS LATER
OBTAIN THE CERTIFICATE OF ENTRY - it records the ship, the member, the terms and limits, the deductibles and any special terms or warranties, and its terms must actually be read
SUBMIT TO A CONDITION SURVEY where the club requires one - commonly for older ships, on entry, or on a change of class or management - and RECTIFY THE RECOMMENDATIONS WITHIN THE TIME ALLOWED

steps.title: Keeping the cover - the continuing conditions
points: MAINTAIN CLASS - the ship must be and remain classed with a society approved by the club; conditions of class and recommendations reported and complied with by their date; any change or withdrawal of class reported at once
this is the single most commonly breached condition of cover, and it is why the survey regime is an insurance matter as well as a technical one

MAINTAIN STATUTORY CERTIFICATION AND FLAG STATE COMPLIANCE - the statutory suite, the Document of Compliance and Safety Management Certificate, the ship security certificate and the maritime labour certification
KEEP THE SHIP SEAWORTHY AND EXERCISE DUE DILIGENCE - want of due diligence is a defence available to the club
PAY THE CALLS - advance, deferred and supplementary, on their due dates; NON-PAYMENT CAN SUSPEND OR TERMINATE COVER
COMPLY WITH THE RULES AND WARRANTIES - trading limits and warranties, crewing warranties, no unapproved contracts, and no carriage on terms less favourable than the applicable regime
NOTIFY MATERIAL CHANGES - ownership, management, flag, class, trade or lay-up; cover is written on a described risk
BEAR THE DEDUCTIBLE on each claim

MAINTAIN THE COMPULSORY CERTIFICATES the club issues on the strength of the entry - the blue cards and certificates required by the civil liability, bunkers, wreck removal and maritime labour financial-security regimes; WITHOUT THESE THE SHIP CANNOT LAWFULLY TRADE

steps.title: Using the cover - conduct after a casualty
points: GIVE PROMPT NOTICE of any casualty, incident or claim likely to give rise to a liability; late notice prejudices the club's ability to defend and can prejudice the cover
PRESERVE THE EVIDENCE - logs, records, charts, printouts, photographs, samples and statements - and take them while they exist
DO NOT ADMIT LIABILITY and do not settle without the club; the club has the conduct of the claim
USE THE CLUB CORRESPONDENT at the port and follow the club's instructions on surveyors, lawyers and security
MITIGATE - take reasonable steps to minimise the loss, which is itself a recoverable head
CO-OPERATE FULLY with the club's investigation and produce the ship's records, which is where the maintenance and survey records are actually tested

PAY TO BE PAID - the general rule is that the member must first DISCHARGE the liability before recovering from the club, subject to the direct rights of action certain compulsory-insurance regimes confer on claimants

THE MINIMUM IN ONE SENTENCE - enter with full disclosure, keep her in class and in certification, keep her seaworthy, pay the calls, obey the rules and warranties, notify changes and casualties promptly, and let the club run the claim

quick_revision.recall_15s: A P&I club is a MUTUAL, non-profit association of owners, operators, managers and demise charterers, covering third-party liabilities — not the ship herself, which is hull and machinery. The members are both the insured and the insurers, so there is no premium: there are calls. Advance call at the start of the year; supplementary call if claims exceed the estimate (the defining mutual feature); release call on leaving, to buy out the open years; overspill call above the reinsurance programme; laid-up returns the other way. Assessed on entered tonnage, ship type and trade, claims record, deductibles and the general increase; policy year from noon on 20 February. Above the club, claims are pooled between the principal clubs with common excess-loss reinsurance above the pool. Protection (from the old hull clubs) — crew injury, illness, death and repatriation; passengers and third parties; the collision liability the hull policy does not cover; fixed and floating objects; wreck removal; pollution; stowaways and life salvage; quarantine and certain fines; legal costs. Indemnity — cargo loss, shortage, damage, delay and mis-delivery; liability under the contract of carriage; cargo's proportion of general average unrecoverable through breach; property on board; approved towage and contractual liabilities; sue and labour. The split is historical, not a division in modern rules. Not covered: the entered ship, war risks, freight demurrage and defence, unapproved contracts, wilful misconduct. The owner's minimum: GET IT — disclose fully, enter, take the certificate of entry, pass the condition survey; KEEP IT — maintain class and statutory certification, stay seaworthy, pay the calls, obey the rules and warranties, notify changes, hold the blue cards; USE IT — prompt notice, preserve evidence, admit nothing, co-operate, mitigate, and remember pay to be paid.
critical_numbers: The policy year conventionally runs from noon on 20 FEBRUARY to noon on 20 February
Four kinds of call: advance, supplementary (additional), release, overspill - plus laid-up returns as a credit
The wreck removal convention has been in force since 14 April 2015
MLC 2006 financial security provisions in force from the 2014 amendments; the 2022 amendments enter into force 23 December 2024 and are FUTURE at this sitting
No monetary figure is stated anywhere in this answer - no retention, pool layer, reinsurance limit, call rate or deductible
quick_revision.critical_regulation: There is no single instrument here: a club is governed by its own Rules, which are private contractual documents between the association and its members and are neither cited nor quoted in this answer. What the law supplies is the framework around the cover — the compulsory-insurance regimes for oil pollution from tankers, for bunker oil pollution, for wreck removal (in force since 14 April 2015) and for maritime labour financial security, all of which require certificates the club issues on the strength of the entry; the Hague-Visby Rules through the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993, which is the carriage regime the indemnity side responds to; and the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, which supplies the duty of utmost good faith relied on at entry. The governing Indian shipping statute at this sitting is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering limb (c) as though it asked what the club does. Every other version of this question in circulation asks how a club handles a claim; this paper asks what the OWNER must minimally do for his ship to have effective cover — disclose fully and enter, maintain class and statutory certification, keep the ship seaworthy, pay the calls, comply with the rules and warranties, notify material changes, and give prompt notice and preserve evidence after a casualty. The paired traps are describing a club as an insurance company when it is a mutual association whose members are both insured and insurers; giving only the advance call and omitting the supplementary, release and overspill calls that make mutuality real; and presenting protection and indemnity as a formal division in the rules when the split is historical and modern rules do not draw it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a P&I club, and how does it differ from a commercial insurer?
retrieval_cards.answer: A mutual, non-profit association of shipowners, operators, managers and demise charterers, providing cover against third-party liabilities arising out of operating their ships. Two differences: mutuality - the members are simultaneously the insured and the insurers, so there is no premium and no profit motive and a member's liability is not capped at what he has paid; and subject matter - the club insures what the owner OWES TO OTHERS, while the hull and machinery underwriter insures the ship herself.
retrieval_cards.why: Mutual, not commercial; liabilities, not the ship - the two lines that carry the whole of limb (a).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the calls a club levies and say when each arises.
retrieval_cards.answer: Advance call at the start of the policy year on an estimated total call, often in instalments and sometimes with a deferred portion. Supplementary or additional call where the year's claims and reinsurance costs exceed the estimate - the defining feature of a mutual. Release call payable by a member leaving, buying out his exposure to future calls on the open policy years. Overspill call across the membership where a single claim exceeds the top of the reinsurance programme. And laid-up returns, which are a credit rather than a call.
retrieval_cards.why: 'Describe how they collect fund' is the half of limb (a) that gets dropped, and four named calls make it undroppable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: On what basis is a member's contribution assessed, and when does the policy year run?
retrieval_cards.answer: On entered tonnage as the primary measure, the ship's type and trade, the member's own claims record, the deductibles he accepts, and any general increase the club applies across its membership. The policy year conventionally runs from noon on 20 February to noon on 20 February, which is why renewals and general increases are an annual February event.
retrieval_cards.why: The 20 February policy year is the one date in this question, and the claims-record element is what makes mutuality reward good operators.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where do the words 'protection' and 'indemnity' come from, and do modern rules still divide them?
retrieval_cards.answer: The clubs grew out of the nineteenth-century mutual hull clubs. Protecting associations were formed to carry the collision liability the hull policy left uncovered and the growing body of personal injury liability; indemnity associations were formed later for cargo claims, which the protecting associations would not take, and the two merged. Modern club rules do NOT divide their cover into two formally separate classes - the words describe the origin of two groups of risk, not a present-day boundary.
retrieval_cards.why: Explaining the split is worth more than another six bullet points of it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name six protection risks.
retrieval_cards.answer: Crew injury, illness, death and repatriation with medical and substitute-crew costs; injury or death of passengers, stevedores, pilots and visitors; the proportion of collision liability not recoverable under the hull policy and liability in excess of hull value; damage to fixed and floating objects such as quays, buoys and submarine cables; wreck removal where compulsory; and pollution liability, clean-up and preventive measures - together with stowaways, life salvage, quarantine, certain fines and the legal costs of all of it.
retrieval_cards.why: Protection is about people and things outside the ship - that phrase recovers the whole list.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the indemnity risks.
retrieval_cards.answer: Cargo loss, shortage, damage, delay, contamination and mis-delivery; liability arising under the contract of carriage; cargo's proportion of general average where it cannot be recovered from the cargo interests because of a breach of the contract of carriage; damage to property on board other than cargo; liabilities under towage and other contracts WHERE THE CLUB HAS APPROVED THE TERMS; and sue and labour costs.
retrieval_cards.why: Indemnity is about what she was carrying and what she promised - cargo and contracts.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name four things a P&I club does NOT cover.
retrieval_cards.answer: Damage to the entered ship herself and her machinery - that is hull and machinery. War risks, which are separately insured. Freight, demurrage and defence, which is a separate class of cover for pursuing and defending commercial disputes. And liabilities under unapproved contracts or assumed by carrying on terms less favourable than the applicable carriage regime - together with wilful misconduct.
retrieval_cards.why: A limb about what is covered is only half answered without what is not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the single most commonly breached condition of P&I cover?
retrieval_cards.answer: Maintenance of class. The ship must be and remain classed with a society approved by the club; any condition of class or recommendation must be reported and complied with by its date; and any change or withdrawal of class must be reported at once, cover being liable to cease under the rules. It is why the classification survey regime is an insurance matter as well as a technical one.
retrieval_cards.why: It links the commercial question directly to the engineer's own responsibilities.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the minimum an owner must do for his ship to have effective P&I cover.
retrieval_cards.answer: GET IT - apply with full disclosure in utmost good faith, obtain and read the certificate of entry, and pass any condition survey. KEEP IT - maintain class and statutory certification, keep the ship seaworthy, pay the calls when due, obey the rules and warranties, notify changes of ownership, management, flag, class or trade, and hold the compulsory certificates. USE IT - prompt notice, preserved evidence, no admission of liability, and co-operation with the club.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the limb that differs from every other version of this question, and the three-stage ordering is what makes it reconstructable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a blue card, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: The club's evidence of insurance, issued on the strength of the entry, which supports the compulsory certificates required by the oil pollution civil liability regime, the bunkers convention, the wreck removal convention and the maritime labour financial-security provisions. Without those certificates the ship cannot lawfully trade, which makes them the most visible practical product of a P&I entry.
retrieval_cards.why: It is where the club's cover becomes a trading requirement rather than a commercial choice.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The paper asks what the owner must do to 'get averages' under a club. Is that the right word?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. 'Average' is a hull and machinery term meaning loss or damage, and general and particular average belong to the hull policy and the adjuster; a club indemnifies third-party liabilities and does not pay averages. The stem is preserved as printed and the point is made in one sentence, then the question the examiner plainly asked is answered. The one genuine overlap is that a club does meet cargo's proportion of general average where it cannot be recovered from cargo interests because of a breach of the contract of carriage.
retrieval_cards.why: Noting a printed looseness once and moving on is a skill; correcting the examiner at length costs marks.
